kubectl delete pod "$POD"                     # clean up when done (nothing respawns it)

Check yourself: three deep facts surfaced at once — (1) a ReplicaSet's membership is the label match, nothing more; (2) the Service dropped the pod for the same reason (selectors again); (3) the orphan didn't respawn when deleted, because no controller claimed it anymore. The quarantine move — relabel to detach, debug, delete — is a genuinely useful production technique built entirely on Chapter 4's mental model.

📌 Chapter 4 Visual Summary — the objects, wired together
   🌍 Ingress/Gateway ─routes─▶ 🔌 Service ─selector(app=easypj)─▶ 📦 Pods
                                    ▲                                ▲ owned by
                               🚀 Deployment ─manages─▶ 🎛️ ReplicaSet ┘ creates (self-heal)
                                    │ pod template pulls in:
                                    ├─ ⚙️ ConfigMap / 🔒 Secret (envFrom)
                                    ├─ 💾 PVC ─▶ PV ─▶ 🧱 StorageClass
                                    └─ 🛡️ ServiceAccount ◀─ RBAC governs access
   🗂️ Namespace contains it all   ·   🧯 NetworkPolicy firewalls it   ·   🔖 LABELS are the glue
   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   You create a Deployment → it owns a ReplicaSet → which owns Pods; a Service finds those Pods
   by LABEL and gives them a stable address. That sentence is 80% of every CKA workload task.

In words: The objects nest. You create a Deployment; it manages a ReplicaSet; the ReplicaSet creates and self-heals the Pods. You never make the lower layers by hand — you describe the top one and ownership cascades down.

A pod's template pulls in everything it needs: ConfigMap/Secret for configuration (envFrom), a PVC → PV → StorageClass chain for storage, and a ServiceAccount (governed by RBAC) for API access. Out front, a Service uses a label selector (app=easypj) to find the ever-changing pods and give them one stable address; Ingress/Gateway routes external traffic to that Service. Around it all, a Namespace contains the objects and a NetworkPolicy firewalls them.

The takeaway: labels are the glue — nothing is wired by name, everything is matched by label. "Create a Deployment → it owns a ReplicaSet → which owns Pods → a Service selects them by label" is the single sentence behind roughly 80% of every CKA workload task.

🟢 Template Part 1 · Recap · Complete

Foundations — What You Now Know

You started unable to picture a cluster; now you can name every component, explain what breaks without each, trace a pod from kubectl apply to Running, and read any easypj manifest. That mental model is the platform the rest of the guide builds on.

🔑 Template Part 1 — Key Takeaways

  • Kubernetes automates deploy / scale / heal via desired-state reconciliation — you declare, control loops deliver (Ch 1).
  • Containers share the host kernel (namespaces + cgroups + union FS); K8s runs them via the CRI, not Docker (Ch 2).
  • Control plane = apiserver + etcd + scheduler + controller-manager; nodes = kubelet + kube-proxy + runtime. Only the apiserver talks to etcd (Ch 3).
  • Core objects: Pod < ReplicaSet < Deployment; Service for stable networking; Namespace for isolation; labels wire it all together (Ch 4).
  • 🎯 Exam: "which component?" thinking powers the whole 25% Architecture + 30% Troubleshooting domains.
  • 🔑 cluster-info · get nodes -o wide · api-resources · explain · crictl
📌 Template Part 1 Visual Summary — easypj source → image → desired state → running pods
   🐍 easypj source ─build─▶ 📀 easypj:v1 ─push─▶ 🏪 registry        (Ch 2: the unit)
                                                     │ pull
   📝 deploy.yaml ──kubectl apply──▶ 📡 apiserver ──▶ 🗄️ etcd          (Ch 1: declare desired)
   (replicas: 3)                       │ authN/Z/admit  (desired state)
                                       ├─ 🔄 controllers: Deployment→ReplicaSet→Pods
                                       └─ 📋 scheduler: bind each Pod → a node       (Ch 3: the brain)
                                              ▼
                            🤖 kubelet ─🐋 run─▶ 📦📦📦 easypj pods ─🌐 CNI gives IPs   (Ch 3: the muscle)
                                              ▼
                            🔌 Service (selector app=easypj) ─load-balances─▶ the pods   (Ch 4: stable net)
   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   one app, described as desired state, that the cluster keeps alive — heal, scale, roll out, repeat. ☸️

In words: You build the easypj app into an image (easypj:v1) and push it to a registry — that image is the portable unit of deployment (Ch 2). You then declare what you want in deploy.yaml (e.g. 3 replicas) and run kubectl apply: the apiserver authenticates, authorizes, and admits the request, then writes that desired state into etcd — the single source of truth (Ch 1).

From there the cluster's brain takes over (Ch 3): controllers expand Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods, and the scheduler picks a node for each Pod. On that node the muscle acts — the kubelet tells the container runtime (via the CRI) to start the containers, and the CNI hands every Pod an IP. A Service with selector app=easypj then gives those churning Pods one stable address and load-balances across them (Ch 4).

The one idea to keep: nothing here is a one-off command — it's all desired state the cluster reconciles toward, continuously. That's why it can heal a dead pod, scale on demand, and roll out a new version on its own. Master this loop and the other 13 parts are just variations on it.

🟢 Part 1 · Foundation

Think Like Helm

Chapters 1–2 · Beginner · "What is Helm, and how do I get it running?"

🟢 Beginner 📖 2 Chapters ⏱️ ~3 hours 🎯 Foundational — supports all 6 exam domains

Before a single helm install makes sense, you need the mental model underneath it: why Helm exists, what a Chart/Release/Repository actually are, and a working helm binary talking to a real cluster. Part 1 builds both — the concepts in Chapter 1, the working setup in Chapter 2 — using easypj (a Django job board app) as the running example throughout this guide.

How the chapters fit — Part 1 mental model
   Ch 1 — WHY & WHAT              Ch 2 — GET IT RUNNING
   the problem Helm solves,  ───▶  install, verify, configure,
   the core concepts                add repos, autocomplete
        │                                  │
        └──────────────────┬───────────────┘
                            ▼
              A working helm CLI + the mental model
              to understand every chapter after this one

Chapter 1 · Understanding Helm — The Kubernetes Package Manager

easypj runs fine on your laptop with python manage.py runserver. Deploying it to Kubernetes for real — across dev, staging, and production, with rollbacks and repeatability — means managing 15+ YAML files by hand, or reaching for the tool built exactly for this problem. That tool is Helm, and this chapter installs the mental model the rest of the guide is built on: what Helm is, why it exists, and how it fits into the Kubernetes ecosystem.

1.1 The Problem Before Helm — YAML Copy-Paste Chaos

Imagine you've built easypj — a Django job board application with the jobpost module where employers post jobs filtered by Skills, Location, and Author. It runs beautifully on your laptop. Now you need to deploy it to Kubernetes. Here's what that looks like without Helm:

The Manual Deployment Nightmare

To deploy easypj to Kubernetes, you'd need to manually create and manage these YAML files — every single one, by hand, for every environment:

easypj Deployment — All the YAML Files You'd Need (Without Helm)
  📁 easypj-k8s-manifests/
  ├── deployment.yaml          ← Django app deployment
  ├── service.yaml             ← Expose app internally
  ├── configmap.yaml           ← App settings (DEBUG, DB_HOST, etc.)
  ├── secret.yaml              ← Database passwords, API keys
  ├── ingress.yaml             ← External access routing
  ├── hpa.yaml                 ← Auto-scaling rules
  ├── pvc.yaml                 ← Persistent storage for uploads
  ├── postgres-deployment.yaml ← Database deployment
  ├── postgres-service.yaml    ← Database service
  ├── postgres-pvc.yaml        ← Database storage
  ├── redis-deployment.yaml    ← Cache deployment
  ├── redis-service.yaml       ← Cache service
  ├── network-policy.yaml      ← Security rules
  ├── service-account.yaml     ← RBAC permissions
  └── namespace.yaml           ← Environment isolation

  😱 15+ YAML files — and that's just ONE environment!
  For dev + staging + prod, you're managing 45+ files.
  Every change = edit in 3 places. Every typo = breakage.

The Pain Points (Before Helm)

📋
YAML Duplication

Dev, staging, and prod need almost identical YAML — just different image tags, replica counts, and config values. You end up copy-pasting 15 files per environment. Change a field in one? You have to chase it down in all the others.

🔢
No Versioning

Which version of easypj is running in production right now? Without Helm, you're checking kubectl describe and hoping the image tag tells you. There's no single source of truth for what's deployed.

🔄
No Rollback

Deployed a bad version of easypj? Without Helm, you're manually reapplying old YAML files — if you can find them. There's no built-in way to go back to the previous working state.

🔀
No Templating

Need to change the app name from "easypj" to "easypj-prod"? You're doing a find-and-replace across 15 files. Helm templates let you define it once and use it everywhere via {{ .Release.Name }}.

⚠️ Without Helm, You're the Package Manager

Every Kubernetes admin eventually writes bash scripts to "manage" their YAML files — sed replacements, kubectl apply loops, custom version tracking. You're reinventing Helm, badly. Helm is the result of the community saying: "There must be a better way."

Before vs After Helm — The easypj Deployment Story
  ❌ BEFORE HELM (Manual Chaos)               ✅ WITH HELM (One Command)
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐            ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │  1. Copy 15 YAML files       │            │  helm install easypj \       │
  │  2. Edit image tag manually  │            │    ./easypj-chart \          │
  │  3. Change DB host in 3 files│            │    --set image.tag=v2.1 \    │
  │  4. Update replica count     │            │    -f values-prod.yaml       │
  │  5. kubectl apply -f file1   │            │                              │
  │  6. kubectl apply -f file2   │            │  🎉 ONE COMMAND.             │
  │  7. ...kubectl apply...file15│            │  Versioned. Reusable.        │
  │  8. Hope nothing broke       │            │  Rollback in seconds.        │
  │  9. No way to rollback       │            │                              │
  │  10. Pray 🙏                 │            │  helm rollback easypj 1      │
  └──────────────────────────────┘            └──────────────────────────────┘

1.2 What is Helm? — The Simple Answer

📖 The Official Definition

Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. It packages Kubernetes YAML manifests into reusable, versioned, configurable units called Charts. One helm install command can deploy an entire application stack — Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Ingresses, PVCs — all at once.

The Elevator Pitch

Think of Helm as "apt-get for Kubernetes" or "npm for Kubernetes" or "brew for Kubernetes." Just like you type apt install nginx to get a web server on Linux, you type helm install myapp ./mychart to deploy an entire application to Kubernetes.

Helm in One Picture — The Core Loop
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                        WHAT HELM DOES                                  │
  │   ┌─────────┐      ┌──────────────┐      ┌─────────────────────────┐ │
  │   │  Chart  │      │    Helm      │      │     Kubernetes          │ │
  │   │  (pkg)  │─────▶│    Engine    │─────▶│     Cluster              │ │
  │   │ • values│      │ 1. Read chart│      │  ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐  │ │
  │   │ • tmpls │      │ 2. Merge vals│      │  │Deploy  │ │Service │  │ │
  │   │ • meta  │      │ 3. Render YML│      │  │easypj  │ │easypj  │  │ │
  │   └─────────┘      │ 4. Apply K8s │      │  └────────┘ └────────┘  │ │
  │                    └──────────────┘      │  ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐  │ │
  │  📦 Chart = package                      │  │Config  │ │Secret  │  │ │
  │  🚀 Release = installed chart            │  │Map     │ │        │  │ │
  │  📋 Repository = chart storage           │  └────────┘ └────────┘  │ │
  │                                          └─────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Helm's Three Core Concepts

📦
Chart

A Helm package — a collection of files that describe a related set of Kubernetes resources. Think of it like a .deb or .rpm file, but for Kubernetes. Contains templates, default values, and metadata.

🚀
Release

A running instance of a chart in a Kubernetes cluster. When you install a chart, Helm creates a release. You can have multiple releases of the same chart (e.g., easypj-dev, easypj-staging, easypj-prod).

📋
Repository

A storage location where charts are collected and shared. Like Docker Hub for container images. Public repos include Artifact Hub, Bitnami, and your own private OCI registries.

💡 The Mental Model

Chart = Template + Default Values. A Helm chart is NOT a running application. It's a blueprint. When you helm install that chart, Helm renders the templates with your values and creates a Release — which IS the running application in your cluster.

Helm Architecture — How It Works Under the Hood

Understanding the architecture is critical for the certification. Here's the complete data flow from your terminal to the Kubernetes cluster:

Helm Architecture (v3+) — Complete Data Flow
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     HELM ARCHITECTURE (v3+)                            │
  │   ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────────┐ │
  │   │  Helm    │     │  Chart       │     │   Kubernetes             │ │
  │   │  CLI     │────▶│  Repository  │────▶│   API Server             │ │
  │   │          │     │  (HTTP repo, │     │                          │ │
  │   │ helm     │     │   OCI,       │     │  ┌────────────────────┐  │ │
  │   │ install  │     │   ChartMuseum│     │  │ Secrets            │  │ │
  │   │ upgrade  │     │   Local .tgz)│     │  │ (Release Storage)  │  │ │
  │   │ rollback │     └──────────────┘     │  └────────────────────┘  │ │
  │   │ uninstall│                          │                          │ │
  │   └────┬─────┘                          │  ┌────────────────────┐  │ │
  │        │  YOUR kubeconfig               │  │ Resources          │  │ │
  │        │  YOUR RBAC rules               │  │ (Deploy, Svc,      │  │ │
  │        │  NO Tiller!                    │  │  CM, Secret...)    │  │ │
  │        ▼                                │  └────────────────────┘  │ │
  │   ┌──────────┐                          └──────────────────────────┘ │
  │   │ Chart    │──▶ Template Engine ──────────────▶ Rendered YAML      │
  │   │ values   │   (values + templates              (kubectl apply)    │
  │   │ + tmpl   │    = rendered YAML)                                   │
  │   └──────────┘                                                        │
  │   🔑 KEY POINTS:                                                      │
  │   • Helm CLI talks DIRECTLY to the K8s API — no intermediary         │
  │   • Uses YOUR kubeconfig credentials (same as kubectl)                │
  │   • Release state stored as K8s Secrets in the release namespace      │
  │   • Template Engine: Go templates + Sprig functions → YAML            │
  │   • No Tiller means: simpler, more secure, no cluster-side component  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

How Helm Differs from kubectl — The Essential Distinction

This is one of the most common points of confusion for beginners. Let's clarify it once and for all:

🔧 kubectl — Imperative Toolkit
  • Creates/modifies individual Kubernetes resources
  • You specify what and how
  • No versioning — apply and forget
  • No built-in rollback capability
  • Great for debugging and one-off tasks
  • Example: kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
⛵ Helm — Declarative Package Manager
  • Manages the entire application lifecycle
  • You declare desired state — Helm figures out how
  • Full versioning — every install/upgrade is tracked
  • Built-in rollback: helm rollback
  • Great for application deployment and management
  • Example: helm install easypj ./chart
📖 When to Use Which

Use kubectl for: quick debugging (kubectl get pods), ad-hoc resource creation, cluster administration tasks.
Use Helm for: deploying applications, managing releases across environments, CI/CD pipelines, sharing application packages with teams.

They're not competitors — they're complementary. Helm actually uses kubectl concepts internally (it submits YAML to the same K8s API). Think of Helm as a layer on top of kubectl, providing packaging, versioning, and lifecycle management.

Helm Release Lifecycle — A Quick Preview

Every Helm operation moves a release through a state machine. Here's a simplified view (we'll go deeper in Chapter 5):

Helm Release State Machine (Simplified)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  HELM RELEASE LIFECYCLE                                           │
  │         ┌─────────┐                                              │
  │         │ unknown │  ← Initial state                              │
  │         └────┬────┘                                              │
  │    ┌─────────▼─────────┐                                         │
  │    │ pending-install   │  ← helm install started                  │
  │    └─────────┬─────────┘                                         │
  │         ┌────▼────┐                                              │
  │         │ deployed│◄──── helm install SUCCESS ✅                  │
  │         └────┬────┘                                              │
  │    ┌─────────▼─────────┐                                         │
  │    │ pending-upgrade    │  ← helm upgrade started                 │
  │    └─────────┬─────────┘                                         │
  │         ┌────▼────┐                                              │
  │         │ deployed│◄──── helm upgrade SUCCESS (prev: superseded)  │
  │         └────┬────┘                                              │
  │    ┌─────────▼─────────┐                                         │
  │    │ failed             │  ← install/upgrade FAILED ❌             │
  │    └─────────┬─────────┘                                         │
  │    ┌─────────▼─────────┐                                         │
  │    │ uninstalled        │  ← helm uninstall                        │
  │    └────────────────────┘                                         │
  │  🔑 helm rollback: superseded → deployed (re-activated)           │
  │  📋 Each revision stored as a K8s Secret for history              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

1.3 The Helm Analogy — apt/yum/brew for Kubernetes

If you've ever used a Linux package manager, you already understand Helm at a conceptual level. The mapping is remarkably direct:

ConceptLinux (apt)JavaScript (npm)Helm (K8s)
Package.deb filepackage.json + codeChart (.tgz file)
Installapt install nginxnpm install expresshelm install easypj ./chart
RegistryAPT repos (Ubuntu)npmjs.comArtifact Hub / OCI
Searchapt search nginxnpm search expresshelm search hub nginx
Upgradeapt upgrade nginxnpm update expresshelm upgrade easypj ./chart
Uninstallapt remove nginxnpm uninstall expresshelm uninstall easypj
List installedapt list --installednpm list -ghelm list
📖 Key Difference from Linux Package Managers

Unlike apt/rpm which install binaries to your system, Helm installs Kubernetes resources (YAML manifests) to a cluster. Helm doesn't put files on your laptop — it talks to the Kubernetes API server and creates Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, etc. in your cluster. You're "installing" an application, not a binary.

1.3a The Shipping Port Analogy — Helm as the Shipping Manifest

Kubernetes concepts are abstract. Physical analogies make them intuitive. The shipping port analogy has become one of the most powerful, widely-used metaphors in the container ecosystem — it maps Helm, Kubernetes, and containers onto real-world logistics.

The Complete Shipping Port Analogy
THE SHIPPING PORT — HOW HELM, KUBERNETES & CONTAINERS WORK TOGETHER
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
                        THE HARBOR (KUBERNETES CLUSTER)
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐              │
    │  │ BERTH A     │    │ BERTH B     │    │ BERTH C     │              │
    │  │ (Namespace: │    │ (Namespace: │    │ (Namespace: │              │
    │  │  dev)       │    │  staging)   │    │  production)│              │
    │  │  ┌───────┐  │    │  ┌───────┐  │    │  ┌───────┐  │              │
    │  │  │ SHIP  │  │    │  │ SHIP  │  │    │  │ SHIP  │  │              │
    │  │  │easypj │  │    │  │easypj │  │    │  │easypj │  │              │
    │  │  │ -dev  │  │    │  │ -stg  │  │    │  │ -prod │  │              │
    │  │  └───────┘  │    │  └───────┘  │    │  └───────┘  │              │
    │  └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘              │
    │              ┌──────────────────────────┐                           │
    │              │  PORT AUTHORITY           │                           │
    │              │  (Kubernetes API Server)  │                           │
    │              │  - Validates manifests    │                           │
    │              │  - Enforces RBAC rules    │                           │
    │              │  - Schedules workloads    │                           │
    │              └──────────────────────────┘                           │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

ANALOGY MAPPINGS:
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
CONCEPT              SHIPPING ANALOGY              WHAT IT DOES
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Helm CLI       =     Harbor Master                 Reads the manifest,
                                                    directs ships to berths
Chart          =     Shipping Manifest             Blueprint: what's in each
                 (Bill of Lading)                  container, how many, where
Release        =     Ship at a Berth               A running instance of the
                 (easypj-dev at Berth A)            application
Values         =     Cargo Instructions             What goes IN the containers
                 (replicaCount, image tag)          (how many crates, which version)
Namespace      =     Berth / Dock                  Isolated parking spot for ships
Repository     =     Warehouse / Depot             Where manifests (charts) are
                 (Artifact Hub)                     stored and retrieved from
K8s API Server =     Port Authority                Validates, authorizes, schedules
kubelet        =     Dock Worker                    Loads/unloads containers at berth
Pod            =     Set of Containers on a Pallet  Containers that travel/dock together
Scheduler      =     Berth Assignment Office        Decides which berth (node) a ship goes to
etcd           =     Port Log Book (the ledger)     Records EVERYTHING — immutable records
Service        =     Ship-to-Ship Radio              Enables comms between ships at berths
Ingress        =     Customs Gate                    Entry point for external traffic
ConfigMap      =     Ship Configuration Sheet        Non-sensitive config data
Secret         =     Sealed Envelope                 Sensitive data (for captain's eyes only)
HPA            =     Automatic Crane                 Scales containers based on cargo demand
Rollback       =     Emergency Return to Port        Ship reverts to last good manifest version
📋
The Chart = Shipping Manifest

A shipping manifest lists everything on the ship — containers, quantities, destination. A Helm Chart lists every Kubernetes resource — Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps — and how they should be configured.

⛵
Helm = Harbor Master

The Harbor Master doesn't build ships or own cargo — they orchestrate: reading manifests, assigning berths, tracking arrivals/departures. Helm does exactly this: reads charts, installs to namespaces, tracks releases. If something goes wrong, the harbor master redirects the ship (rollback) to its last safe position.

💡 How to Use This for the Exam

When you encounter abstract Helm concepts, mentally map them to the shipping analogy. "Install chart X with values Y in namespace Z" becomes "direct ship X carrying cargo Y to berth Z." This makes multi-tenancy (different berths, different rules), release management (ship history), and rollbacks (return to last safe position) intuitive.

⚠️ Common Misunderstanding

Helm is NOT a container registry. Helm stores Kubernetes manifests (YAML), not container images. When a Helm chart says image: easypj:v2.1, Helm just passes that string to Kubernetes. The actual container image is pulled from Docker Hub, ACR, ECR, or GCR — not from Helm.

1.4 Helm 2 vs Helm 3 — The Architecture Revolution

Understanding the difference between Helm 2 and Helm 3 is critical — not just historically, but because the removal of Tiller fundamentally changed Helm's security model.

Helm 2 (With Tiller) vs Helm 3 (Client-Only)
  ❌ HELM 2 (Deprecated — DO NOT USE)          ✅ HELM 3 (Current — USE THIS)

  │  ┌────────┐    ┌────────┐  │            │  ┌────────┐                  │
  │  │  Helm  │───▶│ Tiller │  │            │  │  Helm  │                  │
  │  │  CLI   │    │ (in K8s)│  │            │  │  CLI   │──── DIRECT ────▶ │
  │  └────────┘    └───┬────┘  │            │  └────────┘    CONNECTION    │
  │                    ▼       │            │  ┌──────────────────────────┐ │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐  │            │  │   Kubernetes API Server  │ │
  │  │  Kubernetes API     │  │            │  │  🔐 Uses YOUR kubeconfig │ │
  │  │  Server             │  │            │  │  🔐 Uses YOUR RBAC       │ │
  │  └─────────────────────┘  │            │  │  🔐 No cluster component │ │
  │  ⚠️ PROBLEMS:              │            │  └──────────────────────────┘ │
  │  • Tiller = cluster-wide   │            │  ✅ BENEFITS:                 │

  │    cluster admin           │            │  • Release info in Secrets   │
  │  • Extra component to      │            │    (not ConfigMaps)           │

  └─────────────────────────────┘            └──────────────────────────────┘

1.4a Why Tiller Was Removed — Security Deep Dive

Tiller was Helm 2's server-side component that ran inside the Kubernetes cluster. It received commands from the Helm CLI and executed them against the Kubernetes API. This created a massive security problem:

❌ The Tiller Problem
  • Tiller typically ran with cluster-admin privileges
  • Anyone with network access to Tiller (gRPC port 44134) could deploy anything to the cluster
  • No fine-grained RBAC — Tiller had god-mode
  • Multi-tenant clusters? Impossible — one Tiller, one permission level
  • Tiller's TLS configuration was complex and often skipped entirely
✅ The Helm 3 Solution
  • Helm CLI talks directly to the Kubernetes API
  • Uses your kubeconfig — same permissions you have
  • Your RBAC rules apply — if you can't create Deployments, Helm can't either
  • Multi-tenant safe — each user's permissions are enforced
  • No extra component to install, upgrade, or secure
🚫 CRITICAL: Never Use Helm 2

Helm 2 was deprecated in November 2020 and is no longer supported. This guide (and the certification) uses Helm 3+. If you encounter Helm 2 in any context, migrate immediately — Tiller is a well-known security vulnerability vector.

 Observability      Service Mesh       Security

Helm = The bridge from "I have YAML" to "I have
       a deployable, shareable application"
🐓
Graduated 2020

Helm became the 10th CNCF graduated project, joining Kubernetes, Prometheus, and Envoy at the top tier.

📊
10M+ Downloads/Month

Helm charts are pulled over 10 million times per month from Artifact Hub alone.

Helm History & Evolution — A Timeline

💡
Oct 2015
Helm v1

Created by Deis (acquired by Microsoft). Basic chart packaging. Experimental — not production-ready.

🚀
Nov 2016
Helm v2

Introduced Tiller (server-side component). Charts became mainstream. CNCF incubation.

🐓
Apr 2020
Helm v3 + Graduation

Tiller removed. Client-only architecture. 3-way merge. CNCF graduated — top-tier project.

⛵
Today
Helm v3.x

10K+ charts. OCI support. Library charts. Schema validation. Industry standard for K8s packaging.

📖 Why This History Matters

This guide focuses on Helm v3. Understanding Helm's evolution helps you understand why certain design decisions were made — especially the removal of Tiller. Knowing the v2→v3 transition shows deep understanding, not just command memorization.

1.6 Real-World Helm Use Cases — Who Uses Helm & Why

🏢
Enterprise Deployments

Companies like Spotify, Airbnb, IBM, and Walmart use Helm to manage thousands of microservices across hundreds of clusters. One standardized chart pattern across the entire organization.

🔄
CI/CD Pipelines

GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and Jenkins use Helm to deploy applications after builds pass. helm upgrade --install in your pipeline = automated, versioned deployments.

🏗️
Infrastructure as Code

Deploy Prometheus, Grafana, Istio, cert-manager, and ingress-nginx as Helm charts. Infrastructure components packaged and versioned just like applications.

📦
Software Distribution

ISVs (Independent Software Vendors) distribute their software as Helm charts. Customers run helm install myproduct myrepo/myapp — no manual YAML configuration needed.

🌐
Multi-Environment Management

Same chart, different values files: values-dev.yaml, values-staging.yaml, values-prod.yaml. One codebase, infinite environments.

🔒
GitOps with Argo CD/Flux

Store Helm charts in Git. Argo CD or Flux CD watches Git and syncs to your cluster. Git is the single source of truth — Helm renders the manifests.

💡 Helm by the Numbers (2024–2025)
  • 10,000+ charts on Artifact Hub — the de facto standard for K8s packaging
  • 70%+ of K8s users report using Helm (CNCF Survey 2024)
  • OCI support (Helm 3.8+) means charts live alongside container images
  • All major cloud providers (EKS, AKS, GKE) have native Helm integration

1.7 The Helm Mindset — Think in Charts, Not Files

The biggest shift when learning Helm is moving from a file-based mental model to a chart-based mental model.

❌ File-Based Thinking
  • "I need to edit deployment.yaml"
  • "Let me copy this YAML to staging"
  • "I'll change the image tag in all 3 files"
  • "Where did I put that service.yaml?"
  • "I hope staging is the same as prod"
✅ Chart-Based Thinking
  • "I need to update the chart's values"
  • "I'll create values-staging.yaml"
  • "One value change — all templates updated"
  • "Everything lives in the chart directory"
  • "Dev/staging/prod use the same chart, different values"
The Chart Mindset — Reusable Blueprint
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ONE CHART → MANY RELEASES                                           │
  │                    ┌─────────────────┐                               │
  │                    │  easypj-chart/  │  ← ONE chart (the blueprint)  │
  │                    │  templates/     │                                │
  │                    │  values.yaml    │                                │
  │                    └────────┬────────┘                               │
  │          ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐                     │
  │          ▼                  ▼                  ▼                     │
  │  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐              │
  │  │ easypj-dev   │  │ easypj-stg   │  │ easypj-prod  │              │
  │  │ (namespace:  │  │ (namespace:  │  │ (namespace:  │              │
  │  │  dev)        │  │  staging)    │  │  production) │              │
  │  │ replicas: 1  │  │ replicas: 2  │  │ replicas: 3  │              │
  │  │ image: latest│  │ image: v2.1  │  │ image: v2.0  │              │
  │  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘              │
  │  📋 3 releases = 1 chart × 3 values files                            │
  │  🎯 Same application, different configurations                       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 The Chart Mindset for Certification

On the exam, you'll be asked to do things like "install the same chart in two namespaces with different configurations." If you think in charts (not files), this is trivial: helm install dev ./chart -f values-dev.yaml -n dev and helm install prod ./chart -f values-prod.yaml -n prod. Same chart, different releases.

Under the Hood — how Helm actually renders a chart, and how it compares to the alternatives

"Helm merges values into templates" hides a precise, entirely client-side pipeline — no server component reads or writes anything until the very last step:

   HELM'S RENDER PIPELINE (100% client-side until the final apply)
   ┌────────────┐   ┌───────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌─────────────┐
   │ values.yaml│   │ -f values-    │   │ --set        │   │ Chart.yaml  │
   │ (defaults) │   │  prod.yaml    │   │ image.tag=v2 │   │ (metadata)  │
   └─────┬──────┘   └───────┬───────┘   └──────┬───────┘   └──────┬──────┘
         └──────────────────┴──────────────────┴──────────────────┘
                             │  merged, LAST WINS: --set beats -f beats values.yaml
                             ▼
                  ┌───────────────────────┐
                  │  Go template engine    │   walks every file in templates/,
                  │  + Sprig functions     │   substitutes {{ .Values.x }},
                  │  (text/template)       │   evaluates {{ if }}/{{ range }}
                  └───────────┬───────────┘
                             ▼
                  Rendered, plain Kubernetes YAML (no Helm syntax left)
                             │
                             ▼
                  kubectl-style apply ──▶ Kubernetes API server ──▶ etcd
                             │
                             ▼
                  Release record saved as a Secret (helm.sh/release.v1)

Two things fall out of this that surprise beginners: (1) helm template runs the entire pipeline above except the last two steps — so you can preview exactly what would be applied with zero cluster access; (2) because rendering is pure client-side templating, a chart with a typo in its Go template syntax fails at "render time," before Kubernetes ever sees it — which is why helm lint and --dry-run catch entire classes of errors early.

🔬 Helm vs. Alternatives — a Decision Matrix

Helm isn't the only way to manage Kubernetes YAML at scale. Knowing where it fits — and where a different tool fits better — is exactly the kind of judgment the certification rewards:

ToolApproachStrengthWeakness vs Helm
HelmTemplating + packagingVersioned releases, rollback, dependency management, huge ecosystem (10K+ charts)Go template syntax has a learning curve; whitespace-sensitive
KustomizePatching (overlay-based, no templating)No templating language — pure YAML patches; built into kubectlNo packaging/versioning concept; no release history or rollback
Plain kubectlDirect manifest applySimplest possible mental model; nothing to learnNo reuse, no environment parameterization, no rollback
Operators (Operator SDK)Custom controller + CRDHandles ongoing operational logic (e.g., DB failover), not just deploymentFull software engineering effort to build; overkill for simple apps
Argo CD / FluxGitOps continuous syncContinuously reconciles cluster state to Git — drift detectionNot a packaging format itself — commonly renders Helm charts as its source
🔑 They compose, they don't compete. A very common production pattern is Helm chart (packaging) + Argo CD (continuous GitOps sync) + Kustomize (last-mile patches Argo CD applies on top of the rendered chart). Knowing this saves you from a false "pick one" framing on the exam and in real architecture decisions.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes — it packages YAML manifests into reusable, versioned, configurable Charts, deployable with one command.
  • Three core nouns: Chart, Release, Repository — a Chart is the blueprint, a Release is a running instance of that blueprint, a Repository is where Charts are stored and shared.
  • No Tiller in Helm 3 — the Helm CLI talks directly to the Kubernetes API using your own kubeconfig and RBAC permissions. This is the single biggest architecture change from Helm 2 and the reason Helm 3 is dramatically more secure.
  • Helm ≠ a container registry — Helm stores and renders YAML manifests, not container images. Image pulls still go to Docker Hub/ECR/GCR/ACR.
  • Helm is a Graduated CNCF project (April 2020) — the same top tier as Kubernetes, Prometheus, and etcd, signaling production-grade maturity and governance.
  • Chart-based thinking replaces file-based thinking — one chart, many releases (dev/staging/prod), differentiated only by values. This is the mental model every later chapter builds on.
  • Rendering is entirely client-side — helm template shows you the exact output before anything ever touches the cluster.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • "Helm runs my app." No — Helm deploys Kubernetes resources (Deployments, Services…) that Kubernetes itself then runs. Helm's job ends the moment resources are applied; it doesn't stay in the request path.
  • "Helm is a container registry." It isn't. Charts contain YAML templates and metadata, not container images. The image: field in a chart is just a string passed through to Kubernetes, which pulls from an actual registry.
  • Confusing Chart with Release. The Chart is the reusable package (like a class); the Release is a specific running instance (like an object). One chart can produce many releases.
  • Assuming Helm 2 tutorials/blog posts still apply. Anything mentioning helm init, Tiller, or --tiller-namespace is Helm 2 — deprecated since November 2020. If you see it, it's outdated; ignore it.
  • "Helm and kubectl are competitors." They're complementary — Helm submits the same kind of YAML to the same API server that kubectl apply would. Helm adds packaging, templating, and release tracking on top.
  • Thinking a chart IS a running app. A chart is a blueprint sitting on disk (or in a repository) — nothing runs until you helm install it, which creates a Release.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • For "what is X" concept questions, answer in the Chart / Release / Repository frame first, then add detail — this structure alone earns partial credit and keeps your answer organized under time pressure.
  • "No Tiller" is the fastest way to prove Helm 3 knowledge. Any question probing architecture or security almost always wants you to mention that Helm 3 talks directly to the API server using the caller's own credentials.
  • Mnemonic for the three nouns: Chart = the recipe, Release = the meal you cooked, Repository = the cookbook shelf.
  • helm search hub vs helm search repo — hub searches Artifact Hub (all public charts); repo searches only repositories you've added locally. Mixing these up wastes exam time chasing a chart that was never added.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 1)

orient yourself with Helm — no chart authored yet 
# Confirm the Helm client is installed and its version (must be v3+)
helm version

# Search Artifact Hub for public charts (e.g. a Postgres chart for easypj's DB)
helm search hub postgresql

# Search only repositories you've already added locally
helm search repo bitnami

# List every release currently installed in the current namespace
helm list

# List releases across ALL namespaces
helm list --all-namespaces

# Show a chart's metadata without installing it
helm show chart bitnami/postgresql

🧠 Chapter 1 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of the mental model — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What is the primary purpose of Helm, in one sentence?
Show Answer
Answer

Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes — it packages related Kubernetes manifests into a reusable, versioned unit called a Chart, and installs/upgrades/rolls back that unit as a single Release.

Explanation

The "package manager" framing is deliberate and exam-relevant — it's the same category of tool as apt/npm/brew, just targeting Kubernetes resources instead of binaries or libraries.

Q2
Name Helm's three core concepts and define each in a few words.
Show Answer
Answer
ConceptDefinition
ChartA package of templated Kubernetes manifests + default values + metadata
ReleaseA running instance of an installed chart in a cluster
RepositoryA storage location where charts are published and discovered
Explanation

Every later chapter is really just going deeper on one of these three nouns — Chart authoring (Part 2), Release lifecycle (Part 3), Repository/dependency management (Part 4).

Q3
Using the Shipping Port analogy, what does a Helm Chart correspond to, and what does a Release correspond to?
Show Answer
Answer

A Chart is the Shipping Manifest (the blueprint describing what's in the cargo and how it should be arranged). A Release is a ship docked at a berth — an actual instance created FROM that manifest, in a specific location (namespace).

Explanation

The same manifest (Chart) can produce many ships (Releases) at different berths (namespaces) — exactly like one chart producing easypj-dev, easypj-staging, and easypj-prod releases.

Q4
What is Tiller, and why was it removed in Helm 3?
Show Answer
Answer

Tiller was Helm 2's server-side component, running inside the cluster with (typically) cluster-admin privileges. It was removed in Helm 3 because anyone with network access to it could effectively gain cluster-admin — a severe, well-known security hole.

Explanation

Helm 3 replaced Tiller with direct client-to-API-server communication, using the caller's own kubeconfig and RBAC — no elevated shared component, no extra attack surface.

Q5
Where does Helm 3 store release history/state by default?
Show Answer
Answer

As Kubernetes Secrets, in the same namespace as the release (type helm.sh/release.v1). Helm 2 used ConfigMaps by default.

Explanation

Storing as Secrets (rather than ConfigMaps) reflects that release manifests can contain sensitive rendered values — this is a favorite "what changed from Helm 2" exam probe.

Q6
A team needs to deploy easypj to dev, staging, and production with different replica counts and image tags in each. Describe the Helm-native way to do this.
Show Answer
Answer

Author one chart, then create three environment-specific values files (values-dev.yaml, values-staging.yaml, values-prod.yaml) and install three separate releases: helm install easypj-dev ./chart -f values-dev.yaml -n dev, and similarly for staging/prod.

Explanation

This is the chart-based mindset from §1.7 in practice — one source of truth for structure, environment differences isolated entirely to values.

Q7
Is Helm graded as its own domain on the certification? Explain.
Show Answer
Answer

No — Chapter 1's foundational material isn't a scored domain by itself, but it underpins all 6 official domains (Chart Creation & Anatomy, Template Syntax & Logic, Functions and Pipelines, Dependency Management, Lifecycle Hooks & Releases, Testing & Troubleshooting). Every domain assumes you already know what a Chart/Release/Repository is.

Explanation

Skipping the fundamentals to "save time" backfires — misunderstanding Chart vs Release vocabulary causes misread questions throughout every scored domain.

Q8
What is the difference between a Chart and a Release?
Show Answer
Answer

A Chart is the reusable, static package (templates + default values + metadata) sitting on disk or in a repository. A Release is what you get after running helm install — a specific, named, running instance of that chart in a cluster namespace, with its own revision history.

Explanation

Class vs. object is the closest programming analogy: many Release "objects" can be instantiated from one Chart "class," each with its own state (values, revision, status).

Q9
How does Helm differ from just running docker build / docker push?
Show Answer
Answer

Docker builds and distributes container images — the application binary + its filesystem. Helm distributes Kubernetes deployment configuration — how many replicas, what resources, what environment variables — that reference an already-built image. They operate at different layers and are used together, not instead of each other.

Explanation

A typical pipeline: docker build → docker push → CI updates the chart's image tag → helm upgrade deploys it. Helm never builds or stores images itself.

Q10
What does it mean that Helm is a CNCF "Graduated" project, and why should that matter to you as an operator?
Show Answer
Answer

Graduated is the CNCF's highest maturity tier — reserved for projects proven at production scale with diverse maintainers and strong governance/security processes (Helm reached it in April 2020, alongside Kubernetes itself). For an operator, it signals long-term stability: Helm isn't a fad tool likely to be abandoned, and its security processes have been externally vetted.

Explanation

This is a useful "why should I trust this tool with production" answer — both for the exam and for justifying tooling choices to a team or manager in real work.

⚙️ Chapter 1 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Applied reasoning drills — a situation, and you name the right concept, component, or command.

Q1
A teammate says "I ran helm install and now my app is running." Precisely, WHAT is now running, and where is Helm's own involvement recorded?
Show Answer
Answer

What's "running" are ordinary Kubernetes resources (Pods via a Deployment, a Service, etc.) — Kubernetes itself runs them, not Helm. Helm's own record of the action is a Release, tracked as a Secret of type helm.sh/release.v1 in the target namespace.

Explanation

This distinction (Helm deploys, Kubernetes runs) is the single most common beginner confusion and worth being able to state precisely.

Q2
You need to find a production-ready Redis chart without adding any repositories first. Which command, and why does it work without a prior helm repo add?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm search hub redis

search hub queries Artifact Hub directly over the network — it doesn't depend on any repository you've locally added. search repo, by contrast, only searches repos already registered with helm repo add.

Explanation

Mixing these two up is a classic time-waster: searching repo for a chart you never added returns nothing, even though the chart exists on the Hub.

Q3
Someone on your team is still running Helm 2 and pastes you a command using helm init. What's wrong, and what should they do?
Show Answer
Answer

helm init was the Helm 2 command that installed Tiller into the cluster. It doesn't exist in Helm 3 (no Tiller to install). They should upgrade to Helm 3+ and, if migrating an existing Helm 2 release, use the helm-2to3 plugin.

Explanation

Seeing helm init, --tiller-namespace, or any Tiller reference in a command or tutorial is an immediate signal that the source material is outdated.

Q4
You want to see exactly what YAML a chart would produce for production values — WITHOUT touching the cluster at all. Which command?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart -f values-prod.yaml

helm template runs the full rendering pipeline (merge values → execute Go templates) and prints the resulting plain Kubernetes YAML — entirely client-side, no cluster connection required.

Explanation

This is the fastest way to catch templating mistakes before they ever reach a live cluster, and it's a heavily-used command throughout later chapters on debugging charts.

Q5
Your manager asks "should we replace Helm with Kustomize?" What's the accurate one-sentence answer?
Show Answer
Answer

They solve different problems and are often used together — Kustomize is a patching tool with no templating language or release/versioning concept, while Helm adds packaging, parameterized templating, and release history/rollback; picking one depends on whether you need reusable, parameterized packages (Helm) or simple environment-specific overlays on static YAML (Kustomize).

Explanation

See the full Decision Matrix in this chapter's Under the Hood section for the complete comparison including Operators and GitOps tools.

Q6
You run helm list and see nothing, but you're SURE you installed easypj earlier. What's the most likely cause?
Show Answer
Answer

Wrong namespace. helm list defaults to the current namespace context. Either switch to the correct namespace or add --all-namespaces / -A to search everywhere.

bash
helm list --all-namespaces
Explanation

Namespace scoping trips up beginners constantly — Helm releases, like most Kubernetes resources, are namespace-scoped by default.

Q7
True or False: "Helm requires a special agent installed inside my Kubernetes cluster to function." Justify your answer.
Show Answer
Answer

False (as of Helm 3). This was true in Helm 2 (Tiller ran inside the cluster). Helm 3 is client-only — the helm binary talks straight to the standard Kubernetes API server using your kubeconfig, exactly like kubectl does.

Explanation

This is one of the most exam-relevant facts in the whole chapter — it's frequently tested both directly and indirectly (e.g., via RBAC/permission-scoped questions).

Q8
You want to inspect a chart's metadata (version, description, maintainers) BEFORE installing it. Which command?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm show chart bitnami/postgresql

helm show chart prints just the Chart.yaml content. Related: helm show values (default values.yaml), helm show all (everything).

Explanation

Inspecting before installing is a good habit reinforced throughout this guide — never install a chart blind in production.

Q9
A junior engineer asks why the company standardized on Helm instead of everyone hand-writing kubectl apply scripts. Give two concrete reasons grounded in this chapter.
Show Answer
Answer

Any two of: (1) versioned, trackable Releases with built-in rollback instead of "hope the last-known-good YAML is still on someone's laptop"; (2) one parameterized chart instead of near-duplicate YAML per environment; (3) a huge existing ecosystem (10K+ charts on Artifact Hub) for common infrastructure (databases, ingress controllers, monitoring) instead of writing it all from scratch.

Explanation

This maps directly back to §1.1's "Problem Before Helm" — being able to re-derive the "why" from first principles is stronger than memorizing a features list.

Q10
Someone claims "Helm charts must always come from Artifact Hub." Is this accurate?
Show Answer
Answer

No. Charts can come from a local directory (./my-chart), a packaged .tgz file, any HTTP(S) chart repository, or an OCI registry (Helm 3.8+). Artifact Hub is just the most popular discovery index for public charts, not the only distribution mechanism.

Explanation

OCI registry support is a Helm 3.8+ feature worth remembering — it means charts can live alongside container images in the same registry (ACR, ECR, GCR, Docker Hub, Harbor).

🔬 Practice Drill 1.1 — Sketch the Architecture from Memory

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

In 5 minutes, from memory, sketch the Helm 3 architecture: the Helm CLI, the Kubernetes API server, and where release state is stored. Label the arrow between the CLI and the API server with what credentials it uses. Then explicitly mark where Tiller WOULD have been in Helm 2, and cross it out.

Hint: There should be exactly one arrow, straight from the Helm CLI box to the Kubernetes API server box — no middle box in Helm 3.
View Solution 
   ┌──────────┐   YOUR kubeconfig + RBAC   ┌───────────────────┐
   │ Helm CLI │ ─────────────────────────▶ │ Kubernetes API    │
   └──────────┘   (direct, no middle box)  │ Server             │
        ✗ Tiller (Helm 2 only — REMOVED)   │  └─▶ etcd           │
                                            │  └─▶ Release state  │
                                            │      stored as       │
                                            │      Secrets          │
                                            └───────────────────┘

Check yourself: exactly one arrow from CLI to API server, labeled with kubeconfig/RBAC; Tiller marked as removed; release state landing in Secrets, not ConfigMaps. If you drew all three, you have Helm 3's architecture cold.

🔬 Practice Drill 1.2 — Explore Without Installing

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Using only read-only Helm commands (nothing that installs anything), find a public PostgreSQL chart, inspect its default values, and confirm your local Helm client's version — all in under 5 minutes.

Hint: You need exactly three commands: version check, hub search, and a "show" command.
View Solution
read-only exploration
# 1. Confirm client version (must be v3+)
helm version

# 2. Find a public PostgreSQL chart
helm search hub postgresql

# 3. Add the repo it came from, then inspect default values
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo update
helm show values bitnami/postgresql | less

Check yourself: nothing was installed to any cluster — every command here is safe to run against production without changing a single resource. This read-before-install discipline is worth building now.

🔬 Practice Drill 1.3 — Map easypj onto the Shipping Port Analogy

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Write one sentence each mapping easypj's helm install easypj-prod ./easypj-chart -n production onto the shipping port analogy: what is the Chart, what is the Release, what is the namespace, and who is the Harbor Master?

Hint: The command itself names all four things — chart path, release name, namespace flag, and the tool issuing the command.
View Solution
Command pieceAnalogy role
./easypj-chartThe Shipping Manifest — the blueprint for what gets deployed
easypj-prod (release name)The specific Ship — a named, running instance
-n productionThe Berth — the isolated dock (namespace) the ship is assigned to
helm (the CLI itself)The Harbor Master — reads the manifest and directs the ship to its berth

Check yourself: if you can point at any Helm command and immediately name which analogy role each piece plays, the mental model has fully landed.

🔬 Practice Drill 1.4 — Helm 2 vs Helm 3 Spot-the-Difference

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Below are 4 statements. For each, mark whether it describes Helm 2, Helm 3, or both: (1) "Release state is stored as a ConfigMap." (2) "The CLI talks directly to the Kubernetes API server." (3) "Charts are packaged as .tgz files." (4) "A cluster-side component executes install/upgrade requests."

Hint: Only one of the four is true for BOTH versions — the other three are version-specific.
View Solution
#StatementAnswer
1Release state as ConfigMapHelm 2 (default). Helm 3 defaults to Secrets.
2CLI talks directly to API serverHelm 3 only. Helm 2's CLI talked to Tiller, which talked to the API server.
3Charts packaged as .tgzBoth — chart packaging format didn't change.
4Cluster-side component executes requestsHelm 2 only (Tiller). Removed in Helm 3.

Check yourself: statement 3 is the one constant — chart packaging survived the v2→v3 transition unchanged; everything about how the CLI talks to the cluster changed.

🔬 Practice Drill 1.5 — Explain Helm to a kubectl-Only Colleague

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

A colleague who only uses kubectl apply -f asks "why would I ever need Helm?" Write a 3-sentence answer using easypj as the concrete example, covering: (1) the multi-file problem, (2) multi-environment reuse, (3) rollback.

Hint: Ground every sentence in the easypj example from §1.1 rather than speaking abstractly.
View Solution

Sample answer: "Right now you're hand-editing 15 YAML files for easypj every time something changes, and duplicating all of them for staging and prod — Helm packages those into one chart you install with a single command. Instead of copy-pasting files per environment, you keep one chart and swap a small values file per environment (dev/staging/prod), so a change only has to happen once. And if a bad deploy breaks production, helm rollback easypj 1 reverts to the last known-good release in seconds — with plain kubectl apply, you'd be hunting for the old YAML files by hand."

Check yourself: your answer should be persuasive to someone who has never used Helm — if it relies on Helm-specific jargon they wouldn't know yet, simplify it further.

  │ Chart.yaml   │  ①install  │  values, renders Go    │ ②apply │  (validates, persists)      │
  │ values.yaml  │ ─────────▶ │  templates client-side │ ──────▶│                             │
  │ templates/   │            │  NO Tiller — uses YOUR │        │  ┌───────────────────────┐  │
  │  deploy.yaml │            │  kubeconfig directly    │        │  │ Deployment easypj-web  │  │
  │  svc.yaml    │            └──────────────────────┘        │  │ Service · ConfigMap    │  │
  │  cm.yaml     │                     │③ record            │  └───────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────┘                     ▼                       │  ┌───────────────────────┐  │
                              ┌──────────────────────┐         │  │ Secret: release state  │  │
                              │ 🔐 easypj-prod Release │◀────────│  │ (helm.sh/release.v1)   │  │
                              │ revision 1, "deployed" │         │  └───────────────────────┘  │
                              └──────────────────────┘         └───────────────────────────┘
   ① helm install renders the chart's templates with your values (client-side, no cluster yet)
   ② the rendered YAML is applied straight to the API server — same door kubectl uses
   ③ Helm writes a Release record (as a Secret) so upgrade/rollback/history all work later
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   ONE chart + DIFFERENT values = ONE consistent way to run easypj in dev, staging, and prod —
   versioned, rollback-able, and reproducible. That is the whole point of Helm. ⛵

In words: A Helm Chart is a packaged blueprint — templates plus default values plus metadata — sitting on disk or in a repository, doing nothing on its own. Running helm install renders that blueprint entirely client-side (merging your values into the Go templates) and submits the resulting plain Kubernetes YAML straight to the API server, exactly the way kubectl apply would.

The one addition Helm makes on top of that submission is bookkeeping: it writes a Release record — stored as a Kubernetes Secret — that tracks what was installed, with which values, at which revision. That record is what makes helm upgrade, helm rollback, and helm history possible later.

The takeaway: no Tiller, no hidden server-side magic — Helm 3 is a thin, secure client layer over the same Kubernetes API you already use, adding packaging, environment-parameterized values, and versioned releases. Every chapter after this one is a deeper look at one piece of this picture.

Chapter 2 · Installing & Configuring Helm

Before you can deploy easypj with Helm, you need Helm itself. This chapter walks through installation on every major platform, verifying your setup, configuring Helm's environment, adding chart repositories, extending Helm with plugins, and enabling shell autocompletion — the 10-minute setup tax you pay once so nothing else in this guide stalls on "command not found."

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~45 min 🛠️ Hands-On 🐍 easypj / jobpost 🎯 Foundational — all 6 domains

Foundation Knowledge ALL 6 DOMAINS CLI & Environment Setup PRACTICAL
🎯 Why Setup Speed Matters for the Exam

The certification is performance-based and time-boxed — every second spent fighting a broken helm command is a second not spent solving the actual task. Three things to have automatic before you touch a real task:

  • Know the version check — helm version should show v3.x. If it shows v2.x, stop and fix it first; nothing downstream will behave the way this guide describes.
  • Know the connectivity check — helm list talks to the cluster; a clean (even empty) response means Helm and kubectl share a working kubeconfig.
  • Enable autocompletion in the first 60 seconds of any hands-on task — it pays for itself within 3 commands.

2.1 Installing Helm CLI

Helm is a single binary — no daemon, no database, no background service. Installation is simply downloading the binary and putting it in your PATH. This is a direct consequence of Chapter 1's "no Tiller" architecture: there's nothing server-side to deploy, so there's nothing complicated to install.

Helm Installation — Three Platform Options
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     HELM INSTALLATION METHODS                          │
  │  🐧 LINUX                    🍎 macOS                   🪟 WINDOWS   │
  │  ─────────                  ─────────                 ───────────    │
  │  A) Install script          A) Homebrew                A) Chocolatey  │
  │     curl ... | bash            brew install helm           choco      │
  │  B) Package manager         B) Install script          B) Scoop       │
  │     apt/yum/snap               (same as Linux)             scoop      │
  │                              C) MacPorts                C) Manual .zip│
  │                                 port install helm           from      │
  │                                                              GitHub    │
  │  VERIFY (all platforms): helm version → must show v3.x.x, NOT v2.x.x  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Linux / macOS — install via script or package manager 
# Official install script (Linux or macOS)
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3 | bash

# macOS with Homebrew
brew install helm

# Debian/Ubuntu via apt
curl https://baltocdn.com/helm/signing.asc | sudo apt-key add -
sudo apt-get install apt-transport-https --yes
echo "deb https://baltocdn.com/helm/stable/debian/ all main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/helm-stable-debian.list
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install helm

# RHEL/CentOS/Fedora
sudo dnf install helm
Windows — Chocolatey, Scoop, or manual 
# Chocolatey (run PowerShell as Administrator)
choco install kubernetes-helm

# Scoop
scoop install helm

# Manual: download from https://github.com/helm/helm/releases,
# extract helm.exe, and add its folder to PATH
⚠️ Make Sure You Get v3 — Not v2

The current version is Helm v3.x. If helm version shows v2.x.x, you have the wrong version — Helm 2 is deprecated, uses the removed Tiller architecture, and is incompatible with Kubernetes 1.22+. The certification exam uses Helm v3 exclusively.

2.2 Verifying Installation — helm version

verify the client version AND cluster connectivity 
# Check the Helm client version
helm version
# version.BuildInfo{Version:"v3.16.0", GitCommit:"abcdef1", GitTreeState:"clean", GoVersion:"go1.22.0"}

# Confirm Helm can reach your Kubernetes cluster
helm list
# Empty output is fine — it just means no releases yet, and NO connection error

# If you see "Kubernetes cluster unreachable: the server has asked for
# the client to provide credentials" → check kubectl first:
kubectl cluster-info
📖 What helm version Does (and Doesn't) Tell You

helm version shows only the client version — the Helm binary on your machine. Unlike Helm 2, it does NOT show a server version, because there is no server component (Tiller was removed — Chapter 1, §1.4a). If your Kubernetes cluster is reachable, Helm works. There's nothing else to check.

2.3 Helm Environment & Configuration

📁
HELM_HOME / HELM_CONFIG_HOME

Default: ~/.config/helm/ (Linux/macOS) or %APPDATA%\helm\ (Windows). Stores repositories.yaml and other configuration.

🏷️
HELM_NAMESPACE

Sets a default namespace for all Helm commands, equivalent to kubectl config set-context --namespace. Example: export HELM_NAMESPACE=easypj-dev.

📂
HELM_CACHE_HOME

Where downloaded charts are cached. Default: ~/.cache/helm/. Cleared/refreshed by helm repo update.

🔌
HELM_DATA_HOME / HELM_PLUGINS

Where installed plugins live. Default: ~/.local/share/helm/. Relevant when troubleshooting a plugin that "won't load."

💾
HELM_DRIVER

The backend Helm uses to store release records. Default: secret (Kubernetes Secrets — Chapter 1, §1.4). Can be set to configmap, sql, or memory for special cases.

🎯
HELM_KUBECONTEXT / KUBECONFIG

Override which cluster/context Helm targets, without changing your global kubectl context. Useful when scripting against multiple clusters.

inspect and set Helm's environment 
# View every path and setting Helm is currently using
helm env

# Set a default namespace for all helm commands this session
export HELM_NAMESPACE=easypj-prod

# Filter to just the values you care about
helm env | grep HELM

Registry Authentication (for OCI Chart Repositories)

Since Helm 3.8, charts can be pulled from OCI registries (the same kind Docker images live in). Authenticating to one works exactly like docker login:

OCI registry login 
helm registry login ghcr.io -u USER -p TOKEN
helm registry logout ghcr.io

2.4 Adding Chart Repositories

Repositories are where Helm charts are stored and distributed — the Chapter 1 shipping-port analogy's "Warehouse/Depot." Think of them as Docker registries, but for charts instead of images.

repository management 
# List currently configured repositories
helm repo list

# Add popular repositories
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo add ingress-nginx https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx

# Fetch the latest chart index from every configured repo
helm repo update

# Search only your locally added repos
helm search repo nginx
helm search repo bitnami/postgresql

# Search Artifact Hub — the global chart index (no repo add needed)
helm search hub wordpress

# Remove a repository
helm repo remove ingress-nginx
💡 Repositories You'll Actually Use
  • Bitnami (https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami) — well-maintained charts for databases, caches, and common infrastructure. Used throughout this guide for easypj's PostgreSQL dependency.
  • ingress-nginx (https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx) — the official NGINX ingress controller.
  • cert-manager (https://charts.jetstack.io) — TLS certificate automation.
  • Artifact Hub (artifacthub.io) — not a repo itself, but the global search engine covering nearly every public chart repository.

2.5 Helm Plugins — Extending Helm

Helm has a plugin system that adds new subcommands. Plugins are community-maintained — none are required, but a few are near-universal in production teams.

plugin management 
# Install a plugin from its Git repository
helm plugin install https://github.com/databus23/helm-diff

# List installed plugins
helm plugin list

# Update or remove one
helm plugin update helm-diff
helm plugin uninstall helm-diff
PluginPurposeWhy it matters
helm-diffShows a colored diff of what an upgrade will changeProduction safety — see changes before helm upgrade applies them, similar to terraform plan
helm-secretsEncrypts values files with SOPS/AWS KMSNever commit plain-text secrets to Git
helm-gitInstall charts straight from a Git repositoryUseful when a chart lives in the same repo as the app code, for CI/CD
helm-mapkubeapisMaps deprecated Kubernetes APIs in a release to their supported replacementsPrevents broken upgrades after a Kubernetes version bump deprecates an API
helm-unittestUnit tests for Helm templatesCatches template logic bugs in CI, before helm install ever runs (Part 4)
🎯 Exam Tip

Plugins aren't heavily tested directly, but knowing helm-diff exists is a useful answer for troubleshooting-style questions about detecting configuration drift before an upgrade.

2.6 Shell Autocompletion Setup

Autocompletion dramatically speeds up your workflow — Tab and Helm completes commands, flags, release names, and even chart names. This is worth the 5 seconds it takes to set up, every single session.

enable autocompletion per shell 
# Bash (add to ~/.bashrc)
source <(helm completion bash)

# Zsh (add to ~/.zshrc)
source <(helm completion zsh)

# Fish (add to ~/.config/fish/config.fish)
helm completion fish | source

# PowerShell (add to $PROFILE)
helm completion powershell | Out-String | Invoke-Expression

# After setup, try:
helm <TAB>              # shows all commands: install, upgrade, list…
helm install <TAB>      # shows flags: --set, --namespace, --values…
helm uninstall <TAB>    # shows existing release names
💡 Autocompletion on the Exam

Memorize the one-liner: source <(helm completion bash). Spending 3 seconds enabling it can save minutes of typing and prevent typos in flag names under time pressure.

Under the Hood — the setup validation checklist, step by step

"Make sure Helm is ready" hides six distinct checks, each verifying a different layer of the stack. Running through them in order isolates a failure to one specific layer instead of guessing:

   SETUP VALIDATION — SIX LAYERS, BOTTOM TO TOP
   ① Binary exists & is v3     helm version               (no cluster needed)
   ② kubeconfig is valid       kubectl cluster-info        (no Helm needed)
   ③ Helm ↔ cluster works      helm list                   (both layers together)
   ④ Repos are reachable       helm repo update             (network + repo config)
   ⑤ A real install works      helm install test-nginx …    (end-to-end proof)
   ⑥ Autocompletion is on      helm <TAB><TAB>              (convenience, not correctness)

The ordering is deliberate: each check isolates one additional layer. If ① fails, nothing below it matters — fix the binary first. If ① passes but ② fails, the problem is entirely in kubectl/kubeconfig, not Helm at all — a distinction that saves a lot of misdirected debugging.

CheckCommandWhat it provesWhat it does NOT prove
① Binaryhelm versionThe client binary exists and is v3.xNothing about cluster connectivity — this check needs no cluster at all
② kubeconfigkubectl cluster-infoYour kubeconfig points at a live, reachable API serverNothing about Helm itself — this is pure kubectl
③ Helm↔clusterhelm listHelm can read Release Secrets through the same API server kubectl usedWhether any repos are configured
④ Reposhelm repo updateNetwork access to configured chart repositories, and their indexes are freshWhether an actual install will succeed (RBAC could still block it)
⑤ End-to-endhelm install test-nginx bitnami/nginx --waitEvery previous layer AND your RBAC permissions all work together—(this is the complete proof)
🔑 Debug top-down, not bottom-up. When something's broken, don't jump straight to reinstalling Helm. Walk ①→⑤ in order and stop at the first failure — that's your actual root cause, and everything after it in the list is a false lead.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Helm is a single static binary — no daemon, no database, no cluster-side install step. A direct consequence of the no-Tiller architecture from Chapter 1.
  • helm version only checks the client — there's no server version to check anymore. Cluster connectivity is proven separately, by helm list.
  • Helm reuses your kubeconfig — if kubectl already works, Helm works. There's no separate credential system to configure.
  • HELM_NAMESPACE sets a default namespace for every command that omits -n — convenient, but always double-check it on the exam, where tasks target specific namespaces.
  • Repositories must be added AND updated before charts inside them are visible to search repo — the sequence is always repo add → repo update → search → install.
  • Plugins are optional extensions, not core Helm — helm-diff is the one most teams eventually install for upgrade safety.
  • Autocompletion is a 5-second investment that pays for itself almost immediately under exam time pressure.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • "helm: command not found" — the binary isn't in your PATH. Move it to /usr/local/bin/ (Linux/macOS) or add its folder to PATH (Windows); verify with which helm.
  • "Kubernetes cluster unreachable" — this is almost always a kubectl problem wearing a Helm error message. Check kubectl cluster-info and kubectl get nodes before touching Helm at all.
  • "Error: no repositories found" / a search returns nothing — you haven't run helm repo add yet, or you searched repo when you meant hub (Chapter 1, §1.3). Add the repo, then helm repo update.
  • Stale search results — your local repo cache is old. helm repo update refreshes it; if a repo was removed upstream, helm repo remove <name> cleans it up.
  • "Permission denied" on install — this is usually CORRECT behavior, not a bug. Your RBAC permissions genuinely control what Helm can do (Chapter 1, §1.4a) — check your Role/ClusterRole bindings in the target namespace.
  • Wrong cluster context — helm list shows unexpected (or zero) releases because KUBECONFIG points at the wrong cluster. Check with kubectl config current-context before panicking that releases "disappeared."
  • Running helm init — this was the Helm 2 command that installed Tiller. It doesn't exist in Helm 3 — there's nothing to initialize. Seeing it in a tutorial is an instant sign the material is outdated (Chapter 1, §1.4a).
  • A Linux package manager silently installs Helm 2 — some older/frozen distro repos still ship it. Always run helm version right after any install and confirm v3 before assuming you're set up correctly.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Set aliases + autocompletion in the first 60 seconds of any hands-on task — it pays for itself within 3 commands.
  • helm env is your one-stop debug command — every path, every setting, in one place. Check it before assuming a config file is misplaced.
  • The repo pattern never changes: repo add → repo update → search repo → install. Memorize this exact order, not just the individual commands.
  • Trust kubectl first. Since Helm reuses kubeconfig, any "Helm can't connect" error is fastest diagnosed with plain kubectl commands, which you likely already know well.

# 3. Configure (optional but recommended)

helm test test-nginx
