🧠 Chapter 2 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of setup & configuration — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
You've installed Helm using the install script. How do you verify the installation and confirm it can connect to your cluster?
Show Answer
Answer

Run helm version to verify the client binary version. Run helm list (or helm ls) to verify connectivity — if Helm can reach the API server, it returns cleanly (even an empty list), with no connection error.

Explanation

helm version only checks the client binary — it needs no cluster. helm list actually talks to the Kubernetes API to read Release Secrets. If it returns without a connection error, Helm is properly configured end to end.

Q2
What is the purpose of helm repo update, and when should you run it?
Show Answer
Answer

It fetches the latest chart index from every configured repository. Run it: (1) right after adding a new repo, (2) before searching for a chart, (3) before installing/upgrading, to make sure you're not working off a stale index.

Explanation

Repository indexes are cached locally. Without an update, you're searching stale data — new charts won't appear and versions may be outdated. It's the Helm equivalent of apt update.

Q3
Which environment variable sets the default namespace for all Helm commands, and what's the risk of relying on it during the exam?
Show Answer
Answer

HELM_NAMESPACE, set via export HELM_NAMESPACE=my-namespace. It affects every command that omits an explicit -n/--namespace flag. The risk: exam tasks routinely target different namespaces per question — if you forget you set it, you can deploy to the wrong place without any error.

Explanation

Always re-read the target namespace in each task rather than trusting a session-wide default you set earlier — this is a common self-inflicted exam mistake.

Q4
Explain the difference between helm search hub and helm search repo.
Show Answer
Answer

helm search hub searches Artifact Hub — the global public index of Helm charts. helm search repo searches only the repositories you've already added locally with helm repo add.

Explanation

To install a chart found via search hub, you must first helm repo add its repository — Artifact Hub is a discovery index, not a source Helm installs directly from.

Q5
Which Helm plugin would you use to preview what an upgrade will change, before running it for real?
Show Answer
Answer

helm-diff. Install it, then run helm diff upgrade <release> <chart> to see a colored diff of exactly which resources would be added, changed, or removed.

Explanation

Functionally similar to terraform plan — it's a production safety net against "oops, I didn't mean to delete that" upgrade surprises.

Q6
How do you enable Helm bash autocompletion, and how do you make it permanent?
Show Answer
Answer

Run source <(helm completion bash) for the current shell. To make it permanent, append that same line to ~/.bashrc (or the zsh/fish equivalent for other shells).

Explanation

The completion script is generated by Helm itself at runtime — there's no separate package to install for it.

Q7
Where does Helm store its configuration and cache by default on Linux, and which single command shows you all of these paths at once?
Show Answer
Answer

Configuration: ~/.config/helm/. Cache: ~/.cache/helm/. Data/plugins: ~/.local/share/helm/. helm env prints all of these paths (and more) in one place.

Explanation

helm env is the first command to run when something about repository access or plugin loading seems wrong — it removes the guesswork.

Q8
What command shows every currently configured Helm repository, and where does that data actually live on disk?
Show Answer
Answer

helm repo list. The underlying data lives in ~/.config/helm/repositories.yaml (name + URL per repository).

Explanation

Knowing the actual file matters when scripting a fresh environment setup — you can seed repositories.yaml directly instead of running many repo add commands.

Q9
You need to install the Bitnami PostgreSQL chart for easypj's database. Give the exact commands, in order.
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo update
helm search repo bitnami/postgresql
helm install easypj-db bitnami/postgresql --set auth.database=easypj -n database
Explanation

The pattern is always repo add → repo update → search (confirm it exists) → install. Skipping repo update is the most common reason a just-added repo's charts "aren't found."

Q10
After installing Helm via your distro's package manager, helm version reports v2.16.1. What should you do, and why does it matter?
Show Answer
Answer

Uninstall it and install Helm 3 via the official script. Helm 2 is deprecated (since November 2020), depends on the insecure Tiller component, and is incompatible with modern Kubernetes versions — this guide, and the certification, assume Helm 3 exclusively.

Explanation

Some older or frozen distro package repositories still ship Helm 2. Always confirm the version immediately after any install — don't assume a package manager gave you the current release.

⚙️ Chapter 2 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

A broken setup, and you produce the fix with real commands.

Q1
A teammate runs helm list and gets: Error: Kubernetes cluster unreachable: the server has asked for the client to provide credentials. Diagnose and fix.
Show Answer
Answer

This is a kubeconfig problem, not a Helm problem — Helm reuses whatever kubectl is configured to use.

bash
kubectl cluster-info
echo $KUBECONFIG
kubectl config current-context
kubectl get nodes
Explanation

Fix whatever kubectl reports as broken (expired credentials, wrong context, unreachable cluster) — once plain kubectl commands work, Helm will too, with no separate Helm-side fix needed.

Q2
You run helm search repo redis and get zero results, even though you're sure Bitnami has a Redis chart. What's wrong?
Show Answer
Answer

Either the Bitnami repo was never added, or it was added but never updated. Fix:

bash
helm repo list                    # is bitnami even there?
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo update
helm search repo redis
Explanation

search repo only ever looks at your local index — it can't find a chart from a repository you haven't added and updated, no matter how popular that chart is.

Q3
helm install fails with a permissions/forbidden-style error. Is this necessarily a bug? What do you check first?
Show Answer
Answer

Not necessarily — it's often correct RBAC enforcement. Check whether your identity actually has permission to create the resources the chart contains in that namespace: kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n <namespace> (repeat for the other kinds the chart creates).

Explanation

Because Helm 3 has no Tiller and uses your own credentials, a permission error means YOUR RBAC is genuinely insufficient — the fix is a Role/RoleBinding, not a Helm workaround.

Q4
helm list shows no releases, but you're certain easypj was installed last week. Name the single most likely cause and the command to confirm it.
Show Answer
Answer

Wrong namespace or wrong cluster context. Confirm with:

bash
kubectl config current-context
helm list --all-namespaces
Explanation

helm list defaults to the current namespace only — a release installed into a different namespace, or on a different cluster context, simply won't appear without -A.

Q5
A fresh CI runner needs Helm installed non-interactively as part of a pipeline. Which install method fits best, and why?
Show Answer
Answer

The official install script, piped straight to bash, since it requires no interactive prompts and works identically across Linux distros:

bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3 | bash
helm version --short
Explanation

Package managers (apt/yum) can lag behind or ship Helm 2 on older images — the install script always fetches a current, correct Helm 3 release, and is the most portable choice for CI.

Q6
You want to try a plugin without risking it breaking your daily Helm usage. What's a safe first check before trusting it?
Show Answer
Answer

Install it, confirm it appears in helm plugin list, and test it on a disposable/non-critical release first. If it misbehaves, helm plugin uninstall <name> removes it cleanly with zero effect on core Helm.

Explanation

Plugins are additive subcommands, not modifications to Helm's core binary — uninstalling one always returns you to stock behavior.

Q7
You need every Helm command in this terminal session to default to the easypj-staging namespace, without typing -n every time. One command?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
export HELM_NAMESPACE=easypj-staging
Explanation

Remember this is session-scoped and easy to forget about later — always sanity-check helm env | grep NAMESPACE if a command's behavior seems to target the "wrong" place unexpectedly.

Q8
Before doing a risky helm upgrade on a production release, what single extra step would a careful operator take, and what tool enables it?
Show Answer
Answer

Run helm diff upgrade <release> <chart> -f values-prod.yaml (the helm-diff plugin) to preview exactly what would change, before actually running helm upgrade.

Explanation

This is the closest Helm equivalent to terraform plan, and the single highest-value plugin for production safety covered in this chapter.

Q9
A junior engineer wants to pull a chart from your company's private OCI registry at myregistry.io. What do they need to do before helm pull will work?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm registry login myregistry.io -u USER -p TOKEN
Explanation

OCI-based chart repositories (Helm 3.8+) authenticate exactly like a container registry — helm registry login/logout mirror docker login/logout directly.

Q10
Design a 4-command "prove Helm is fully working end-to-end" smoke test — not just installed, but genuinely able to deploy and clean up.
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami && helm repo update
helm install smoke-test bitnami/nginx --wait --timeout 2m
helm test smoke-test
helm uninstall smoke-test
Explanation

This exercises every layer from Under the Hood's checklist at once: repo access, install, RBAC, and a working cleanup — a real install/uninstall cycle is the only check that proves everything together, end to end.

🔬 Practice Drill 2.1 — Zero to Verified in Under 5 Minutes

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Starting from a terminal with a working Kubernetes cluster but NO Helm installed, get to a fully verified setup: Helm v3 installed, version confirmed, cluster connectivity confirmed, and autocompletion enabled — in under 5 minutes.

Hint: You need exactly 4 commands — install, two verification checks, and one completion line.
View Solution
zero to verified
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3 | bash
helm version
helm list
source <(helm completion bash)

Check yourself: helm version shows v3.x, helm list returns without a connection error, and helm <TAB><TAB> shows a command list. If all three are true, you're genuinely ready for Chapter 3.

🔬 Practice Drill 2.2 — Connect to Bitnami and Find easypj's Database Chart

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Add the Bitnami repository, refresh it, and confirm a PostgreSQL chart is available for easypj's database — without installing anything yet.

Hint: repo add → repo update → search repo, in that exact order.
View Solution
bash
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo update
helm search repo bitnami/postgresql

Check yourself: the search returns at least one row with a chart version and app version. If it returns nothing, you skipped repo update — go back and run it.

🔬 Practice Drill 2.3 — Diagnose a Simulated Broken Setup

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Deliberately break your own setup to understand the failure signature: temporarily set export KUBECONFIG=/nonexistent/path, then try helm list. Read the exact error, then fix it and confirm recovery.

Hint: unset KUBECONFIG restores the default ~/.kube/config lookup.
View Solution
bash
export KUBECONFIG=/nonexistent/path
helm list                          # errors — file doesn't exist
unset KUBECONFIG
helm list                          # works again

Check yourself: the error message you saw should now be instantly recognizable in real troubleshooting — deliberately breaking things once is the fastest way to learn to read error text quickly under pressure.

🔬 Practice Drill 2.4 — Install and Test a Real Plugin

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Install the helm-diff plugin, confirm it's listed, then use it to preview (not apply) a change to a test release.

Hint: You'll need an existing release to diff against — install a throwaway one first if you don't have one.
View Solution
bash
helm plugin install https://github.com/databus23/helm-diff
helm plugin list

helm install diff-test bitnami/nginx --wait
helm diff upgrade diff-test bitnami/nginx --set replicaCount=2

helm uninstall diff-test

Check yourself: the diff output should show a ~ (changed) line for replicaCount — and critically, running helm diff should NOT have actually changed anything; only helm upgrade would.

🔬 Practice Drill 2.5 — Write a One-Screen Onboarding Cheat Sheet

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

A new teammate joins the easypj team tomorrow. Write the exact sequence of commands (no explanations, just commands) they should run on day one to go from a bare laptop to a fully verified, autocompletion-enabled Helm setup connected to the team's Bitnami repo.

Hint: This is exactly the Commands to Know block above, in the right order — the exercise is recalling that order from memory, not looking it up.
View Solution
day-one onboarding
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3 | bash
helm version
kubectl cluster-info
helm list
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo update
source <(helm completion bash)

Check yourself: if you could write this from memory without re-reading the chapter, Chapter 2's material has genuinely landed — this exact sequence recurs at the start of nearly every real Helm engagement.

📌 Chapter 2 Visual Summary — from bare laptop to a verified Helm setup
  📥 INSTALL              ✅ VERIFY                  ⚙️ CONFIGURE
  ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────────┐      ┌───────────────────┐
  │ install script│  ①    │ helm version       │  ②  │ HELM_NAMESPACE     │
  │ or brew/choco │ ─────▶│  → v3.x.x           │────▶│ helm env           │
  │ single binary,│        │ helm list          │      │ registry login     │
  │ no daemon     │        │  → no conn. error  │      └───────────────────┘
  └──────────────┘        └──────────────────┘               │
                                                               ▼
  ⌨️ SPEED UP              🔌 EXTEND                  📋 CONNECT
  ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────────┐      ┌───────────────────┐
  │ helm         │  ⑤    │ helm plugin        │  ④  │ helm repo add       │
  │ completion   │◀───────│ install helm-diff  │◀────│ helm repo update    │
  │ bash/zsh     │        │ (optional)         │      │ helm search repo    │
  └──────────────┘        └──────────────────┘      └───────────────────┘
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   ⑥ PROVE IT END-TO-END:  helm install test-nginx bitnami/nginx --wait
                            helm test test-nginx  →  helm uninstall test-nginx
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   6 steps, ~10 minutes, done ONCE. Every later chapter assumes this works. ⛵

In words: Getting Helm production-ready is a short, linear checklist, not an ongoing chore. Install the single binary for your platform, then verify two separate things — the client version (helm version) and cluster connectivity (helm list) — because they can fail independently and point to entirely different fixes.

From there, configuration is optional convenience: a default namespace, plugin extensions like helm-diff, and shell autocompletion all make daily work faster without changing what Helm fundamentally does. Connecting to a repository (Bitnami, in easypj's case, for its PostgreSQL dependency) is the one step that's actually required before Chapter 3's chart work can pull in real dependencies.

The takeaway: a full install-to-verified cycle — including a real helm install/helm uninstall round-trip — takes about 10 minutes and only needs to happen once per machine. Skipping the verification step is the single most common cause of confusing errors three chapters later.

Chapter 3 · Charts — The Heart of Helm

A Chart is the fundamental unit of Helm — everything you do with Helm revolves around charts: creating them, packaging them, installing them, sharing them. This chapter dissects the chart structure file by file, showing exactly what each component does, then builds a real chart for easypj from scratch. By the end you'll be able to create, understand, and navigate any Helm chart with confidence.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~2 hours 📦 Core 🐍 easypj / jobpost 🎯 Chart Creation & Anatomy

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Work with values.yaml — the default configuration layer

🎓 Helm Certification Relevance
Chart Creation & Anatomy CORE DOMAIN
🎯 Chart Structure Is the Foundation of Every Other Domain

Template Syntax, Functions/Pipelines, Dependency Management, Lifecycle Hooks — every one of them is really "do something specific with a file inside the chart you're about to learn here." Get the anatomy solid now:

  • Know what's required vs optional in Chart.yaml — apiVersion, name, version are the only three the exam can't let you skip.
  • Know what's a template vs what isn't — NOTES.txt and _helpers.tpl live in templates/ but are never submitted to Kubernetes as resources.
  • Always scaffold with helm create, never an empty folder — deleting what you don't need is faster than typing from scratch under exam time pressure.

3.1 What is a Chart? — Structure Deep Dive

A Helm chart is a directory tree containing every file needed to describe a Kubernetes application — the "source code" of your deployment. Templates, default configuration, metadata, and dependency declarations all live together in one organized structure.

Complete Chart Anatomy — Every File Explained
  📁 easypj-chart/                              ← Chart root directory
  │
  ├── 📄 Chart.yaml          ← METADATA
  │   ├── apiVersion: v2     ← Chart API version (v2 = Helm 3)
  │   ├── name: easypj       ← Chart name
  │   ├── version: 0.1.0     ← Chart version (SemVer)
  │   ├── appVersion: "2.1"  ← Application version
  │   ├── type: application  ← "application" or "library"
  │   ├── description: ...   ← Human-readable description
  │   └── dependencies: []   ← Subchart declarations
  │
  ├── 📄 values.yaml         ← DEFAULT CONFIGURATION
  │   ├── replicaCount: 2
  │   ├── image: {repository, tag, pullPolicy}
  │   ├── service: {type, port}
  │   ├── ingress: {enabled}
  │   └── resources: {}
  │
  ├── 📄 values-dev.yaml / values-staging.yaml / values-prod.yaml   ← ENV OVERRIDES
  │
  ├── 📁 templates/          ← YAML GENERATION ENGINE
  │   ├── deployment.yaml · service.yaml · configmap.yaml · secret.yaml
  │   ├── ingress.yaml · hpa.yaml
  │   ├── NOTES.txt          ← POST-INSTALL MESSAGE (not a K8s resource)
  │   ├── _helpers.tpl       ← REUSABLE TEMPLATE HELPERS (not deployed)
  │   └── tests/test-connection.yaml
  │
  ├── 📁 charts/             ← SUBCHART DEPENDENCIES (postgresql-*.tgz, redis-*.tgz)
  ├── 📄 Chart.lock          ← DEPENDENCY LOCK FILE
  └── 📄 .helmignore         ← EXCLUDE PATTERNS (for helm package)
📖 Chart = Blueprint, Release = Building

The chart directory contains templates, not actual Kubernetes resources. When you run helm install, Helm reads the chart, injects values into templates, renders complete YAML manifests, and submits them to Kubernetes. The resulting running application is a Release (Chapter 1, §1.2).

3.1a Chart.yaml — Metadata, Versioning & apiVersion

Chart.yaml is the identity card of your chart — it tells Helm what this chart is called, what version it is, what application it deploys, and what other charts it depends on.

Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2              # REQUIRED: Chart API version (v2 = Helm 3+)
name: easypj                # REQUIRED: Chart name
description: A Helm chart for the easypj Django job board application
type: application            # REQUIRED: "application" or "library"
version: 0.1.0               # REQUIRED: Chart version (SemVer 2)
appVersion: "2.1.0"          # OPTIONAL: Version of the app being deployed
kubeVersion: ">= 1.19.0-0"   # OPTIONAL: Supported K8s versions
home: https://easypj.example.com
sources:
  - https://github.com/easypj/easypj
maintainers:
  - name: DevOps Team
    email: devops@easypj.com
keywords:
  - django
  - job-board
dependencies:
  - name: postgresql
    version: "12.x.x"
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    condition: postgresql.enabled
📌
apiVersion: v2

Always v2 for Helm 3. v1 was Helm 2. If you see v1 in the wild, the chart is outdated.

🏷️
version vs appVersion

version = chart version (changes when templates change). appVersion = application version. They're independent.

🔀
type: application/library

application = standard deployable chart. library = reusable template snippets (not directly installable — §3.6).

Chart.yaml — Every Field Explained

FieldRequired?TypeDescription
apiVersionYESstringMust be v2 for Helm 3. v1 was Helm 2.
nameYESstringMust match the directory name. Lowercase + hyphens only.
versionYESsemverMust follow SemVer 2. Increment on every change (§3.5).
kubeVersionNosemver rangeK8s version constraint, e.g. >=1.25.0-0 blocks old clusters.
descriptionNostringSingle-line description shown in helm search.
typeNostringapplication (default, deployable) or library (template-only).
appVersionNostringVersion of the deployed app. Informational only — never affects behavior.
dependenciesNoarraySubchart declarations with version constraints (Part 4).
maintainersNoarrayName + email of chart maintainers.
iconNoURLIcon shown in Artifact Hub. SVG or PNG.
annotationsNomapArbitrary metadata, used by Artifact Hub for categorization.
keywordsNoarraySearch keywords for helm search and Artifact Hub.
⚠️ Common Mistake: Confusing version and appVersion

Beginners often assume version and appVersion must match. They don't. You can release chart version 5.2.0 that still deploys appVersion 1.0.0, if only the templates changed. version tracks the chart; appVersion tracks the app.

3.1b values.yaml — Default Configuration & Documentation

values.yaml is the single source of default configuration — every value that can be customized lives here.

values.yaml for easypj
replicaCount: 2
image:
  repository: easypj/easypj
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent
  tag: "v2.1"
nameOverride: ""
fullnameOverride: ""
serviceAccount:
  create: true
  name: ""
service:
  type: ClusterIP
  port: 80
ingress:
  enabled: false
  hosts:
    - host: easypj.local
      paths: [{ path: /, pathType: Prefix }]
resources: {}
autoscaling:
  enabled: false
  minReplicas: 1
  maxReplicas: 10
  targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 80
postgresql:
  enabled: true
  auth:
    database: easypj_db
    username: easypj_user
    password: changeme
💡 values.yaml as Documentation

Comments in values.yaml serve as self-documentation. A well-commented values.yaml tells users exactly what each setting does and what the valid options are — this becomes a formal best practice in Chapter 4.

3.1c templates/ — The YAML Generation Engine

The templates/ directory is where the rendering happens. Each file is a Go template that Helm renders into Kubernetes YAML. Anything in this directory (except NOTES.txt and files starting with _) gets processed and submitted to Kubernetes.

📄
deployment.yaml

Defines the Deployment — replica count, image, ports, health checks, resource limits, volumes.

🌐
service.yaml

Exposes the app internally (ClusterIP) or externally (NodePort/LoadBalancer).

⚙️
configmap.yaml

Non-sensitive configuration — env vars, app settings, feature flags.

🔐
secret.yaml

Sensitive data — passwords, API keys, TLS certs. Base64-encoded at rest.

🚪
ingress.yaml

External HTTP/HTTPS routing. Usually conditional (if ingress.enabled).

📈
hpa.yaml

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler — auto-scales based on CPU/memory.

📖 Special Template Files
  • NOTES.txt — displayed to the user after install/upgrade. NOT a Kubernetes resource.
  • _helpers.tpl — reusable template functions (Chapter 7). NOT deployed.
  • tests/ — test pod definitions, run via helm test.

3.1d charts/ — Subchart Dependencies

The charts/ directory holds dependent charts — other charts your application needs. For easypj, that's PostgreSQL (database) and Redis (cache). When you declare dependencies in Chart.yaml and run helm dependency update, Helm downloads the dependency charts as .tgz files into charts/. Chart.lock (§3.1f) records exact versions for reproducible builds — full dependency management is Part 4.

3.1e .helmignore — Excluding Files from Packaging

Similar to .gitignore, .helmignore tells Helm which files to exclude when packaging a chart with helm package.

.helmignore
# Patterns to ignore when packaging
.git/
.gitignore
.idea/
*.swp
*.bak
*tmp*
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db
tests/
.github/
.gitlab-ci.yml

3.1f Chart.lock — Reproducible Dependency Builds

Chart.lock is automatically generated by helm dependency update. It records the exact versions and digests of all dependency charts — critical for reproducible deployments.

⚠️ Never Delete Chart.lock

Deleting Chart.lock means helm dependency update re-resolves versions from scratch, potentially pulling different ones. Always commit Chart.lock to Git — "same versions, every time" instead of "it worked yesterday, broken today."

3.2 Creating Your First Chart — helm create

create and explore your first chart
# Create a new chart with default scaffolding
helm create my-first-chart

# See what was created
tree my-first-chart/

# Customize for easypj:
helm create easypj-chart
vim easypj-chart/Chart.yaml
vim easypj-chart/values.yaml

# Verify the chart is valid
helm lint easypj-chart/

# See what YAML the chart would generate
helm template easypj-chart/

# Install it!
helm install easypj-dev ./easypj-chart --namespace dev --create-namespace
💡 helm create is Your Exam Friend

On the certification exam, always use helm create to scaffold charts. It gives you a working template immediately. Never start from an empty directory — it wastes precious exam time.

Bonus: helm show — Inspecting Charts Without Installing

helm show lets you peek inside any chart — local or from a repository — without installing it.

helm show — chart inspection
# Show chart metadata (Chart.yaml content)
helm show chart ./easypj-chart
helm show chart bitnami/nginx

# Show the chart's README
helm show readme bitnami/postgresql

# Show all values with documentation — prints the entire values.yaml with comments
helm show values bitnami/postgresql

# Show everything (chart info + readme + values)
helm show all bitnami/nginx

Bonus: helm package — Distributing Your Chart

When you're ready to share a chart, helm package creates a versioned .tgz archive — this is what gets pushed to chart repositories.

packaging and verifying charts
# Package a chart (creates easypj-0.1.0.tgz)
helm package ./easypj-chart

# Package to a specific destination
helm package ./easypj-chart -d ./releases/

# Sign a chart package (requires GPG key)
helm package ./easypj-chart --sign --key 'devops@easypj.com'

# Verify a signed chart
helm verify easypj-0.1.0.tgz

# Lint before packaging (good CI practice)
helm lint ./easypj-chart && helm package ./easypj-chart
1
Lint

helm lint ./chart — validate syntax and best practices.

2
Template

helm template ./chart --debug — render YAML locally to verify output.

3
Package

helm package ./chart — create the .tgz archive.

4
Push

helm push ./chart-0.1.0.tgz oci://registry.example.com/charts — distribute to a registry.

3.3 Chart Structure for easypj — Step by Step Walkthrough

Let's walk through creating a production-ready chart for easypj, our Django job board application. It needs: a Django web deployment, PostgreSQL, a Redis cache, and optional ingress.

1
Scaffold

helm create easypj-chart — creates the standard skeleton.

2
Metadata

Set name: easypj, appVersion: "2.1.0", add PostgreSQL/Redis dependencies in Chart.yaml.

3
Configure

Set image, service port 8000, enable ingress with host jobs.example.com in values.yaml.

4
Templates

Write deployment.yaml with Django/Gunicorn settings, env vars sourced from ConfigMap/Secret.

5
Config

configmap.yaml for DEBUG/DB_HOST. secret.yaml for SECRET_KEY/DB_PASSWORD.

6
Dependencies

helm dependency update downloads PostgreSQL + Redis into charts/.

7
Deploy

helm lint → helm template --debug → helm install easypj-dev ./easypj-chart -n dev --create-namespace

3.5 Semantic Versioning for Charts (SemVer 2)

SemVer: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
  MAJOR . MINOR . PATCH          Example:  2  .  1  .  5
    │       │       │
    │       │       └── PATCH: backward-compatible bug fixes
    │       │            fix typo in NOTES.txt → 2.1.5 → 2.1.6
    │       │            update default resource limits → 2.1.6
    │       │
    │       └── MINOR: backward-compatible new features
    │            add new template (hpa.yaml) → 2.1.5 → 2.2.0
    │            add new values section → 2.2.0
    │
    └── MAJOR: incompatible / breaking changes
         rename a values key → 2.1.5 → 3.0.0
         remove a template → 3.0.0

  🔑 If users must change their values.yaml to upgrade, it's MAJOR.
1
SemVer for Charts

Increment MAJOR for breaking template changes, MINOR for new backward-compatible features, PATCH for bug fixes. appVersion tracks the application independently.

2
kubeVersion Constraints

kubeVersion: ">=1.25.0-0" prevents installation on unsupported clusters. The -0 suffix allows pre-release versions.

3
Deprecation Strategy

Set deprecated: true in Chart.yaml when a chart is no longer maintained. Users see a warning on install. Remove the chart entirely after a deprecation period.

3.6 Chart Types — Application vs Library Charts

📦 Application Chart

Default chart type. Deployable — helm install myapp ./chart WORKS. Contains complete Kubernetes resources.

Chart.yaml: type: application

templates/
  deployment.yaml  ✅ Creates resources
  service.yaml     ✅ Creates resources
  NOTES.txt        ✅ Post-install message
📚 Library Chart

NOT deployable directly — helm install mylib ./chart FAILS with "library charts are not installable." Contains only named templates (define blocks), imported by other charts via dependencies.

Chart.yaml: type: library

templates/
  _labels.tpl    {{ define "easypj.labels" }}
  _security.tpl  {{ define "easypj.security" }}
  # NO deployment.yaml, service.yaml, etc.
⚠️ Library Chart Gotcha

Running helm install on a library chart produces an error. Library charts are imported with {{ include "name" . }} from another chart's templates — they cannot be installed standalone. Used for shared helpers/patterns across a family of related charts.

Under the Hood — what helm package actually produces, byte by byte

"helm package creates a chart archive" hides a precise transformation: your entire chart directory becomes one gzipped tarball (.tgz), with .helmignore patterns applied before anything is bundled.

   CHART DIRECTORY → PACKAGE → ARCHIVE → REPOSITORY → INSTALL
   ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

   easypj/                       helm package
   ├── Chart.yaml                ./easypj
   ├── values.yaml          →    easypj-0.1.0.tgz
   ├── templates/                 (gzipped tar archive)
   │   ├── deployment.yaml
   │   └── service.yaml
   └── charts/
       └── postgresql-12.x.tgz

   The .tgz archive contains:
   1. All template files (templates/)
   2. Chart.yaml (metadata)
   3. values.yaml (defaults)
   4. charts/ (bundled dependencies)
   5. .helmignore patterns applied — matching files never enter the archive
   6. OPTIONAL: .prov (provenance signature file, from --sign)
PropertyWhat it means in practice
ImmutableOnce published, a version should never change — republishing the same version with different content is a well-known way to break caches and confuse users
SemVer 2 versionedMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (§3.5) — repositories index charts by this exact string
SignableGPG-signed via --sign --key; verified later with helm verify
OCI-native storageOCI registries (Helm 3.8+) store charts as OCI artifacts, not literal .tgz files on disk — same registry, same auth as container images
🔑 The archive IS the chart, frozen. Once you understand that helm install bitnami/postgresql is really "download a specific immutable .tgz, then run the exact same render pipeline as a local chart," a huge amount of "how do remote charts even work" confusion disappears — there's no special remote-only code path, just a download step in front of the same local pipeline.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Chart.yaml has exactly three required fields — apiVersion (always v2), name (must match the directory), and version (SemVer). Everything else is optional metadata.
  • templates/ isn't purely "resources to deploy" — NOTES.txt and _helpers.tpl live there but are never submitted to Kubernetes.
  • Always scaffold with helm create, then delete what you don't need — never start from an empty directory.
  • Chart naming rules are strict: lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens only, and the name in Chart.yaml must exactly match the chart's directory name.
  • A chart should deploy sensible defaults — helm install myapp ./chart with no extra flags should produce a working application. Overrides are for customization, not for fixing broken defaults.
  • One chart, one application — bundle immediate dependencies (PostgreSQL, Redis) as subcharts, not unrelated services.
  • Application vs Library is a one-line distinction with a hard consequence: only application charts are installable; library charts exist purely to be imported.
  • Chart.lock should always be committed to Git — it's the difference between "same versions every time" and "it worked yesterday, broken today."
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Chart name ≠ directory name. A mismatch between name: in Chart.yaml and the actual folder name causes silent packaging/publishing issues down the line — keep them identical always.
  • Forgetting to bump version after a template change. Helm won't warn you — an unchanged version republished with different content breaks the "immutable archive" assumption every chart repository relies on.
  • Invalid SemVer strings. version: 1.0 (missing PATCH) or version: v1.0.0 (leading "v") are both invalid — Helm requires strict MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, no prefix.
  • Assuming appVersion affects behavior. It's purely informational/cosmetic — changing it alone does not change what gets deployed. Only the actual image.tag value does that.
  • Treating NOTES.txt/_helpers.tpl as deployed resources. They're processed by the template engine but never submitted to Kubernetes — a common source of "why isn't this showing up as a resource" confusion.
  • Trying to helm install a library chart. It will fail outright — library charts (§3.6) only work when included from another chart's templates.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Never type a chart from scratch. helm create then delete unneeded files — always faster than typing boilerplate under time pressure.
  • helm lint --strict before every package/install — catches naming, syntax, and best-practice violations in one command.
  • helm show values <chart> beats guessing. When installing an unfamiliar chart (e.g. Bitnami PostgreSQL), print its full commented values.yaml first instead of trial-and-error --set flags.
  • Recall the required-field mnemonic: "A-N-V" — ApiVersion, Name, Version. Everything else in Chart.yaml is optional.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 3)

the full chart lifecycle: create → inspect → package 
# Scaffold a new chart
helm create easypj-chart

# Validate before you do anything else
helm lint easypj-chart/
helm lint --strict easypj-chart/

# Preview the rendered YAML, no cluster needed
helm template easypj-chart/ --debug

# Inspect any chart (local or remote) without installing
helm show chart bitnami/postgresql
helm show values bitnami/postgresql
helm show readme bitnami/postgresql
helm show all bitnami/postgresql

# Package for distribution
helm package ./easypj-chart
helm package ./easypj-chart -d ./releases/
helm package ./easypj-chart --sign --key 'devops@easypj.com'
helm verify easypj-0.1.0.tgz

# Push to an OCI registry
helm push easypj-0.1.0.tgz oci://registry.example.com/charts

🧠 Chapter 3 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of chart anatomy — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What command creates a new Helm chart with default scaffolding?
Show Answer
Answer

helm create <chart-name>. Generates a complete chart with Chart.yaml, values.yaml, templates/, and helper files.

Explanation

The scaffolded chart deploys nginx by default. You customize Chart.yaml, values.yaml, and the templates for your own application (easypj, in this guide).

Q2
What's the difference between version and appVersion in Chart.yaml?
Show Answer
Answer

version = chart version (templates/metadata), REQUIRED. appVersion = application version (the software being deployed), optional. They're completely independent.

Explanation

version tracks changes to the chart itself (template logic, structure); appVersion tracks the container image version. A chart bump doesn't require an app bump, and vice versa.

Q3
What is the purpose of the charts/ directory?
Show Answer
Answer

It holds dependency charts (subcharts), populated by helm dependency update based on the dependencies: list in Chart.yaml.

Explanation

Chart.lock then pins the exact resolved versions, so a later helm dependency build can reproduce charts/ without hitting the network again.

Q4
Which file's rendered content is displayed to the user after a successful helm install?
Show Answer
Answer

templates/NOTES.txt. It is NOT a Kubernetes resource — it's rendered text shown directly to the user with post-install instructions.

Explanation

NOTES.txt goes through the exact same Go-template rendering as every other file in templates/ (so {{ .Release.Name }} etc. all work), but its output is displayed, never applied to the cluster.

Q5
What SemVer bump is required for renaming a key in values.yaml, and why?
Show Answer
Answer

MAJOR (e.g. 2.1.5 → 3.0.0). Renaming a values key breaks any existing user's values.yaml that still references the old key — a breaking change by definition.

Explanation

The general rule from §3.5: if users must edit their own values.yaml to keep working after upgrading the chart, that's always a MAJOR bump, no exceptions.

Q6
What's the practical difference between an Application chart and a Library chart?
Show Answer
Answer

Application charts are deployable (helm install works and creates resources). Library charts are NOT deployable — they only provide reusable named templates, imported by other charts.

Explanation

Attempting helm install on a library chart fails with an explicit "library charts are not installable" error — this is by design, not a bug.

Q7
What command validates a chart WITHOUT installing it?
Show Answer
Answer

helm lint <chart-path> — checks Chart.yaml syntax, template rendering, and best practices. Add --strict for stricter, exam-level validation.

Explanation

helm lint catches structural problems before you ever touch a cluster — it should be the very first command run against any chart you've just edited.

Q8
What is the purpose of .helmignore?
Show Answer
Answer

It excludes files from the packaged chart archive (helm package), working exactly like .gitignore. Common entries: .git/, *.swp, CI config files.

Explanation

Excluded files never affect chart *logic* — helm install still works identically. It only controls what physically ends up inside the .tgz.

Q9
Should Chart.lock be committed to version control? Why or why not?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes, always. It pins exact dependency versions and digests for reproducible builds. Without it, helm dependency update may resolve to different versions on a later run.

Explanation

helm dependency build reads the lock file with no network call (fast, reproducible); helm dependency update regenerates the lock file from scratch (slower, can drift).

Q10
After running helm create mychart, which three files do you typically edit first?
Show Answer
Answer

(1) Chart.yaml — set your metadata. (2) values.yaml — set your defaults. (3) templates/deployment.yaml — customize for your actual application.

Explanation

This is the fastest path from generic scaffold to a working, app-specific chart — everything else in the scaffold (service.yaml, hpa.yaml, etc.) is usually close enough to reuse as-is initially.

⚙️ Chapter 3 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

A broken or incomplete chart, and you produce the fix with real commands.

Q1
helm install on your freshly-created chart fails immediately with a chart-loading error, before anything is even submitted to Kubernetes. What do you run first to isolate the cause?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm lint --strict ./easypj-chart
helm template ./easypj-chart --debug
Explanation

Both commands are entirely client-side — no cluster needed — so they isolate whether the problem is in the chart itself (YAML syntax, template logic) before you even consider a cluster-side cause.

Q2
You renamed your chart's folder from easypj-chart to easypj but forgot to update Chart.yaml. What breaks, and what fixes it?
Show Answer
Answer

Packaging/publishing can silently misbehave since the chart name: in Chart.yaml no longer matches the directory name. Fix: edit name: easypj in Chart.yaml to match the new folder exactly.

Explanation

Helm doesn't hard-fail loudly on every mismatch scenario — this is exactly the kind of "silent gotcha" §3.1a warns about, and worth checking any time you rename a chart directory.

Q3
A teammate wants to see exactly what a Bitnami PostgreSQL chart's default configuration looks like before writing any override values. One command?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm show values bitnami/postgresql
Explanation

This prints the chart's complete values.yaml with its original comments — the fastest way to discover every configurable key without installing anything.

Q4
You made a template-only fix (no values.yaml changes) to easypj-chart, currently at version 1.3.2. What should the new version be?
Show Answer
Answer

1.3.3 — a PATCH bump, since it's a backward-compatible bug fix with no new features and no breaking changes.

Explanation

Reserve MINOR for new backward-compatible capability (a new optional template or values key) and MAJOR only when existing users' values.yaml would need to change.

Q5
Someone accidentally runs helm install mylib ./mylib-chart where mylib-chart is type: library. What happens, and what's the correct way to use that chart?
Show Answer
Answer

The install fails outright — library charts are not installable by design. The correct usage is declaring it as a dependencies: entry in another (application) chart's Chart.yaml, then calling its templates via {{ include "mylib.someHelper" . }}.

Explanation

Library charts exist purely to share template logic across a family of charts — think of them as an imported function library, never a standalone deployable unit.

Q6
Your CI pipeline needs to package easypj-chart and place the resulting archive into a dedicated ./releases/ folder, not the current directory. One command?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm package ./easypj-chart -d ./releases/
Explanation

The -d/--destination flag controls where the .tgz lands — useful in CI to keep build artifacts separate from source.

Q7
A chart repository maintainer accidentally re-published version 2.0.0 with different (fixed) content after a bug was found. What principle did they violate, and what's the correct fix instead?
Show Answer
Answer

They violated chart immutability — a published version should never change. The correct fix is publishing a new version, e.g. 2.0.1, with the fix.

Explanation

Immutability is what lets Chart.lock and pinned dependency versions actually guarantee reproducibility — silently mutating a published version breaks that guarantee for everyone who already pulled it.

Q8
You want to confirm a downloaded chart archive hasn't been tampered with, and it was published with a GPG signature. Which command?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm verify easypj-0.1.0.tgz
Explanation

helm verify checks the archive against its accompanying .prov provenance file, which was produced when the maintainer packaged it with --sign --key.

Q9
Your chart's charts/ directory is missing entirely after a fresh git clone, even though Chart.yaml declares PostgreSQL and Redis dependencies. Is this a bug? What do you run?
Show Answer
Answer

Not a bug — downloaded subchart .tgz files are typically not committed to Git. Run:

bash
helm dependency build ./easypj-chart
Explanation

Since Chart.lock IS committed, dependency build can re-download the exact pinned versions with no network resolution step, restoring charts/ deterministically.

Q10
Design the minimal command sequence to go from a fresh helm create scaffold to a signed, verified, packaged easypj chart ready for distribution.
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm create easypj-chart
# ...edit Chart.yaml, values.yaml, templates/...
helm lint --strict ./easypj-chart
helm template ./easypj-chart --debug
helm package ./easypj-chart --sign --key 'devops@easypj.com'
helm verify easypj-0.1.0.tgz
Explanation

This is the full four-stage cycle from Under the Hood's own process-steps: lint → template → package → push, with signing/verification layered on for distribution safety.

🔬 Practice Drill 3.1 — Scaffold and Rename a Chart Correctly

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Create a new chart called my-first-chart, then rename its directory to easypj-chart and correctly update every field that referenced the old name so nothing is silently broken.

Hint: The directory name and Chart.yaml's name: field must always match exactly.
View Solution
bash
helm create my-first-chart
mv my-first-chart easypj-chart
sed -i 's/^name: my-first-chart/name: easypj-chart/' easypj-chart/Chart.yaml
helm lint easypj-chart/

Check yourself: helm lint should report no warnings about a name mismatch. If you only renamed the folder and skipped Chart.yaml, this drill just reproduced Scenario Drill Q2's exact bug.

🔬 Practice Drill 3.2 — Inspect Three Charts Without Installing Any

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Using only helm show, find the default replica count, the default service type, and whether ingress is enabled by default in the Bitnami nginx chart — without running helm install.

Hint: One command shows everything you need — you're just reading its output carefully.
View Solution
bash
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo update
helm show values bitnami/nginx | less

Check yourself: you should be able to answer all three questions from the printed values.yaml alone — no install, no cluster touched.

🔬 Practice Drill 3.3 — Build a Minimal easypj Chart.yaml from Scratch

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Without looking back at §3.1a, write a valid Chart.yaml for easypj from memory: the 3 required fields, plus description, type, and appVersion.

Hint: Remember the "A-N-V" mnemonic from Speed Tips — apiVersion, Name, Version.
View Solution
Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: easypj-chart
version: 0.1.0
description: A Helm chart for the easypj Django job board application
type: application
appVersion: "2.1.0"

Check yourself: helm lint against a chart using this Chart.yaml should pass with zero errors related to metadata — if it complains about a missing required field, you dropped one of apiVersion/name/version.

🔬 Practice Drill 3.4 — Package, Sign, and Verify

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Take a chart you scaffolded earlier, package it into a versioned archive, and (conceptually, if you don't have a real GPG key handy) walk through the exact commands you'd run to sign and then verify it.

Hint: Package with --sign --key, verify with a separate command entirely.
View Solution
bash
helm package ./easypj-chart --sign --key 'devops@easypj.com'
# produces: easypj-chart-0.1.0.tgz  +  easypj-chart-0.1.0.tgz.prov

helm verify easypj-chart-0.1.0.tgz

Check yourself: notice that signing produces a companion .prov file alongside the .tgz — that's what helm verify actually checks against, not some hidden metadata inside the archive itself.

🔬 Practice Drill 3.5 — Application vs Library, Decide and Justify

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Your team wants to share a set of common labels/annotations logic across FIVE different application charts (easypj, and four others). Should this shared logic be its own application chart or a library chart? Justify in two sentences.

Hint: Ask: does this thing ever get installed on its own?
View Solution

Sample answer: "It should be a library chart, because it's never meant to be deployed standalone — it only exists to be imported by other charts via {{ include }}. Making it an application chart would be misleading (implying it's independently installable) and wouldn't actually prevent someone from accidentally running helm install on it."

Check yourself: the deciding question is always "does this get installed on its own, ever?" — if no, it's a library chart, full stop.

📌 Chapter 3 Visual Summary — the six files that make a chart
  📄 Chart.yaml         ⚙️ values.yaml          🔧 templates/
  ┌──────────────┐      ┌──────────────┐       ┌──────────────────┐
  │ apiVersion: v2│      │ replicaCount  │       │ deployment.yaml   │
  │ name (=dir!)  │      │ image: {...}  │       │ service.yaml      │
  │ version SemVer│      │ service: {...}│       │ NOTES.txt (not a  │
  │ appVersion    │      │ (self-docs    │       │  K8s resource!)   │
  │ (informational)│     │  via comments)│       │ _helpers.tpl      │
  └──────────────┘      └──────────────┘       └──────────────────┘
        3 REQUIRED             DEFAULTS               THE ENGINE

  📦 charts/            🔒 Chart.lock            🚫 .helmignore
  ┌──────────────┐      ┌──────────────┐       ┌──────────────────┐
  │ postgresql.tgz│      │ exact pinned  │       │ .git/  *.swp      │
  │ redis.tgz     │      │ dep versions  │       │ excluded from     │
  │ (subcharts)   │      │ COMMIT TO GIT │       │ helm package      │
  └──────────────┘      └──────────────┘       └──────────────────┘
    DEPENDENCIES         REPRODUCIBILITY          PACKAGING ONLY
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   helm create → edit these 6 pieces → helm lint → helm package →
   a versioned, immutable .tgz ready for a repository or OCI registry

In words: A chart is six kinds of files working together, not one monolithic thing. Chart.yaml is identity (only 3 fields are actually required); values.yaml is the single source of configurable defaults; templates/ is the Go-template engine that turns those values into real Kubernetes YAML — plus two special files, NOTES.txt and _helpers.tpl, that live there but are never deployed as resources.

charts/ and Chart.lock exist together for one purpose: reproducible subchart dependencies — the lock file is what lets helm dependency build restore charts/ deterministically with zero network resolution. .helmignore is the odd one out, purely cosmetic — it only trims what physically enters the packaged archive, never affects chart behavior.

The takeaway: helm create gives you all six pieces at once as a working scaffold. Everything from here forward — Chapter 4's values patterns, Chapter 6's templating, Part 4's dependencies — is going deeper into one of these six files, not introducing a seventh.

Chapter 4 · Values & Configuration — The Control Panel of Helm

Values are how you tell Helm what to deploy. Without values, every installation would be identical — same image, same replica count, same config. Values are what make a chart reusable across environments, teams, and use cases. This chapter covers the complete values system: defaults, overrides, precedence rules, multiple files, and schema validation — the mechanism behind "one chart, many releases" from Chapter 1.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~1.5 hours ⚙️ Config 🐍 easypj / jobpost 🎯 Chart Creation & Anatomy

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Master values.yaml as the single source of default configuration
  • ✅ Override values with --set, --values, --set-file, and --set-json
  • ✅ Understand the complete value precedence chain — what overrides what, and why
  • ✅ Manage environment-specific configurations with multiple values files
  • ✅ Validate values with JSON Schema (values.schema.json)
  • ✅ Build real dev, staging, and prod configurations for easypj
🎓 Helm Certification Relevance
Chart Creation & Anatomy CORE DOMAIN
🎯 The Exam Tests the Separation, Not Just the Syntax

When a task says "change the replica count," the correct move is never editing templates/deployment.yaml — it's changing a value. Internalize three things now:

  • Templates are a function of values — f(values) = Kubernetes YAML. Change the input, never the function, to reconfigure a deployment.
  • The precedence chain is memorizable and gets tested directly — --set beats -f files, and among multiple -f files, the last one wins.
  • Values merge deep, not shallow — overriding one nested key preserves its siblings, UNLESS you replace the entire parent object at once.
