4.1 values.yaml — The Single Source of Configuration

values.yaml is the default configuration file in every Helm chart. It defines sensible defaults so that helm install myapp ./chart works without any additional flags. Every template accesses these values through the .Values object.

How Values Flow Into Templates
  ┌──────────────────┐
  │  values.yaml     │  ← Chart defaults (lowest priority)
  │  ─────────────   │
  │  replicaCount: 2 │
  │  image.tag: v2.1 │
  │  service.port: 80│
  └────────┬─────────┘
           │
           ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────────────┐
  │  Template Engine │────▶│  Rendered YAML          │
  │  {{ .Values.     │     │  apiVersion: apps/v1    │
  │    replicaCount  │     │  kind: Deployment       │
  │  }}              │     │  spec:                  │
  │  {{ .Values.     │     │    replicas: 2          │  ← From values.yaml
  │    image.tag     │     │    template: {spec: ...}│
  │  }}              │     │      containers:        │
  │                  │     │      - image: easypj:v2.1│  ← From values.yaml
  └──────────────────┘     └─────────────────────────┘
📖 Values Are NOT Secrets

values.yaml is plain text — never put passwords or API keys here. Use Kubernetes Secrets, the helm-secrets plugin (Mozilla SOPS), or an External Secrets Operator for sensitive data. Values get stored in release history as Secrets, but the source values.yaml itself should never contain actual secrets.

4.2 Overriding Values — --set, --values, --set-file

Helm provides four ways to override default values, each suited to a different use case:

MethodSyntaxBest ForExample
--set--set key=valueQuick overrides, CI/CD--set image.tag=v3.0
--values / -f-f file.yamlEnvironment configs-f values-prod.yaml
--set-file--set-file key=pathLarge config files--set-file config=app.conf
--set-string--set-string key=valForce string type--set-string port="80"
overriding values — examples
# --set: quick overrides (good for CI/CD pipelines)
helm install easypj ./chart --set image.tag=v3.0 --set replicaCount=5

# --set for nested values (dot notation)
helm install easypj ./chart --set service.port=8080 --set ingress.enabled=true

# -f: use a values file
helm install easypj-prod ./chart -f values-prod.yaml

# Multiple -f flags (later files override earlier ones)
helm install easypj ./chart -f values-base.yaml -f values-prod.yaml

# Combine --set and -f (--set wins for conflicting keys)
helm install easypj ./chart -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=hotfix

# --set-string: force string (prevents YAML type coercion)
helm install easypj ./chart --set-string appVersion="2.0"
⚠️ Gotcha: --set Type Coercion

--set replicaCount=5 sets it as a number. --set-string replicaCount="5" sets it as a string. If a template expects a number but gets a string, rendering can fail. Use --set-string only when you explicitly need a string.

--set-json — Setting Complex Values (Helm 3.7+)

Need to set an entire array or nested object from the command line? --set-json accepts raw JSON — for complex structures that are awkward with dot notation.

--set-json examples
# Set an array (impossible with plain --set)
helm install easypj ./chart \
  --set-json 'ingress.hosts=[{"host":"easypj.local","paths":[{"path":"/","pathType":"Prefix"}]}]'

# Set resource limits as a complex object
helm install easypj ./chart \
  --set-json 'resources={"limits":{"cpu":"500m","memory":"256Mi"},"requests":{"cpu":"100m","memory":"128Mi"}}'

# Set an array of environment variables
helm install easypj ./chart \
  --set-json 'env=[{"name":"DEBUG","value":"false"},{"name":"LOG_LEVEL","value":"info"}]'

--set: When to Use, and When to Avoid

✅ Use --set for
  • Quick overrides during development
  • CI/CD pipelines (injecting a build tag)
  • Secrets injection from an environment variable
  • One-off testing
  • Simple scalar values
❌ Avoid --set for
  • Complex nested structures
  • Production deployments (not reproducible — nothing to review in a diff)
  • Multiple values at once (hard to read/audit)
  • Lists and arrays (use --set-json instead)
  • Anything you'd want tracked in version control

Troubleshooting Values — Common Issues

🔍
"nil pointer evaluating interface"

You referenced a nested value that doesn't exist. Check the parent key exists in values.yaml, or use {{ .Values.x | default "fallback" }} as a safety net.

🔍
Wrong type error

Template expects an integer but got a string. Use --set (not --set-string) for numbers, or add explicit conversion: {{ int .Values.replicaCount }}.

🔍
Values not taking effect

Check precedence — are you using --reuse-values on an upgrade? Old --set values can outlive new defaults. Use helm get values <release> --all to see what's actually applied.

🔍
Schema validation fails

Values don't match values.schema.json. Run helm lint to see validation errors — check required fields, types, and enum values.

4.3 Value Precedence — What Overrides What

One of the most exam-relevant concepts in this guide. When multiple value sources conflict, Helm uses a strict precedence chain:

Value Precedence — Highest to Lowest Priority
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  VALUE PRECEDENCE (Highest → Lowest Priority)                │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  🔴 HIGHEST — User-supplied --set values              │   │
  │  │  helm install easypj ./chart --set image.tag=v3.0     │   │
  │  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
  │  │  🟠 --set-file / --set-string                         │   │
  │  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
  │  │  🟡 User-supplied -f values files (LAST FILE WINS)    │   │
  │  │  -f base.yaml -f prod.yaml  → prod.yaml overrides     │   │
  │  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
  │  │  🟢 Parent chart's values (for subcharts)             │   │
  │  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
  │  │  🔵 This chart's own values.yaml (built-in defaults)  │   │
  │  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
  │  │  ⚪ LOWEST — a subchart's own values.yaml              │   │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │  🔑 KEY RULE: --set always beats -f files.                  │
  │  🔑 KEY RULE: Multiple -f: LAST file wins.                  │
  │  🔑 KEY RULE: A user's -f file outranks a PARENT chart's    │
  │     own values — easy to get backwards, verify vs docs.     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
precedence in action
# values.yaml has image.tag: "v2.0"
# values-prod.yaml has image.tag: "v2.1"

# What image tag is deployed?
helm install easypj ./chart -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=v3.0
# Answer: v3.0 (--set wins over everything)

helm install easypj ./chart -f values-prod.yaml
# Answer: v2.1 (-f overrides values.yaml)

helm install easypj ./chart
# Answer: v2.0 (just the chart default)

4.4 Multiple Values Files — Environment-Specific Config

The real power of Helm values is using multiple files for different environments. The same chart can deploy to dev, staging, and production with drastically different configurations — no template changes required.

Multi-Environment Values Strategy
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ONE CHART → THREE ENVIRONMENTS                            │
  │  easypj-chart/                                              │
  │  ├── values.yaml          ← BASE (common defaults)          │
  │  │   replicaCount: 2                                        │
  │  │   image.repository: easypj/easypj                        │
  │  │                                                          │
  │  ├── values-dev.yaml      ← DEV OVERRIDE                    │
  │  │   replicaCount: 1         (minimal resources)             │
  │  │   image.tag: latest                                       │
  │  │   ingress.enabled: false                                  │
  │  │                                                          │
  │  ├── values-staging.yaml  ← STAGING OVERRIDE                │
  │  │   replicaCount: 2         (like prod, not public)         │
  │  │   image.tag: v2.1-rc1                                     │
  │  │                                                          │
  │  └── values-prod.yaml     ← PRODUCTION OVERRIDE             │
  │      replicaCount: 5         (high availability)             │
  │      image.tag: v2.0                                         │
  │      ingress.enabled: true                                   │
  │      resources: {limits: {cpu: 1, memory: 512Mi}}            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  DEPLOY:
  helm install easypj-dev  ./chart -f values-dev.yaml -n dev
  helm install easypj-stg  ./chart -f values-staging.yaml -n staging
  helm install easypj-prod ./chart -f values-prod.yaml -n production

4.5 Schema Validation — values.schema.json

Helm 3 supports JSON Schema validation for values. Create a values.schema.json file in the chart root, and Helm validates user-supplied values against it before installing or upgrading — catching configuration errors early, before anything touches the cluster.

values.schema.json — basic constraints
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["replicaCount", "image"],
  "properties": {
    "replicaCount": {
      "type": "integer",
      "minimum": 1,
      "maximum": 50,
      "description": "Number of application replicas"
    },
    "image": {
      "type": "object",
      "required": ["repository", "tag"],
      "properties": {
        "repository": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 },
        "tag": { "type": "string", "pattern": "^v?\\d+\\.\\d+" },
        "pullPolicy": { "type": "string", "enum": ["Always", "IfNotPresent", "Never"] }
      }
    },
    "service": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "type": { "enum": ["ClusterIP", "NodePort", "LoadBalancer"] },
        "port": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 65535 }
      }
    }
  }
}

Conditional Validation

JSON Schema also supports if/then conditional rules — useful when one field's requirement depends on another's value:

values.schema.json — conditional rule
{
  "properties": {
    "ingress": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "enabled": {"type": "boolean"},
        "tls": {"type": "boolean"},
        "host": {"type": "string"}
      },
      "allOf": [{
        "if": { "properties": {"tls": {"const": true}} },
        "then": { "required": ["host"] }
      }]
    }
  }
}
// If tls is enabled, host MUST be provided
💡 Schema Validation on the Exam

Schema validation may appear as a task: "Add a values.schema.json that requires replicaCount to be between 1 and 10." Know the basic JSON Schema vocabulary: type, required, properties, minimum/maximum, enum, pattern.

4.6 easypj: dev vs staging vs prod Values

Real values files for our Django job board, put together:

🛠️
values-dev.yaml

replicaCount: 1
image.tag: latest
ingress.enabled: false
debug: true
Single replica, latest code, no ingress — fast iteration.

🧪
values-staging.yaml

replicaCount: 2
image.tag: v2.1-rc1
ingress.enabled: true
debug: false
Mirrors production shape, tests release candidates.

🏭
values-prod.yaml

replicaCount: 5
image.tag: v2.0
ingress.enabled: true
autoscaling.enabled: true
HA, stable version, auto-scaling.

deploying easypj to all three environments
# Deploy to all environments with appropriate values
helm install easypj-dev  ./easypj-chart -f values-dev.yaml -n dev --create-namespace
helm install easypj-stg  ./easypj-chart -f values-staging.yaml -n staging --create-namespace
helm install easypj-prod ./easypj-chart -f values-prod.yaml -n production --create-namespace

# Verify each deployment
helm list -n dev
helm list -n staging
helm list -n production

# Check what values are actually being used
helm get values easypj-prod -n production
Under the Hood — deep merge mechanics, the values/templates contract, and subchart scoping

Three mechanisms make the values system work the way it does. Understanding all three prevents the majority of "why didn't my override take effect" confusion.

① Deep Merge vs Shallow Replace

When you provide values from multiple sources, Helm doesn't just overwrite — it performs a deep merge.

  VALUES.YAML (base):              OVERRIDE YAML (-f file):        MERGED RESULT:
  ┌─────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────┐
  │ image:              │         │ image:              │         │ image:              │
  │   repository: easypj│    +    │   tag: v3.0         │    =    │   repository: easypj│
  │   tag: v2.1         │         │   pullPolicy: Always│         │   tag: v3.0         │
  │   pullPolicy: IfNot..│        └─────────────────────┘         │   pullPolicy: Always│
  └─────────────────────┘                                         └─────────────────────┘

  🔑 Deep Merge: nested keys are merged, not replaced.
     The override file only specified 'tag' and 'pullPolicy' — 'repository' was
     preserved automatically from the base.

  ⚠️ BUT: overriding an ENTIRE parent key replaces ALL its children:
  --set 'image={"repository":"newrepo","tag":"v4.0"}'
  This REPLACES the whole 'image' object — 'pullPolicy' is lost!
debugging value merging
# See what values were ACTUALLY used (after all merging)
helm get values easypj --all

# Compare: user-supplied only vs all values
helm get values easypj         # just what the user provided
helm get values easypj --all   # user values merged with chart defaults

# See the rendered templates with values
helm template ./chart --debug 2>&1 | head -100

# Install with --dry-run to preview rendered manifests
helm install test ./chart --dry-run --debug | less
🔑 Incomplete override is usually correct, not a bug. If values-prod.yaml sets only image.tag, the other image sub-keys (repository, pullPolicy) come from values.yaml — that's the deep merge working as designed. Only reach for --set-json when you genuinely need to replace an entire object wholesale.
② The Values/Templates Contract

This is arguably the most important conceptual shift in Helm: separating WHAT gets deployed (templates) from HOW it's configured (values). This separation is what makes charts reusable across environments, teams, and organizations.

   THE HELM CONTRACT
   ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
   values.yaml (INPUT)          templates/ (TRANSFORM)       K8s YAML (OUTPUT)
   ─────────────────────        ─────────────────────        ─────────────────
   replicaCount: 3        →     replicas: {{ .Values.  →     replicas: 3
                                  replicaCount }}

   image:                        containers:                   containers:
     repository: easypj    →     - image: {{ .Values.  →      - image: myreg.io/
     tag: v2.0                    image.repository }}:              easypj:v2.0
     pullPolicy: Always           {{ .Values.image.tag }}

   THE KEY INSIGHT: the template is a FUNCTION: f(values) = K8s YAML
   Change the values → change the output → WITHOUT touching templates.
   Same principle as function parameters in ordinary programming.

Why this matters for the exam: when a question asks "change the number of replicas from 2 to 5," never edit templates/deployment.yaml. Use --set replicaCount=5, or edit values.yaml and run helm upgrade. The exam tests this separation constantly — editing a template when you should have changed a value is a common, costly mistake.

③ Subchart Values — The Global Scope Pattern

When a chart has subcharts (dependencies — Part 4), values are scoped. A subchart cannot see its parent's arbitrary top-level values — only its own dedicated section, plus one special exception: global.

   VALUES SCOPE VISUALIZATION
   ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
   Parent Chart (easypj) values.yaml:
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ replicaCount: 3         ← Parent only        │
   │ image: {repository: easypj}  ← Parent only   │
   │                                               │
   │ postgresql:              ← SCOPE GATE        │
   │   enabled: true                              │
   │   auth: {password: secret123}  ← subchart sees this section only │
   │                                               │
   │ global:                  ← GLOBAL SCOPE      │
   │   imageRegistry: my.io   ← ALL subcharts see this │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

   HOW SUBCHARTS ACCESS VALUES (in order):
   1. Subchart's OWN values.yaml (lowest priority)
   2. Parent's dedicated section for that subchart (.Values.postgresql.auth.password)
   3. Parent's global section (.Values.global.imageRegistry)

   KEY: subcharts CANNOT access the parent's arbitrary top-level values —
   the postgresql subchart cannot see .Values.replicaCount, but it CAN
   see .Values.global.imageRegistry.
🔑 Use global for cross-cutting concerns only. Registry URLs, image pull secrets, and common labels are good global candidates because every subchart genuinely needs them. Application-specific settings belong in each subchart's own dedicated section — this scoping is covered fully in Part 4's dependency management chapters.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • values.yaml is the single source of defaults — a chart should install successfully with zero extra flags, using sensible defaults alone.
  • Four override methods, one clear hierarchy — --set (quick, CI-friendly) > -f files (environment configs, last file wins) > --set-file (large blobs) > --set-string (force string type).
  • Precedence is memorizable, not guessable — --set beats everything; among multiple -f files, the last one specified wins.
  • Merging is deep, not shallow — an override only replaces the keys it explicitly sets; everything else survives from the layer below, unless an entire parent object is replaced at once.
  • One chart, three (or more) environments — dev/staging/prod differ only in their values file, never in the chart's templates.
  • Schema validation catches mistakes before the cluster does — a well-written values.schema.json turns a bad deploy into an immediate, readable local error.
  • The template is a pure function of values — f(values) = K8s YAML. Reconfigure by changing the input, never the function.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Incomplete override read as a bug. If values-prod.yaml only sets image.tag, the other image sub-keys survive from values.yaml — this is deep merge working correctly, not data loss.
  • Storing secrets in values.yaml. It's plain text and typically committed to Git. Use Kubernetes Secrets, the helm-secrets plugin, or an External Secrets Operator instead — never a real password in a tracked file.
  • Forgetting --reset-values on upgrade. Without it, a previous --set from install "sticks" across upgrades even if you don't repeat it — surprising anyone expecting the chart's plain defaults to apply.
  • Assuming a subchart can see the parent's arbitrary values. It can't — only its own dedicated section and the special global namespace are visible to it.
  • Confusing which -f file "wins." With multiple -f flags, the LAST file specified takes priority for conflicting keys — order on the command line matters.
  • Editing templates to "just quickly" reconfigure something. If it's a value that changes between environments, it belongs in values.yaml/an override — not hardcoded into a template file.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • helm get values <release> --all beats re-tracing precedence by hand — it shows the FINAL merged values directly. Use it instead of mentally re-deriving what won.
  • Precedence mnemonic: "set beats files, last file wins" — that one phrase covers the two rules the exam tests most.
  • Validate three ways before installing for real: helm lint --strict → helm template -f values.yaml → helm install --dry-run --debug. All three are free — no cluster state changes.
  • Reach for --set-json the moment you need an array or a fully-replaced object — don't fight dot-notation --set syntax past its limits.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 4)

the helm get family — inspecting a release's values & output 
# The full rendered YAML that was actually applied to the cluster
helm get manifest easypj -n prod

# Values used for this release — user-supplied only, by default
helm get values easypj -n prod
helm get values easypj -n prod --all        # + chart defaults, merged
helm get values easypj -n prod --revision 3 # values from a specific past revision

# Hook resources, and the post-install NOTES.txt output
helm get hooks easypj -n prod
helm get notes easypj -n prod

# Everything combined in one call
helm get all easypj -n prod

# Validate before touching the cluster
helm lint --strict ./easypj-chart
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart -f values-prod.yaml
helm install --dry-run --debug easypj ./easypj-chart -f values-prod.yaml
💡 Exam Pattern for helm get

"What was deployed?" → helm get manifest. "What values were used?" → helm get values --all. "Why did the hook fail?" → helm get hooks. "What did the user see after install?" → helm get notes.

🧠 Chapter 4 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (15)

Quick recall of the values system — 15 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What command overrides the image tag to v3.0 during install?
Show Answer
Answer

helm install myapp ./chart --set image.tag=v3.0

Explanation

--set overrides individual values inline. For nested keys, use dot notation: --set service.port=8080.

Q2
What is the value precedence order, highest to lowest?
Show Answer
Answer

1. --set/--set-string → 2. -f files (last wins) → 3. Parent chart values → 4. This chart's values.yaml → 5. Subchart values.yaml (lowest).

Explanation

--set always beats every file-based source — this is the single most tested precedence fact in the chapter.

Q3
You run -f base.yaml -f override.yaml --set image.tag=hotfix. Which image tag is actually used?
Show Answer
Answer

hotfix. --set has the highest priority, ahead of both files regardless of their order.

Explanation

Resolution order here: base.yaml loses to override.yaml (last file wins among the two), and --set beats both files outright.

Q4
Which file provides JSON Schema validation for a chart's values?
Show Answer
Answer

values.schema.json, placed in the chart root. Helm validates user-supplied values against it before install/upgrade.

Explanation

Key JSON Schema keywords worth memorizing: type, required, enum, minimum/maximum, pattern.

Q5
How do you deploy the same chart to dev and prod with different configurations?
Show Answer
Answer

Create values-dev.yaml and values-prod.yaml, then helm install app-dev ./chart -f values-dev.yaml -n dev and helm install app-prod ./chart -f values-prod.yaml -n prod.

Explanation

The templates never change between environments — only which values file is passed via -f.

Q6
Why shouldn't secrets be stored in values.yaml?
Show Answer
Answer

values.yaml is plain text and typically committed to Git. Use Kubernetes Secrets, the helm-secrets plugin (SOPS), or an External Secrets Operator instead.

Explanation

Override sensitive values at deploy time instead, e.g. --set dbPassword="$SECRET" sourced from a CI secret store, never hardcoded in a tracked file.

Q7
What does --set-string do differently from plain --set?
Show Answer
Answer

--set auto-detects the type (number, boolean, string). --set-string forces the value to be a string regardless — use it when a template genuinely expects a string, like "8080" instead of 8080.

Explanation

--set enabled=false yields boolean false; --set-string enabled=false yields the string "false" — which is truthy in most template logic. Mixing these up is a subtle, easy-to-miss bug.

Q8
How do you view the actual, final values used by a deployed release?
Show Answer
Answer

helm get values <release> shows user-supplied values; helm get values <release> --all shows the complete merged set, including chart defaults.

Explanation

This is the fastest way to confirm precedence resolved the way you expected, instead of re-tracing the chain by hand.

Q9
Where should you document what each value in a chart does?
Show Answer
Answer

In values.yaml itself, via YAML comments — they serve as inline, always-in-sync documentation. Complex configurations also belong in the chart's README.md.

Explanation

A well-commented values.yaml is self-documenting — a user should never have to read template source to understand what a value controls.

Q10
How do you validate a chart's values without actually installing anything?
Show Answer
Answer

Three layers, from fastest to closest-to-real: helm lint --strict (structure/syntax), helm template --debug (render output), helm install --dry-run --debug (full simulation).

Explanation

All three are entirely client-side / dry-run — none of them mutate cluster state, so there's no reason to skip straight to a real install.

Q11
You use -f file1.yaml -f file2.yaml and both define replicaCount. What happens?
Show Answer
Answer

The LAST file's value wins — file2.yaml's replicaCount is used. Non-conflicting keys from BOTH files are preserved via deep merge.

Explanation

Multiple -f files merge left to right; each subsequent file only overrides the keys it actually specifies.

Q12
How do you prevent a chart from being installed on Kubernetes versions older than 1.25?
Show Answer
Answer

Set kubeVersion: ">=1.25.0-0" in Chart.yaml. Helm refuses to install on clusters older than that constraint. The -0 suffix allows pre-release Kubernetes versions.

Explanation

This is a chart-load-time check via Chart.yaml, distinct from a runtime check via {{ if semverCompare ">=1.25-0" .Capabilities.KubeVersion.Version }} inside a template.

Q13
What does --set-json do, and when should you reach for it?
Show Answer
Answer

It sets a value from a raw JSON string, preserving complex types (arrays, nested objects) that plain --set dot-notation can't express — e.g. an array of environment variables.

Explanation

Available since Helm 3.7+. Use it any time you need an array, or need to set a fully-structured nested object in one shot.

Q14
You install with --set image.tag=v1.0, then later run helm upgrade app ./chart --reset-values. What image tag ends up deployed?
Show Answer
Answer

The chart's default image.tag from values.yaml — --reset-values discards ALL previously-set values, including the original install-time --set.

Explanation

Without --reset-values (or with --reuse-values), Helm remembers previous --set values across upgrades — a "sticky" behavior that surprises people expecting a clean default.

Q15
How do you share a common image registry across all subcharts without repeating it in each one?
Show Answer
Answer

Use the global key in the parent chart's values.yaml. All subcharts automatically have access to .Values.global with no explicit import needed.

Explanation

The global namespace is the one exception to normal subchart scoping (Under the Hood, §③) — reserved for genuinely cross-cutting concerns like registry URLs, pull secrets, and shared labels.

⚙️ Chapter 4 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

A values conflict or misconfiguration, and you produce the fix with real commands.

Q1
You expected replicaCount: 5 after an upgrade, but the release still shows 2. Diagnose without guessing.
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm get values easypj --all -n production
helm history easypj -n production
Explanation

get values --all shows exactly what's active right now — if it still shows 2, your upgrade command's precedence didn't do what you thought (e.g. a stale sticky --set, or the wrong -f file).

Q2
Your values-prod.yaml sets a brand new image: object with only tag, and after deploying, pullPolicy reverted to its chart default instead of staying as you'd set it via an earlier --set image.pullPolicy=Never. Why?
Show Answer
Answer

Because -f files replace at the level they specify, and here the --set from a PREVIOUS install wasn't reused — without --reuse-values, an upgrade starts from the chart+file merge only, ignoring prior ad-hoc --set flags unless reapplied.

Explanation

This is exactly why production upgrades shouldn't rely on "sticky" --set history — put anything you need preserved into a tracked values file instead.

Q3
A teammate wants to inject a database password from a CI secret store at deploy time, without ever writing it to a file. One command pattern?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm upgrade easypj ./chart --set dbPassword="$DB_PASSWORD" --reuse-values
Explanation

--set from a shell variable never touches disk — the value only exists in the process's argument list and in the resulting release Secret, which is exactly the right amount of exposure for a CI-injected credential.

Q4
You need to set resources.limits as a full nested object AND an array of env vars in one install command. Which flag, and what does the syntax look like?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm install easypj ./chart \
  --set-json 'resources={"limits":{"cpu":"500m","memory":"256Mi"}}' \
  --set-json 'env=[{"name":"DEBUG","value":"false"}]'
Explanation

Both are structures plain --set dot-notation can't cleanly express — --set-json is the correct tool the moment you need an array or a fully-formed nested object.

Q5
Someone accidentally commits a real database password into values-prod.yaml and pushes it to Git. What's the actual security-relevant fact here, beyond "rotate the credential"?
Show Answer
Answer

The credential is now in Git history permanently, even if the file is later edited or deleted — anyone with repo access (or who ever cloned it) can retrieve it from a past commit. Rotating the credential is necessary; rewriting Git history is a separate, much harder cleanup.

Explanation

This is precisely why §4.1's "values are NOT secrets" rule exists — the failure mode isn't hypothetical, it's a permanent, hard-to-undo Git history leak.

Q6
A chart install fails immediately with a schema validation error before anything touches the cluster. What's the fastest way to see exactly which rule failed?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm lint --strict ./easypj-chart -f values-prod.yaml
Explanation

helm lint surfaces schema violations with the specific field and constraint that failed — far faster than trial-and-error against a real helm install.

Q7
Design a values.schema.json rule requiring replicaCount to be an integer between 1 and 10, and Chart.yaml/values fields to be present for image.repository and image.tag.
Show Answer
Answer
json
{
  "required": ["replicaCount", "image"],
  "properties": {
    "replicaCount": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 10},
    "image": {
      "required": ["repository", "tag"],
      "properties": {
        "repository": {"type": "string"},
        "tag": {"type": "string"}
      }
    }
  }
}
Explanation

This exact shape — a top-level required array plus nested required for sub-objects — is the pattern most exam schema-validation tasks expect.

Q8
A subchart's template references .Values.imageRegistry but it's actually set as global.imageRegistry in the parent. What breaks, and what's the one-line fix?
Show Answer
Answer

The reference resolves to nothing (nil), because subcharts don't see arbitrary parent top-level keys. Fix the template to reference .Values.global.imageRegistry instead.

Explanation

This is the Global Scope Pattern from Under the Hood in practice — only a subchart's own section and global are visible; nothing else from the parent leaks through.

Q9
You need a large NGINX config file injected as a value, too long to reasonably paste with --set. Which flag, and what's the syntax?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm install easypj ./chart --set-file nginxConf=./nginx.conf
Explanation

--set-file reads a file's entire contents into a single value, ideal for config blobs that would otherwise need painful shell escaping via plain --set.

Q10
You want production installs to be 100% reproducible from Git — no ad-hoc flags at all. Design the install command.
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm install easypj-prod ./easypj-chart -f values-prod.yaml -n production --create-namespace
Explanation

No --set flags at all — every configurable value lives in a version-controlled values-prod.yaml, so the exact same command always produces the exact same result, and the diff of any future change is fully visible in Git.

🔬 Practice Drill 4.1 — Predict the Precedence Winner

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Without running anything, predict the final image.tag for: helm install easypj ./chart -f values-base.yaml -f values-staging.yaml -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=canary, given each file sets a different tag.

Hint: Only one source in this command can possibly win, regardless of file order.
View Solution

Answer: canary — --set always beats every -f file, no matter how many are chained or in what order. The three files' relative order (base → staging → prod) would only matter if --set weren't present.

Check yourself: if you predicted anything other than "canary," re-read §4.3's precedence diagram — --set sits at the very top, unconditionally.

🔬 Practice Drill 4.2 — Build All Three easypj Environment Files

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Write values-dev.yaml, values-staging.yaml, and values-prod.yaml from scratch for easypj, each differing only in replicaCount, image.tag, and ingress.enabled.

Hint: dev = smallest/loosest, prod = largest/strictest — staging sits between them.
View Solution
3 values files
# values-dev.yaml
replicaCount: 1
image: {tag: latest}
ingress: {enabled: false}

# values-staging.yaml
replicaCount: 2
image: {tag: v2.1-rc1}
ingress: {enabled: true}

# values-prod.yaml
replicaCount: 5
image: {tag: v2.0}
ingress: {enabled: true}

Check yourself: your three files should be small — only the fields that genuinely differ per environment. Everything else stays in the shared values.yaml base.

🔬 Practice Drill 4.3 — Diagnose a Deep-Merge Surprise

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

A teammate ran --set-json 'image={"tag":"v4.0"}' expecting only the tag to change, but pullPolicy reverted to Kubernetes' own default instead of the chart's configured value. Explain exactly why, referencing deep merge vs shallow replace.

Hint: --set-json on a whole object behaves differently than --set on individual dot-notation keys.
View Solution

Answer: --set-json 'image={...}' replaces the ENTIRE image object wholesale — it isn't a deep merge at that key, it's a full substitution. Since the JSON only contained tag, every other sibling (including pullPolicy) was wiped, not preserved.

Check yourself: the fix would be either including every needed sub-key in the JSON, or using individual dot-notation --set image.tag=v4.0 instead, which DOES deep-merge and leaves siblings untouched.

🔬 Practice Drill 4.4 — Write a Real values.schema.json

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Write a values.schema.json for easypj requiring: replicaCount is an integer 1-20, service.type is one of ClusterIP/NodePort/LoadBalancer, and if ingress.tls is true, ingress.host must be provided.

Hint: The conditional rule needs an if/then inside allOf, exactly like §4.5's example.
View Solution
values.schema.json
{
  "properties": {
    "replicaCount": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 20},
    "service": {"properties": {"type": {"enum": ["ClusterIP","NodePort","LoadBalancer"]}}},
    "ingress": {
      "properties": {"tls": {"type": "boolean"}, "host": {"type": "string"}},
      "allOf": [{"if": {"properties": {"tls": {"const": true}}}, "then": {"required": ["host"]}}]
    }
  }
}

Check yourself: test it by intentionally installing with ingress.tls=true and no host — helm lint should reject it with a clear schema error.

🔬 Practice Drill 4.5 — Trace a Value Through the Global Scope

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

The parent easypj chart sets global.imageRegistry: myregistry.io. Write the exact template expression a PostgreSQL subchart would use to read it, and explain why it can't instead reference .Values.imageRegistry.

Hint: Global values live under one specific, reserved key from the subchart's perspective.
View Solution
subchart template
image: "{{ .Values.global.imageRegistry }}/postgresql:15"

Check yourself: .Values.imageRegistry (without global.) would resolve to nil inside the subchart, because subcharts only ever see their own dedicated section plus the reserved global namespace — never the parent's arbitrary top-level keys.

📌 Chapter 4 Visual Summary — one chart, endless configurations
  ⚙️ values.yaml          🔝 --set              📁 -f values-*.yaml
  ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────┐      ┌───────────────────┐
  │ chart's own   │  ④    │ HIGHEST       │  ①  │ environment configs│
  │ defaults      │◀───────│ priority       │────▶│ LAST file wins      │
  │ (lowest prio) │        │ override       │      └───────────────────┘
  └──────────────┘        └──────────────┘               │
                                                           ▼
  📐 values.schema.json   🏗️ Multi-env         🔒 Secrets
  ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────┐      ┌───────────────────┐
  │ validates     │  ②    │ 1 chart ×      │  ③  │ NEVER in values.   │
  │ BEFORE install│◀───────│ N environments │────▶│ yaml — use Secrets │
  └──────────────┘        └──────────────┘      └───────────────────┘
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   PRECEDENCE (memorize this order):
   --set  >  -f files (last wins)  >  parent chart values  >  values.yaml
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   ONE chart + DIFFERENT values-*.yaml = dev/staging/prod, safely and
   reproducibly — never a template edit, only ever a values change. ⚙️

In words: Every value a chart uses ultimately comes from values.yaml's defaults, unless something overrides it. Overrides stack in a strict, memorizable order — --set wins over everything, multiple -f files resolve last-one-wins, and the whole stack deep-merges rather than replacing wholesale, so an override only changes what it explicitly sets.

values.schema.json is the safety net on top of all of this — it validates whatever the final merged result looks like, before Kubernetes ever sees it, turning a bad deploy into an immediate, readable local error instead of a half-applied cluster mess.

The takeaway: "one chart, many environments" isn't a Helm feature you have to opt into — it falls directly out of this precedence system. dev/staging/prod are just three small values files layered on top of one shared chart, and Chapter 5 is where that chart becomes a real, trackable, rollback-able Release.

Chapter 5 · Installing, Upgrading & Managing Releases

This is where Helm comes alive. Installing, upgrading, rolling back, and uninstalling — these are the commands used every single day. A Release is an instance of a chart running in a cluster, and Helm tracks every change through a complete lifecycle. This chapter closes out Part 2: by the end, easypj won't just be a chart on disk — it'll be a tracked, rollback-able, running application.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 🚀 Operations 🐍 easypj / jobpost 🎯 Lifecycle Hooks & Releases

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Install releases with helm install — names, atomic, wait, timeout
  • ✅ Upgrade releases with helm upgrade — reuse-values, three-way merge
  • ✅ Rollback to previous versions with helm rollback
  • ✅ Uninstall releases with helm uninstall — the keep-history option
  • ✅ List and inspect releases with helm list and helm history
  • ✅ Understand the complete release state machine
  • ✅ Inspect releases with helm get and helm status
🎓 Helm Certification Relevance
Lifecycle Hooks & Releases HEAVILY TESTED
🎯 The Release Lifecycle Is the Single Most-Tested Topic

Three facts anchor almost every exam question in this domain:

  • Rollback doesn't rewind time — helm rollback creates a brand-new revision using an old revision's config. Revision numbers only ever go up; nothing is ever "re-activated" in place.
  • helm upgrade --install is always safe — it works whether the release exists yet or not, making it the standard CI/CD pattern.
  • Helm 3 has no --name flag — that's a Helm 2 relic. The release name is a plain positional argument: helm install <name> <chart>.

5.1 helm install — Your First Release (easypj)

helm install deploys a chart for the first time, creating a new Release. This is the command that turns a chart blueprint into a running application.

helm install — basic usage
# Basic install (release name is a plain positional argument)
helm install easypj ./easypj-chart

# Install to a specific namespace
helm install easypj-dev ./easypj-chart --namespace dev --create-namespace

# Install with a custom values file
helm install easypj-prod ./easypj-chart -f values-prod.yaml -n production

# Install with --set overrides
helm install easypj ./chart --set image.tag=v3.0 --set replicaCount=5

# Dry-run: see what would be deployed without actually deploying
helm install easypj ./chart --dry-run --debug

# Generate a random release name
helm install ./chart --generate-name
# Creates: easypj-chart-1689273

5.1a Release Names — --generate-name vs. Named Releases

✅ Named Releases (Recommended)
  • helm install easypj-prod ./chart
  • Predictable, meaningful names
  • Easy to reference in scripts
  • Best for production environments
🎲 --generate-name
  • helm install ./chart --generate-name
  • Random name: chartname-timestamp
  • Useful for CI/CD transient deploys
  • Avoids name conflicts automatically
📖 CORRECTED: There Is No --name Flag

Helm 2 used helm install --name myapp ./chart. In Helm 3, the release name is a plain positional argument: helm install myapp ./chart — no flag at all. Seeing --name anywhere is an instant sign the material is Helm 2-era.

5.1b Atomic Installations — --atomic, --wait, --timeout

⚛️
--atomic

If the install fails, automatically roll back to the previous state. All-or-nothing — critical for production.

⏳
--wait

Wait until all resources are ready before returning — Pods Running, Services with endpoints.

⏱️
--timeout

How long to wait for --wait/--atomic. Default: 5 minutes. Set with --timeout 10m.

production-grade install
helm install easypj-prod ./easypj-chart \
  -f values-prod.yaml \
  -n production \
  --create-namespace \
  --atomic \
  --wait \
  --timeout 10m

5.2 helm upgrade — Updating Deployed Releases

When a running release needs a change — new image, more replicas, updated config — use helm upgrade.

helm upgrade examples
# Upgrade to a new chart version
helm upgrade easypj ./easypj-chart

# Upgrade with new values
helm upgrade easypj ./easypj-chart -f values-prod.yaml

# Upgrade with --set
helm upgrade easypj ./easypj-chart --set image.tag=v3.0 --set replicaCount=5

# Install if not exists, upgrade if it does (idempotent!)
helm upgrade --install easypj ./easypj-chart -f values-prod.yaml

# Atomic upgrade: rollback on failure
helm upgrade easypj ./easypj-chart --atomic --wait --timeout 10m

# Dry-run to see what would change
helm upgrade easypj ./easypj-chart --dry-run --debug
💡 Always Use --install for CI/CD

helm upgrade --install is idempotent: it installs if the release doesn't exist, upgrades if it does. This is the standard CI/CD pattern — one command that works regardless of current state.

5.2a --reuse-values vs --reset-values

❌ --reuse-values (use with care)

Reuses ALL previously set values, including --set flags from the LAST install/upgrade. Can cause unexpected config if you've forgotten what was set before.

# First install:
helm install app ./chart --set image.tag=v1.0
# Later upgrade (INTENT: change replicas only):
helm upgrade app ./chart --reuse-values --set replicaCount=5
# RESULT: image.tag STILL v1.0 (reused!) + replicaCount=5
✅ --reset-values (predictable)

Discards ALL previous --set values. Uses ONLY the chart's values.yaml plus any new -f/--set flags given right now.

# First install:
helm install app ./chart --set image.tag=v1.0
# Later upgrade (INTENT: start fresh):
helm upgrade app ./chart --reset-values -f values-v2.yaml
# RESULT: ALL previous --set values discarded.
# Only values-v2.yaml + chart defaults are used.
🎯 Exam Pattern

"Upgrade the release but keep all previously configured values" → --reuse-values. "Start fresh with new values" → --reset-values. These flags are mutually exclusive — never combine them.

5.2b Three-Way Strategic Merge Patch

Helm 3 uses a three-way merge to determine what changes during an upgrade. It compares: (1) the old manifest, (2) the new manifest, and (3) the current live state in Kubernetes. This prevents Helm from overwriting changes made by other controllers (like an HPA or an admission webhook).

Three-Way Merge — How It Works
  ┌──────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────┐
  │  OLD MANIFEST    │   │  NEW MANIFEST    │   │  LIVE STATE      │
  │  (previous rev)  │   │  (what we want)  │   │  (in K8s now)    │
  │  replicas: 2     │   │  replicas: 3     │   │  replicas: 4     │
  │  image: v2.0     │   │  image: v2.1     │   │  image: v2.0     │
  └────────┬─────────┘   └────────┬─────────┘   └────────┬─────────┘
           └──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┘
                                  ▼
                    ┌─────────────────────────┐
                    │  THREE-WAY MERGE RESULT  │
                    │  replicas: 3  (new wins) │
                    │  image: v2.1  (new wins) │
                    │  If old=new but live      │
                    │  differs → keep live      │
                    └─────────────────────────┘

5.3 helm rollback — Going Back in Time

One of Helm's most powerful features: instant rollback to any previous revision. Every install/upgrade creates a new numbered revision.

rollback commands
# See revision history
helm history easypj
# REVISION  UPDATED                   STATUS      CHART          DESCRIPTION
# 1         Mon Jun 8 10:00:00 2026   superseded  easypj-0.1.0   Install complete
# 2         Mon Jun 8 10:30:00 2026   superseded  easypj-0.1.0   Upgrade complete
# 3         Mon Jun 8 11:00:00 2026   deployed    easypj-0.1.0   Upgrade complete

# Rollback to the previous revision
helm rollback easypj
# Rolls back to revision 2

# Rollback to a specific revision
helm rollback easypj 1
# Rolls back to revision 1

# Check what happened
helm history easypj
# REVISION 4 = the rollback (deployed)
⚠️ MAX HISTORY LIMIT

Helm stores only 10 revisions by default (--history-max). If you deploy frequently, increase it: helm install --history-max 50. Old revisions beyond the limit are automatically deleted — you can't rollback to a deleted revision.

5.4 helm uninstall — Cleaning Up

uninstall commands
# Uninstall a release
helm uninstall easypj-dev

# Uninstall from a specific namespace
helm uninstall easypj-stg -n staging

# Dry-run to see what would be deleted
helm uninstall easypj --dry-run

5.4a --keep-history — Uninstall Without Deleting History

By default, helm uninstall deletes all release history. Use --keep-history to preserve it for auditing or a potential future re-install.

--keep-history usage
# Uninstall but keep history records
helm uninstall easypj --keep-history

# The release status becomes "uninstalled" but history remains
helm list --all
# NAME     NAMESPACE  STATUS        ...
# easypj   default    uninstalled   ...

# History is still visible
helm history easypj

# Re-install with the same name — works because the name was preserved
helm install easypj ./chart

5.5 helm list — Viewing All Releases

helm list options
# List releases in the current namespace
helm list
helm ls          # short form

# List all releases across all namespaces
helm list --all-namespaces
helm list -A     # short form

# Show all releases, including "uninstalled" and "failed"
helm list --all

# Show only failed / only deployed releases
helm list --failed
helm list --deployed

# Sort by date or by revision
helm list --date
helm list -r

5.6 helm history — Tracking Release Changes

view release history
# View revision history
helm history easypj

# Output format: yaml or json
helm history easypj --output yaml
helm history easypj -o json
⚠️ History Max Is Per-Release

With 10 stored revisions and one more upgrade, revision 1 is permanently deleted — you cannot rollback to it. Increase --history-max if you need a longer rollback window.

5.7 Release Lifecycle — Understanding the State Machine

Complete Release State Machine
  HELM RELEASE STATE MACHINE
         ┌─────────┐
         │ unknown │  ← state cannot be determined
         └────┬────┘
    ┌─────────▼─────────┐
    │ pending-install   │  ← helm install started
    └─────────┬─────────┘
         ┌────▼────┐
         │ deployed│◄──── helm install SUCCESS · helm upgrade SUCCESS · helm rollback SUCCESS
         └────┬────┘
    ┌─────────▼─────────┐
    │ pending-upgrade    │  ← helm upgrade started
    └─────────┬─────────┘
         ┌────▼────┐
         │ deployed│◄──── previous revision → "superseded"
         └────┬────┘
    ┌─────────▼─────────┐
    │ pending-rollback   │  ← helm rollback started
    └─────────┬─────────┘
    ┌─────────▼─────────┐
    │ failed             │  ← install/upgrade/rollback FAILED
    └─────────┬─────────┘
    ┌─────────▼─────────┐
    │ uninstalling       │  ← helm uninstall in progress
    └─────────┬─────────┘
    ┌─────────▼─────────┐
    │ uninstalled        │  ← helm uninstall complete
    └────────────────────┘

5.7a Release Status Codes — What Each State Means

StatusMeaningCan helm install (same name)?Recovery action
deployedRelease is running normally❌ Name in useUse helm upgrade
failedInstall/upgrade/rollback failed❌ Name in usehelm rollback or helm uninstall
supersededOld revision replaced by a newer oneN/A (historical)A valid rollback target
pending-installInstall in progress❌ LockedWait, or delete the pending release Secret
pending-upgradeUpgrade in progress❌ LockedWait, or delete the pending release Secret
pending-rollbackRollback in progress❌ LockedWait, or delete the pending release Secret
uninstalledRelease removed (with --keep-history)✅ Can re-installUse helm install — the name is free
unknownHelm can't determine the stateCheck history firstInvestigate the release's Secrets directly

5.8 helm get — Inspecting Releases

helm get subcommands
# Get all information about a release
helm get all easypj

# Get computed values (merged from all sources)
helm get values easypj
helm get values easypj --all         # include chart defaults
helm get values easypj --revision 2  # a specific past revision

# Get the rendered Kubernetes manifests
helm get manifest easypj
helm get manifest easypj --revision 3

# Get the hooks that ran, and the NOTES.txt output
helm get hooks easypj
helm get notes easypj

5.9 helm status — Current Release State

check release status
# Check current status
helm status easypj

# Show status of a specific past revision
helm status easypj --revision 2

# Show status with detailed resource info
helm status easypj --show-resources

# Output in different formats
helm status easypj -o yaml
helm status easypj -o json
Under the Hood — the revision timeline, and what rollback actually does

"helm rollback reverts to a previous version" is slightly misleading phrasing. Here's precisely what happens, and why it matters for how you reason about release history:

   RELEASE: easypj-prod (namespace: production)
   ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
   REV  STATUS       DEPLOYED    CHART    APP VER   DESCRIPTION
   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   1    SUPERSEDED   10:00 AM    0.1.0    v1.0.0    Initial install
   2    SUPERSEDED   10:30 AM    0.1.1    v1.0.1    Bug fix
   3    SUPERSEDED   11:00 AM    0.2.0    v2.0.0    Major upgrade
   4    FAILED       11:15 AM    0.2.1    v2.0.1    BROKEN - rolled back
   5    DEPLOYED     11:16 AM    0.2.0    v2.0.0    Rollback to rev 3 ← CURRENT

   MAX HISTORY: 10 (default) — oldest revisions auto-deleted!
   Set with: helm install --history-max 20

   KEY INSIGHT: helm rollback CREATES a new revision (here, 5) with
   the config from revision 3. Revision 3 itself is NOT re-activated —
   it stays exactly as it was, permanently marked "superseded."
🔑 Revision numbers only ever go up. There's no way to "go back" to revision 3 in the sense of making the counter say 3 again — every rollback is really a forward-moving install using old config. This is why helm history always tells a complete, chronological, tamper-evident story: nothing is ever secretly rewritten.
Release Management: Detecting and Recovering from Drift
🔧
Detecting Release Drift

Someone modified resources directly with kubectl? Use helm diff upgrade <release> <chart> (helm-diff plugin) or helm get manifest <release> | kubectl diff -f - to compare live state vs Helm's last known state.

🔧
Recovering Failed Releases

helm rollback <release> works even from a failed state. If that itself fails: helm uninstall <release> --keep-history, then helm install <release> ./chart --reuse-values to recreate with the previous values.

🔧
Safe Production Upgrades

The full sequence: helm diff upgrade → review → helm upgrade --dry-run → helm upgrade --atomic --wait --timeout 10m. --atomic is the safety net — a failed upgrade becomes an automatic rollback.

🔧
Finding Stale Releases

helm list --all --all-namespaces surfaces everything, including failed and pending releases. helm list --failed -A narrows straight to broken ones. Clean up with helm uninstall, or fix with helm rollback.

   Release broken? ──YES──▶ helm rollback <name> ──SUCCESS──▶ 🎉 Done!
        │                                 │
        NO                               FAILED
        │                                 │
        ▼                                 ▼
   Everything OK?              helm uninstall --keep-history
        │                      helm install <name> ./chart
        ▼
   🎉 Production healthy!

   🔑 GOLDEN RULE: always test with --dry-run first.
      helm upgrade <name> ./chart --dry-run --debug

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • A Release is a running, tracked instance of a Chart — install creates one, upgrade changes it, rollback undoes a change, uninstall removes it.
  • Rollback creates a new revision — it doesn't rewind time. Revision numbers only ever climb; nothing already-superseded is ever re-activated in place.
  • --atomic is the production safety net — a failed install/upgrade automatically reverts, instead of leaving a broken release stuck mid-deploy.
  • helm upgrade --install is the standard CI/CD pattern — idempotent, safe to run repeatedly regardless of whether the release already exists.
  • Only 10 revisions are kept by default — --history-max controls this, and rollback to a deleted revision is simply impossible.
  • The three-way merge protects out-of-band changes — Helm compares old manifest, new manifest, and live state, so it won't blindly clobber what an HPA or webhook changed live.
  • helm get/helm status/helm history are your inspection toolkit — always investigate before guessing when a release misbehaves.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Assuming rollback "restores" the old revision. It creates a brand-new revision with the old config — the old revision number is never reactivated, and helm history will show a NEW, higher revision number after rolling back.
  • Looking for a --name flag. It doesn't exist in Helm 3 — the release name is a plain positional argument. Any material using --name is Helm 2-era.
  • --reuse-values silently carrying forward an old --set. An upgrade with --reuse-values can reapply a value you set months ago and forgot about — always confirm with helm get values --all before trusting the result.
  • Assuming helm list shows everything. By default it only shows currently-deployed releases in the current namespace — failed, uninstalled, and other-namespace releases need --all/--all-namespaces.
  • Not realizing history has a cap. With the default --history-max 10, frequent deployers can silently lose the ability to roll back past a certain point — old revisions are deleted, not archived.
  • Trying to reinstall a release name that's still "deployed" or "failed." Both states lock the name — only uninstalled (or a genuinely free name) allows a fresh helm install.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • helm upgrade --install is always safe to use instead of plain install — it works whether the release exists yet or not, so you never have to branch your logic on release state.
  • Default to --atomic --wait --timeout 10m on any production install/upgrade — three flags that turn "hope it works" into "guaranteed to end in a known-good state."
  • "Keep values" vs "start fresh" reflex: --reuse-values for the former, --reset-values for the latter — say the exam's exact wording back to yourself to pick the right flag under pressure.
  • When a release misbehaves, always run helm status first — it's the fastest single command for "what's actually going on right now."

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 5)

the three most common release workflows 
# WORKFLOW 1 — Fresh deploy
helm install easypj ./chart -f values-prod.yaml -n production --create-namespace --atomic --wait

# WORKFLOW 2 — Update in place
helm upgrade easypj ./chart --set image.tag=v3.0 --atomic --wait

# WORKFLOW 3 — CI/CD idempotent (installs OR upgrades)
helm upgrade --install easypj ./chart -f values-prod.yaml -n production --atomic --wait --timeout 10m

# Emergency rollback
helm rollback easypj <revision> --wait

# Safe preview — ALWAYS before applying for real
helm upgrade easypj ./chart --dry-run --debug

🧠 Chapter 5 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of release lifecycle management — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What command installs a chart and creates a new release named "easypj-prod" in the "production" namespace?
Show Answer
Answer

helm install easypj-prod ./easypj-chart -n production --create-namespace

Explanation

Namespace accuracy is critical on the exam — a wrong namespace scores zero even if everything else is correct. Verify with kubectl config view --minify or helm list -n production.

Q2
What does --atomic do during an install or upgrade?
Show Answer
Answer

If the operation fails, Helm automatically rolls back to the previous successful state — all-or-nothing.

Explanation

Without --atomic, a failed upgrade leaves the release stuck in "failed" state with the app potentially down. With it, a broken upgrade automatically reverts and the app stays up.

Q3
How do you upgrade a release while keeping all previously set values?
Show Answer
Answer

helm upgrade easypj ./chart --reuse-values. This keeps all existing values and applies chart defaults only to genuinely NEW fields.

Explanation

Without --reuse-values, an upgrade with no explicit -f/--set resets everything to the chart's plain values.yaml defaults — a common source of "why did my replica count change?!" surprises.

Q4
What is the three-way merge in Helm 3?
Show Answer
Answer

Helm compares (1) the old manifest, (2) the new manifest, and (3) the live state in Kubernetes to determine exactly what to change — preventing overwriting changes made by other controllers.

Explanation

Example: if an HPA changed live replicas to 7, but old=3 and new=5 (unchanged by the user), Helm leaves replicas alone — the HPA still owns that field in practice.

Q5
How do you rollback to revision 2 of a release?
Show Answer
Answer

helm rollback easypj 2. Use helm history easypj first to see which revisions are actually available.

Explanation

This doesn't reactivate revision 2 — it creates a new revision (e.g. revision 4) using revision 2's exact configuration.

Q6
What is the default maximum number of stored revisions per release?
Show Answer
Answer

10. Increase it with the --history-max flag at install/upgrade time. Beyond the limit, the oldest revisions are auto-deleted and can no longer be rolled back to.

Explanation

Frequent deployers should set a higher --history-max deliberately if they need a longer rollback window — the default silently trims history otherwise.

Q7
How do you uninstall a release but keep its history?
Show Answer
Answer

helm uninstall easypj --keep-history. The release status becomes "uninstalled," but its history records remain intact.

Explanation

A normal helm uninstall (without the flag) deletes all revision Secrets permanently — the release is gone with no trace.

Q8
What single command makes install/upgrade idempotent, ideal for a CI/CD pipeline?
Show Answer
Answer

helm upgrade --install easypj ./chart. It installs if the release doesn't exist, upgrades if it does — safe to run on every pipeline execution, no branching needed.

Explanation

First run: "Release does not exist. Installing..." Second and later runs: "Release has been upgraded." Same command, same safe outcome, every time.

Q9
What does helm get values show, versus helm get values --all?
Show Answer
Answer

helm get values shows only user-supplied values. --all shows the complete merged set — user values plus chart defaults.

Explanation

This distinction is essential for debugging: "what did I explicitly set?" vs "what's actually running right now?" are genuinely different, useful questions.

Q10
A release is in "failed" state. What's the fastest way to see exactly what went wrong?
Show Answer
Answer

helm status easypj shows the current state and any error message. helm history easypj shows the full revision history. helm get manifest easypj --revision <n> shows the exact YAML that was submitted for the failed revision.

Explanation

Layer these three commands together: status tells you IT failed, history tells you WHICH revision, get manifest shows you WHAT was actually attempted.

⚙️ Chapter 5 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

A release in trouble, and you produce the fix with real commands.

Q1
A production upgrade just failed halfway through, and the release now shows "failed" status. The team needs the app back up in the next 60 seconds. What do you run?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm rollback easypj --wait -n production
Explanation

helm rollback works even from a failed state — with no revision number, it rolls back to the previous deployed revision, and --wait confirms resources are actually healthy before returning.

Q2
You try helm install easypj ./chart and get an error that the name is already in use, but kubectl get pods shows nothing running for it. What's the likely release status, and how do you confirm?
Show Answer
Answer

Likely failed or a stuck pending-* state — both lock the name without anything actually running. Confirm with:

bash
helm status easypj
helm list --all
Explanation

Only uninstalled (or a truly free name) allows a fresh install — a failed or stuck-pending release still occupies the name and needs helm rollback or helm uninstall first.

Q3
Your CI pipeline needs one command that works whether this is the very first deploy or the hundredth. Design it, production-safe.
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm upgrade --install easypj ./chart -f values-prod.yaml -n production --atomic --wait --timeout 10m
Explanation

--install handles the "does it exist yet" branching for you; --atomic --wait --timeout means a bad deploy self-heals instead of leaving a half-broken release for a human to notice later.

Q4
You deployed 15 times this week to a fast-moving release and now can't roll back to last Monday's known-good revision. Why not, and how do you prevent this going forward?
Show Answer
Answer

The default --history-max 10 deleted it — only the 10 most recent revisions are kept. Going forward, set a higher limit:

bash
helm upgrade easypj ./chart --history-max 50
Explanation

This is a per-release setting applied at install/upgrade time, not a one-time global config — it needs to be part of your standard deploy command if frequent deploys are expected.

Q5
Someone ran kubectl scale deployment easypj --replicas=10 directly, bypassing Helm entirely. Your next helm upgrade — will it silently undo that change?
Show Answer
Answer

Only if the chart's own values also changed replicaCount. If the chart's desired replicaCount is unchanged between the old and new manifest, the three-way merge leaves the live value (10) alone — Helm only overwrites fields where its OWN desired value actually changed.

Explanation

This is exactly the HPA-protection scenario from §5.2b, generalized: any out-of-band live change survives an upgrade UNLESS the upgrade itself also touches that same field.

Q6
A teammate asks to see exactly what YAML was applied for a release's revision 3, which has since been superseded twice. One command?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm get manifest easypj --revision 3
Explanation

Every revision's manifest is preserved (up to --history-max) — you don't need the release to currently be AT revision 3 to inspect what it looked like then.

Q7
You need to remove a staging release entirely but preserve the ability to audit exactly what was deployed, for compliance. What's the right uninstall flag, and what does it NOT let you do afterward?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm uninstall easypj-stg --keep-history -n staging

This preserves history for auditing (helm history still works), but the release no longer has running resources — it can't be "resumed," only re-installed fresh (which would create new resources, not restore the old ones).

Explanation

"Keeping history" preserves the record, not the live application — a useful distinction the exam sometimes probes directly.

Q8
You want to preview EXACTLY what an upgrade would change before running it for real, beyond what helm template alone shows (which doesn't know about live cluster state). What do you run?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm diff upgrade easypj ./chart -f values-prod.yaml
Explanation

The helm-diff plugin (Chapter 2, §2.5) is aware of both the rendered chart AND the live cluster state, so it shows a true add/change/remove diff — helm template alone only renders in isolation, with no live-state comparison.

Q9
List every release across the entire cluster that is currently in a broken state, in one command.
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm list --failed --all-namespaces
Explanation

Combining --failed with -A is the fastest cluster-wide triage command for "what needs my attention right now" during an incident.

Q10
Design the complete, safe sequence for a risky production upgrade, from first check to final verification.
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm diff upgrade easypj ./chart -f values-prod.yaml   # 1. preview the real diff
helm upgrade easypj ./chart -f values-prod.yaml --dry-run --debug  # 2. dry-run
helm upgrade easypj ./chart -f values-prod.yaml --atomic --wait --timeout 10m  # 3. apply, safely
helm status easypj  # 4. verify
Explanation

This is the "Golden Rule" from Under the Hood's decision flowchart, spelled out as four concrete steps — diff, dry-run, apply-with-atomic, verify.

🔬 Practice Drill 5.1 — Full Lifecycle, One Release

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Install a release, upgrade it once, view its history, rollback to revision 1, and uninstall it with history preserved — five commands, one continuous flow, on any test cluster.

Hint: install → upgrade → history → rollback → uninstall --keep-history, in that exact order.
View Solution
full lifecycle
helm install easypj bitnami/nginx --set replicaCount=1
helm upgrade easypj bitnami/nginx --set replicaCount=2
helm history easypj
helm rollback easypj 1
helm uninstall easypj --keep-history

Check yourself: after the rollback, helm history should show a NEW revision (3) with replicaCount=1 — not a jump back to revision 1 itself. That's the "rollback creates, never rewinds" rule in action.

🔬 Practice Drill 5.2 — Simulate and Recover From a Failed Upgrade

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Install a release, then deliberately upgrade it to a nonexistent image tag WITH --atomic, and confirm the release survives in a healthy state instead of getting stuck broken.

Hint: An intentionally-bad --set image.tag=does-not-exist plus --atomic --wait --timeout 1m should trigger an automatic rollback.
View Solution
bash
helm install easypj bitnami/nginx
helm upgrade easypj bitnami/nginx --set image.tag=does-not-exist --atomic --wait --timeout 1m
# Expect: "upgrade failed... rolling back to revision 1"
helm status easypj  # should show "deployed", not "failed"

Check yourself: the release should end at deployed status, not failed — that's --atomic working exactly as designed.

🔬 Practice Drill 5.3 — Reuse vs Reset, Predict the Outcome

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

You install with --set replicaCount=5. Predict the replica count after each of these, run independently: (a) helm upgrade ./chart with no flags, (b) helm upgrade ./chart --reuse-values, (c) helm upgrade ./chart --reset-values.

Hint: Only one of the three preserves the value 5 automatically.
View Solution
CommandResulting replicaCountWhy
(a) no flagschart default (e.g. 1)Neither reuse nor reset was specified — Helm 3's default behavior resets to chart values unless told otherwise
(b) --reuse-values5Explicitly carries forward the prior --set value
(c) --reset-valueschart default (e.g. 1)Explicitly discards prior --set values — functionally same result as (a) here, but declared intentionally

Check yourself: only (b) reliably keeps replicaCount=5 — if you predicted otherwise for (b), re-read §5.2a.

🔬 Practice Drill 5.4 — Build the Release Status Decision Table From Memory

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Without looking back at §5.7a, list all 8 release status codes and, for each, whether helm install with that same name would succeed.

Hint: Only one status genuinely frees up the name for a plain install.
View Solution

Answer: deployed (❌), failed (❌), superseded (N/A, historical only), pending-install (❌ locked), pending-upgrade (❌ locked), pending-rollback (❌ locked), uninstalled (✅), unknown (investigate first).

Check yourself: uninstalled is the only status that frees the name — every "pending-*" state is locked, not available, which is a common point of confusion.

🔬 Practice Drill 5.5 — Explain Three-Way Merge With a Concrete easypj Example

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

easypj's HPA scaled live replicas to 8. The chart's desired replicaCount was 3 in the old release and stays 3 in a new upgrade that only changes image.tag. What does the three-way merge do to replicas, and why?

Hint: Compare what actually CHANGED between old and new manifest, field by field.
View Solution

Answer: Replicas stay at 8 (the live/HPA value) — untouched. Since replicaCount is unchanged between old (3) and new (3) manifests, Helm doesn't touch that field at all, leaving whatever the live cluster currently has (8, set by the HPA) exactly as-is. Only image.tag, which genuinely changed, gets applied.

Check yourself: if you predicted replicas would reset to 3, you've mixed up "unchanged in the desired manifest" with "Helm re-applies every field every time" — the three-way merge specifically avoids that.

📌 Chapter 5 Visual Summary — a release's complete lifecycle
  📥 install            🔄 upgrade             ⏪ rollback
  ┌──────────────┐      ┌──────────────┐       ┌──────────────────┐
  │ create a NEW  │  →  │ change a      │  →   │ NEW revision with  │
  │ release       │      │ running      │       │ OLD config — never │
  │ (rev 1)       │      │ release      │       │ "rewinds" in place │
  └──────────────┘      └──────────────┘       └──────────────────┘
                                                          │
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ▼
  🗑️ uninstall           📋 list                 🔍 status / get / history
  ┌──────────────┐      ┌──────────────┐       ┌──────────────────┐
  │ remove       │      │ what's        │       │ inspect ANY detail │
  │ (optionally  │      │ running       │       │ of ANY revision,    │
  │ --keep-history)│    │ right now?    │       │ any time            │
  └──────────────┘      └──────────────┘       └──────────────────┘
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   THE ONE RULE THAT EXPLAINS EVERYTHING:
   revision numbers only go UP. install=1, upgrade=2, rollback=3 (using
   rev-1's config), never back to "1" again. History is a ledger, not a
   rewindable tape. 🚀

In words: A Release moves through a small, predictable set of operations — install creates it, upgrade changes it, rollback reverts a bad change, uninstall removes it. Every one of the first three creates a NEW numbered revision; nothing is ever edited in place, and nothing is ever truly "undone" in the sense of erasing history.

Five inspection tools — list, history, get, status, and the state machine itself — let you answer "what's running," "what changed," "what exactly was deployed," and "is it healthy right now" at any point, for any past revision, without guessing.

The takeaway: once you accept that revision numbers only go up and rollback is really "install with old config," the entire release lifecycle stops being mysterious — it's one small, closed set of operations, fully observable at every step. Part 2 is complete: a chart (Ch3), configured per environment (Ch4), now fully manageable as a running release (Ch5). Part 3 goes inside the template engine itself.

Chapter 6 · Go Templating Fundamentals — The YAML Generation Engine

Templates are where Helm transforms from a simple package manager into a powerful code generator. Using Go's text/template library with Sprig's 70+ functions, a template produces different Kubernetes YAML based on values, conditions, and loops. This chapter covers the foundational building blocks — without it, "parameterized chart" is just a folder of static files.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🔧 Core 🐍 easypj / jobpost 🎯 Template Syntax & Logic

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Master the {{ }} template syntax and delimiter/whitespace rules
  • ✅ Understand all six Built-in Objects: .Release, .Values, .Chart, .Files, .Capabilities, .Template
  • ✅ Access nested configuration through the .Values object
  • ✅ Use release metadata through the .Release object
  • ✅ Embed static files and detect Kubernetes cluster capabilities
🎓 Helm Certification Relevance
Template Syntax & Logic CORE DOMAIN
🎯 A Template File Is a Mad Libs Page

The {{ }} blanks get filled in with values at render time, and the rest of the YAML around them never moves. Three things to internalize before going further:

  • The exam calls this "dot notation." {{ .Values.image.tag }} is accessing a value via dot notation — each . walks one level deeper into the values tree, always left-to-right, root to leaf.
  • The dot (.) changes meaning inside range/with. Referencing .Values inside one of these blocks without saving the root context first ({{ $root := . }}) silently loses access to .Release/.Chart — this is the single most common template bug (Under the Hood covers it in full).
  • helm template ./chart --debug renders locally in under a second. Use it to check syntax before any cluster call — there's no reason to debug templating issues against a live cluster.
