6.1 Template Syntax — {{ }} Delimiters

Helm templates use Go's text/template syntax. Everything between {{ and }} is evaluated as a template expression. Everything outside is literal text (plain YAML).

template syntax basics
# This is a Helm template file (e.g., deployment.yaml)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-deployment    # ← template expression
  labels:
    app: {{ .Chart.Name }}                # ← chart name from Chart.yaml
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}    # ← value from values.yaml
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
        image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
📖 Whitespace Control

Use {{- to trim leading whitespace and -}} to trim trailing whitespace. {{- .Values.name -}} removes spaces on both sides — crucial for clean YAML output.

6.2 Built-in Objects — The Template Context

Helm provides six built-in objects that give templates access to all configuration and metadata:

⚙️
.Values

All values from values.yaml, -f files, and --set flags. The primary data source — accessed with dot notation.

🚀
.Release

Release info: Name, Namespace, Revision, IsUpgrade, IsInstall, Service.

📦
.Chart

Metadata from Chart.yaml: Name, Version, AppVersion, Description, Type, ApiVersion.

📁
.Files

Static files bundled in the chart (not in templates/). Useful for ConfigMaps built from config files.

🔍
.Capabilities

Kubernetes cluster info: version, available API versions. Used for version-conditional templates.

📋
.Template

Info about the current file being rendered: .Name and .BasePath. Rarely used directly.

Complete Object Reference

ObjectKey propertiesExampleWhen to use
.Release.Name, .Namespace, .Revision, .IsUpgrade, .IsInstall, .Service{{ .Release.Name }}Release-specific metadata; labeling resources
.ValuesYour values.yaml structure{{ .Values.image.tag }}Accessing user configuration
.Chart.Name, .Version, .AppVersion, .Type, .ApiVersion{{ .Chart.Version }}Chart metadata in labels/annotations
.Files.Get(name), .GetBytes(name), .Glob(pattern), .AsConfig(), .AsSecrets(){{ .Files.Get "config.json" }}Embedding static files in ConfigMaps/Secrets
.Capabilities.KubeVersion, .APIVersions.Has(){{ .Capabilities.KubeVersion.GitVersion }}K8s version detection; API availability check
.Template.Name, .BasePath{{ .Template.Name }}Rarely used directly; template identification

6.3 The .Values Object — Accessing Configuration

.Values is the primary interface to user-supplied configuration — everything from values.yaml plus overrides (Chapter 4).

accessing .Values
# Given this values.yaml:
# replicaCount: 3
# image:
#   repository: easypj/easypj
#   tag: v2.1
# service:
#   port: 80

replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}           # → 3
image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"  # → easypj/easypj:v2.1
port: {{ .Values.service.port }}               # → 80

# Accessing a key that doesn't exist = RUNTIME ERROR
# Use default() for safety:
port: {{ .Values.service.port | default 8080 }}

6.4 The .Release Object — Name, Namespace, Revision

.Release fields
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-easypj      # release name, e.g. easypj-prod
  namespace: {{ .Release.Namespace }}    # target namespace
  annotations:
    revision: "{{ .Release.Revision }}"   # current revision number
    isUpgrade: "{{ .Release.IsUpgrade }}" # true/false
    isInstall: "{{ .Release.IsInstall }}" # true/false
    service: {{ .Release.Service }}      # always the literal string "Helm"

6.5 The .Chart Object — Metadata Access

Access Chart.yaml fields directly in templates — useful for labels and annotations that should match the chart's own metadata.

.Chart usage
labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
    app.kubernetes.io/version: {{ .Chart.AppVersion }}
    helm.sh/chart: {{ .Chart.Name }}-{{ .Chart.Version }}

6.6 The .Files Object — Embedding Static Files

Include files from the chart (config files, scripts, certificates) inside ConfigMaps or Secrets. .Files cannot reach anything under templates/, anything excluded by .helmignore, or files outside the chart directory.

.Files examples
# Embed a file's content in a ConfigMap
data:
  nginx.conf: |
{{ .Files.Get "config/nginx.conf" | indent 4 }}

# Get a file as base64 (for Secrets)
data:
  cert.pem: {{ .Files.Get "certs/cert.pem" | b64enc }}

# List and embed every non-template file matching a glob
{{ range $path, $_ := .Files.Glob "config/**" }}
  {{ $path }}: |
{{ $.Files.Get $path | indent 4 }}
{{ end }}
⚠️ .Files.Get Throws If the File Doesn't Exist

Unlike a safe default lookup, .Files.Get errors out on a missing path. Check existence first with .Files.Glob, or wrap the call in an if.

6.7 The .Capabilities Object — K8s Version & API Detection

Detect what the target cluster supports at render time — essential for backward-compatible charts that need to work across a range of Kubernetes versions.

.Capabilities usage
# Check Kubernetes version
{{ if semverCompare ">=1.25-0" .Capabilities.KubeVersion.GitVersion }}
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1  # use v1 Ingress (K8s 1.19+)
{{ else }}
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1beta1  # legacy Ingress
{{ end }}
kind: Ingress

# Check if a specific API is available
{{ if .Capabilities.APIVersions.Has "monitoring.coreos.com/v1" }}
# deploy a ServiceMonitor — Prometheus Operator is installed
{{ end }}
🎯 Exam Tip

Questions about API version compatibility are common. Always check the cluster's K8s version BEFORE deciding which API version to use. .Capabilities.KubeVersion.GitVersion returns something like v1.29.0 — use semverCompare for the comparison.

Under the Hood — the full rendering pipeline, and the dot (.) — Helm's most important concept

"Helm substitutes values into templates" hides a precise six-stage pipeline, and one single concept — the dot — that trips up more beginners than anything else in this guide.

① The Complete Rendering Pipeline

When helm install runs, Helm doesn't just substitute values — it runs a full pipeline that transforms templates + values into valid Kubernetes YAML:

1
Load Chart

Helm reads Chart.yaml, values.yaml, and every file in templates/ recursively. Files matching .helmignore are excluded. The chart is loaded into memory as a Go struct.

2
Build Values

Helm merges values in precedence order (Chapter 4): chart's values.yaml → parent chart values → -f files in order → --set overrides. This produces one merged .Values object.

3
Execute Templates

Each file in templates/ is processed by Go's text/template engine plus the Sprig function library (Chapter 7). The dot (.) is set to the root context — containing .Values, .Release, .Chart, .Files, .Capabilities, and .Template.

4
Concatenate & Parse as YAML

All rendered template output is concatenated into one big YAML stream, then split back into individual Kubernetes resource objects (separated by ---).

5
Sort & Apply

Resources are sorted by kind (Namespaces first, then Secrets, ConfigMaps, Services, Deployments…) so dependencies are created in the right order, then kubectl apply-equivalent submission happens per resource.

6
Store Release

The rendered manifest, computed values, and chart metadata are compressed, base64-encoded, and stored as a Kubernetes Secret named sh.helm.release.v1.<name>.v<rev> — this IS the Release record Chapter 5 works with.

② The Dot (.) — Helm's Most Important Concept

In Go templates, . (dot) is the current context. Its meaning changes depending on where you are in the template — mastering this is essential for writing correct templates.

   DOT CONTEXT VISUALIZATION
   ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
   TOP LEVEL:
   {{ .Values.image.tag }}    . = {Values: {...}, Release: {...}, Chart: {...}}
                                 ↑ the ENTIRE root object

   INSIDE with:
   {{ with .Values.image }}     . = .Values.image = {repository: "easypj", tag: "v2.0"}
     {{ .repository }}          .repository = "easypj" ✓ (dot is now the image object)
     {{ .tag }}                 .tag = "v2.0" ✓
   {{ end }}

   INSIDE range:
   {{ range .Values.env }}      . = each element of the env list
     {{ .name }}                .name = "DEBUG" (dot is the current env item)
     {{ .value }}               .value = "true"
   {{ end }}

   DOT IS REBOUND INSIDE: with, range, define blocks
   DOT IS PRESERVED BY: if/else blocks

   CRITICAL: inside {{ range }} or {{ with }}, you CANNOT access .Values
   anymore — . now points to the loop variable / narrowed scope, not the root.
   FIX: save the root FIRST: {{ $root := . }} before range/with, then use
   {{ $root.Values.xxx }} anywhere inside the block.
🔑 The #1 template error in Helm. Accessing .Values.something (or .Release/.Chart) inside a range or with block without saving the root context first. The fix is one line at the top of any template using range/with: {{- $root := . -}} — then use $root.Values.xxx (or the shorthand $.Values.xxx, since $ ALWAYS refers to the root, everywhere, with no setup required) instead of the now-rebound ..

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Everything inside {{ }} is a Go template expression — everything outside is literal YAML that never changes.
  • Six built-in objects give every template its data: .Values, .Release, .Chart, .Files, .Capabilities, .Template.
  • The dot (.) is context-sensitive — it means the root object at the top level, but gets REBOUND inside range/with blocks (never inside if/else).
  • $ always refers to the root, unconditionally — the escape hatch for accessing .Values/.Release/.Chart from anywhere, even deep inside a range/with block.
  • Whitespace control ({{-/-}}) isn't cosmetic — sloppy whitespace produces YAML with stray blank lines that can fail to parse.
  • The render pipeline is entirely deterministic and inspectable — helm template --debug shows exactly what six stages of processing would produce, with zero cluster involvement.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Missing whitespace control. {{ .Values.name }} renders as " easypj " with surrounding whitespace intact; {{- .Values.name -}} renders clean as "easypj".
  • Nil pointer when a key doesn't exist. {{ .Values.missing }} crashes with "nil pointer evaluating interface." {{ .Values.missing | default "safe" }} doesn't.
  • Scope loss inside with/range. Once inside {{ with .Values.db }}, plain .Release.Name is unreachable — only $.Release.Name works, because $ is the one symbol that's never rebound.
  • Forgetting to quote strings with special characters. value: {{ .Values.special }} can produce a YAML parse error if the value contains a colon or hash; value: {{ .Values.special | quote }} is always safe.
  • Assuming .Files.Get fails gracefully. It throws a hard error on a missing path — check with .Files.Glob first, don't assume a try/catch-style fallback.
  • Confusing .Chart.Version with .Chart.AppVersion. The chart's own SemVer version and the deployed application's version are two entirely independent fields (Chapter 3, §3.1a).
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Always use default(). Never assume a key exists — {{ .Values.x | default "fallback" }} prevents the single most common Helm template error.
  • Always quote dynamic strings. {{ .Values.name | quote }} prevents YAML parsing errors from special characters like colons, hashes, and brackets.
  • Use $ for root scope, unconditionally. Inside with or range, $ always refers to the root context — {{ $.Release.Name }} works anywhere, no setup required.
  • Trim whitespace with {{- -}} as a default habit, not an afterthought — critical for clean YAML output every single time.
  • Prefer include over template. include returns a string and is pipeline-friendly (| nindent 4); template writes inline with no pipeline support (Chapter 7).
  • nindent N for block insertion — newline plus N-space indent in one function, e.g. {{ include "labels" . | nindent 4 }}.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 6)

debugging templates — entirely client-side, no cluster needed 
# Render the full chart's output locally, with debug detail
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart --debug

# Render just one specific template file
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart --show-only templates/deployment.yaml

# Simulate a full install without touching the cluster
helm install easypj ./easypj-chart --dry-run --debug

# Validate structure/syntax before rendering at all
helm lint --strict ./easypj-chart

🧠 Chapter 6 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (15)

Quick recall of syntax and built-in objects — 15 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What delimiters does Helm use for template expressions?
Show Answer
Answer

{{ and }}. Everything between them is a Go template expression. {{- trims leading whitespace, -}} trims trailing.

Explanation

Without {{-/-}}, template expressions leave blank lines that can break YAML parsing — whitespace control is not optional polish.

Q2
Name three of Helm's six Built-in Objects.
Show Answer
Answer

Any three of: .Values, .Release, .Chart, .Files, .Capabilities, .Template.

Explanation

All six form the complete template context — the dot (.) at the top level of any template is the root object containing all of them.

Q3
How do you access a nested value like image.tag from values.yaml?
Show Answer
Answer

{{ .Values.image.tag }}. For safety against a missing key: {{ .Values.image.tag | default "latest" }}.

Explanation

Dot notation chains through nested YAML structures left to right, root to leaf — there's no other traversal order in Helm templates.

Q4
How do you embed a file from the chart into a ConfigMap?
Show Answer
Answer

{{ .Files.Get "path/to/file" | indent 4 }}. Place the file anywhere in the chart except templates/, then reference it with .Files.Get.

Explanation

indent 4 is essential here — without it, the embedded file's own indentation won't align correctly inside the surrounding YAML block.

Q5
How do you check if the cluster supports a specific Kubernetes API version?
Show Answer
Answer

{{ if .Capabilities.APIVersions.Has "networking.k8s.io/v1/Ingress" }}...{{ end }} — use this for version-conditional templates.

Explanation

This check happens entirely at render time, against whatever cluster helm install/upgrade is currently targeting.

Q6
What does .Release.IsUpgrade return, and when would you use it?
Show Answer
Answer

true if the current operation is an upgrade, false for a fresh install. Use it to run upgrade-only logic, like backing up data before applying a change.

Explanation

Its counterpart .Release.IsInstall is the mirror case — both are false during a plain helm template render, since no real install/upgrade is happening.

Q7
How do you reference the chart's name from Chart.yaml inside a template?
Show Answer
Answer

{{ .Chart.Name }}. Also available: .Chart.Version, .Chart.AppVersion, .Chart.ApiVersion, .Chart.Type.

Explanation

These are used constantly in standard Kubernetes labels, e.g. helm.sh/chart: {{ .Chart.Name }}-{{ .Chart.Version }}.

Q8
What happens if you reference .Values.missingKey when that key doesn't exist?
Show Answer
Answer

A runtime error — rendering fails with "nil pointer evaluating interface." Always guard with default: {{ .Values.missingKey | default "fallback" }}.

Explanation

For a value that MUST be supplied (no sensible default exists), use required "message" .Values.x instead — it fails with a clear, custom error rather than a generic nil-pointer crash.

Q9
How do you base64-encode a file's content for a Kubernetes Secret?
Show Answer
Answer

{{ .Files.Get "certs/cert.pem" | b64enc }}. b64enc is a Sprig function (Chapter 7) that base64-encodes a string.

Explanation

Secret data fields require base64 values — combining .Files.Get with b64enc is the standard pattern for embedding a cert/key file into a Secret at render time.

Q10
Which built-in objects would you combine to generate standard Kubernetes recommended labels?
Show Answer
Answer

.Chart.Name, .Chart.Version/.Chart.AppVersion, and .Release.Name/.Release.Service — feeding app.kubernetes.io/name, helm.sh/chart, app.kubernetes.io/instance, and app.kubernetes.io/managed-by.

Explanation

In practice, this exact combination is almost always defined once in _helpers.tpl as a named labels template and reused everywhere via include (Chapter 7) — never retyped per-resource.

Q11
What does the dash in {{- do in a template?
Show Answer
Answer

It trims whitespace. {{- trims LEFT whitespace, -}} trims RIGHT, {{- ... -}} trims BOTH sides.

Explanation

The dash "chomps" adjacent whitespace including newlines — without it, expressions leave stray blank lines in the rendered YAML that can, in the worst case, break parsing.

Q12
How do you access a file's content inside a template, and what's the safety check before doing so?
Show Answer
Answer

{{ .Files.Get "config.json" }}. Check existence first with {{ if .Files.Glob "config.json" }}, since .Files.Get throws if the path doesn't exist.

Explanation

.Files.AsConfig and .Files.AsSecrets go one step further, producing ready-to-use ConfigMap/Secret YAML automatically instead of raw content you'd have to wrap yourself.

Q13
What is the difference between .Chart.Version and .Chart.AppVersion?
Show Answer
Answer

.Chart.Version is the chart's own SemVer version (required in Chart.yaml). .Chart.AppVersion is the deployed application's version (optional, purely informational).

Explanation

Bump .Chart.Version on every chart change (templates, structure); bump the underlying appVersion only when the application itself changes — the two numbers move independently.

Q14
How do you conditionally include an entire resource, using if?
Show Answer
Answer

Wrap the whole resource in {{ if .Values.ingress.enabled }}...{{ end }}. When false, the resource is completely omitted from the rendered output — not just emptied, genuinely absent.

Explanation

This is the standard pattern for optional resources like Ingress, HPA, and PVC — combine with else for an alternative resource instead of simple omission.

Q15
What are .Release.IsInstall and .Release.IsUpgrade useful for in practice?
Show Answer
Answer

Differentiating install-vs-upgrade behavior: running a full DB migration only on IsInstall, or backing up data first when IsUpgrade is true — logic that shouldn't run on every single deploy.

Explanation

.Release.Revision pairs naturally with these booleans — it increments on every install/upgrade/rollback, giving templates a full picture of "what kind of change is this, and how many have happened before."

⚙️ Chapter 6 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

A broken template, and you diagnose it using the dot-context and built-in-object mental model.

Q1
A template fails with "nil pointer evaluating interface {}.Release" — but ONLY inside a {{ range .Values.env }} block, and only for that one line. Diagnose it.
Show Answer
Answer

Inside the range, the dot (.) has been rebound to each env-list item — .Release no longer means the root's Release object. Fix by using $.Release instead of .Release inside the loop.

Explanation

This is the #1 template error from Under the Hood, in the wild — always reach for $ the moment you're inside range/with and need something from the root.

Q2
Rendered YAML has an unexpected blank line right before every image: field, breaking a downstream YAML parser. What's the fix, in general terms?
Show Answer
Answer

Add whitespace-trimming dashes to the surrounding template expressions — likely {{- on the line producing the blank, or -}} on the line before it.

Explanation

Run helm template ./chart --debug and inspect the exact rendered output around that field — the stray newline is always traceable to a missing dash nearby.

Q3
You need to embed configs/redis.conf into a ConfigMap, but you're not 100% sure the file exists in every version of the chart. Write the safe pattern.
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
{{ if .Files.Glob "configs/redis.conf" }}
data:
  redis.conf: |
{{ .Files.Get "configs/redis.conf" | indent 4 }}
{{ end }}
Explanation

.Files.Glob is truthy only when at least one file matches, making it a safe existence check before the error-prone .Files.Get.

Q4
A chart must support both Kubernetes 1.18 (legacy Ingress API) and 1.29+ (stable Ingress API) with the same template. Write the conditional.
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
{{ if .Capabilities.APIVersions.Has "networking.k8s.io/v1/Ingress" }}
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
{{ else }}
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1beta1
{{ end }}
kind: Ingress
Explanation

Checking a specific resource's API availability (rather than just a raw version number) is more robust — it directly answers "does THIS cluster support what I'm about to submit," not just "is the version number high enough."

Q5
You want migrations to run only on the very first install of easypj, never on subsequent upgrades. Sketch the guard.
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
{{ if .Release.IsInstall }}
# migration Job definition here
{{ end }}
Explanation

This is a preview of Lifecycle Hooks territory (Part 4) — in real charts, this pattern is more often expressed as a post-install hook rather than a bare if, but the underlying boolean is the same one covered here.

Q6
A teammate writes secret: {{ .Values.apiKey }} and it renders fine in dev but breaks YAML parsing in prod, where the key happens to contain a colon. What's the one-word fix?
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
secret: {{ .Values.apiKey | quote }}
Explanation

Unquoted dynamic values are a YAML parsing time bomb — they work by luck until a value happens to contain a character (colon, hash, leading special char) that YAML treats specially.

Q7
You need the chart's own version AND its name in one Kubernetes-standard label, without hardcoding either. Write it.
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
helm.sh/chart: {{ .Chart.Name }}-{{ .Chart.Version }}
Explanation

This exact label is part of the Kubernetes-recommended label set — worth memorizing verbatim since it appears in almost every real-world chart's _helpers.tpl.

Q8
Before submitting anything to a real cluster, you want to see the exact rendered YAML for just templates/deployment.yaml. One command?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart --show-only templates/deployment.yaml
Explanation

--show-only narrows a multi-template chart's output to exactly the one file you're debugging, instead of scrolling through every resource the chart produces.

Q9
A base64-encoded Secret field renders as an empty string instead of the certificate content. List two things to check.
Show Answer
Answer

(1) Does the file path passed to .Files.Get actually match a real file relative to the chart root (typos are common)? (2) Is the file excluded by .helmignore or does it sit inside templates/ (both make it invisible to .Files)?

Explanation

An empty-but-not-erroring result usually means the path resolved to nothing rather than that b64enc itself misbehaved — b64enc of an empty string is still valid base64, just useless.

Q10
Design a template snippet that safely reads .Values.database.password, with NO default fallback allowed — it must be provided by the user or fail loudly at render time.
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
password: {{ required "database.password is required!" .Values.database.password | quote }}
Explanation

required is the deliberate opposite of default — it turns a missing value into an immediate, readable error with a custom message instead of a silent fallback or a generic nil-pointer crash.

🔬 Practice Drill 6.1 — Fix the Scoping Bug

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

The following template fails to render. Find and fix the bug:

{{ range .Values.env }}
- name: {{ .name }}
  value: {{ .value }}
  release: {{ .Release.Name }}
{{ end }}
Hint: Inside the loop, what does the dot currently refer to?
View Solution 
{{ range .Values.env }}
- name: {{ .name }}
  value: {{ .value }}
  release: {{ $.Release.Name }}   ← fixed: $ instead of .
{{ end }}

Check yourself: .name and .value work correctly because the dot IS each env item — but .Release was never part of an env item, so it must go through $, the one symbol that always means the root regardless of how deep you are.

🔬 Practice Drill 6.2 — Render and Read the Debug Output

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Using any chart you have locally (or helm create test-chart), run helm template with --debug and identify, from the output alone, exactly what value was used for replicaCount.

Hint: --debug prints the computed values BEFORE the rendered YAML — look at the top of the output.
View Solution
bash
helm create test-chart
helm template test-chart --debug | head -30

Check yourself: the debug output's "COMPUTED VALUES" section shows the exact merged .Values object BEFORE any template runs — this is the fastest way to confirm precedence resolved as expected, without reading a single line of rendered YAML.

🔬 Practice Drill 6.3 — Write a Version-Conditional Template

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Write a template snippet for an HPA that uses autoscaling/v2 if available, falling back to autoscaling/v2beta2 on older clusters.

Hint: Check the specific resource's API availability, not just a raw version number.
View Solution
yaml
{{ if .Capabilities.APIVersions.Has "autoscaling/v2/HorizontalPodAutoscaler" }}
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
{{ else }}
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2beta2
{{ end }}
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler

Check yourself: this exact pattern generalizes to every "old API vs new API" situation a chart will ever face — same shape, different resource string.

🔬 Practice Drill 6.4 — Trace the Six-Stage Pipeline From Memory

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Without looking back at Under the Hood, list the six stages of the rendering pipeline, in order, from helm install to a stored Release.

Hint: Load → Build → Execute → Concatenate → Sort → Store.
View Solution

Answer: (1) Load Chart, (2) Build Values (merge precedence), (3) Execute Templates (Go template engine + Sprig), (4) Concatenate & Parse as YAML, (5) Sort & Apply (by kind, dependency order), (6) Store Release (as a Kubernetes Secret).

Check yourself: if you can explain WHY each stage exists (not just recite the name), you understand the pipeline — e.g. stage 5 exists because Namespaces must exist before anything can be created inside them.

🔬 Practice Drill 6.5 — Build a Safe Values Access Checklist

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Write a 3-item checklist a code reviewer should run through for every {{ .Values.x }} reference in a new template, based on this chapter's gotchas.

Hint: Existence, quoting, and root-scope access are the three recurring failure modes covered this chapter.
View Solution

Sample checklist: (1) Does this key always exist, or does it need | default / required? (2) Could this value ever contain YAML-special characters, and does it need | quote? (3) Is this reference inside a range/with block, and if so, should it be $.Values.x instead of .Values.x?

Check yourself: these three questions catch the large majority of real-world Helm template bugs — worth running through habitually, not just when something breaks.

📌 Chapter 6 Visual Summary — syntax + six objects = the complete template vocabulary
  {{ }} DELIMITERS         ⚙️ .Values              🚀 .Release
  ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐        ┌───────────────────┐
  │ expression =  │        │ user config,  │        │ Name, Namespace,    │
  │ {{ ... }}     │        │ your primary  │        │ Revision, IsUpgrade,│
  │ {{- trims -}} │        │ data source   │        │ IsInstall, Service  │
  └──────────────┘         └──────────────┘        └───────────────────┘

  📦 .Chart                📁 .Files               🔍 .Capabilities
  ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐        ┌───────────────────┐
  │ Chart.yaml    │        │ static files,  │       │ K8s version &      │
  │ metadata      │        │ NOT templates/ │       │ API availability   │
  └──────────────┘         └──────────────┘        └───────────────────┘
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   THE ONE RULE THAT EXPLAINS MOST BUGS:
   . = root at the top level, REBOUND inside range/with, but $ ALWAYS
   means the root, everywhere, no exceptions. When in doubt, use $. ⚙️

In words: Every Helm template is plain YAML with {{ }} expressions dropped in — the six built-in objects (.Values, .Release, .Chart, .Files, .Capabilities, .Template) are the entire vocabulary of data available to fill those blanks. Learn what each one holds, and you can read (and mostly write) any Helm template in this guide.

The one genuinely tricky concept is the dot itself: it means "the whole root object" at the top of a template, but gets narrowed — rebound — the moment you enter a range or with block. $ is the escape hatch that always means the root, no matter how deeply nested you are.

The takeaway: syntax and objects alone only get you static substitution. Chapter 7 adds the 70+ functions and pipeline (|) syntax that turn this into genuine logic — conditionals, loops, string manipulation, and reusable named templates.

Chapter 7 · Template Functions & Pipelines — The Power Tools

Go templates alone are limited. Helm supercharges them with 70+ Sprig functions plus custom Helm functions. This chapter covers string manipulation, type conversion, control structures (if/range/with), named templates, pipelines, and the tpl function — the actual vocabulary needed to DO something useful inside the {{ }} braces Chapter 6 introduced.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~3 hours 🔧 Functions 🐍 easypj / jobpost 🎯 Functions and Pipelines

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Master string, type, math, and date transformation functions
  • ✅ Use default, required, and empty for safe value handling
  • ✅ Control template flow with if/else, with, and range
  • ✅ Create reusable templates with define, template, and include
  • ✅ Chain functions with pipelines |
  • ✅ Evaluate templates dynamically with tpl, and query the cluster with lookup
🎓 Helm Certification Relevance
Functions and Pipelines HEAVILY TESTED
🎯 Functions Are Kitchen Tools, Pipelines Are the Assembly Line

A raw ingredient goes in one end, a plated dish comes out the other — each tool's output feeds the next tool's input. Three things to internalize before going further:

  • The exam names default "the fail-safe function." {{ .Values.x | default "safe-value" }} — if .Values.x is nil, "", 0, or false, the fallback is used instead of crashing the render. Without it: "nil pointer evaluating interface" — the #1 template failure on the exam AND in production.
  • indent vs nindent is a top "why did my YAML fail to parse" gotcha. indent 4 adds 4 spaces to EVERY line, including the first — usually leaving that first line under-indented relative to its YAML key. nindent 4 adds a newline FIRST, then indents every line — the correct choice right after a key: on its own line.
  • Reflex-wrap every optional .Values reference in | default the moment you type it — don't wait for the crash to remind you.

🧭 Section Map — the Chapter 7 Learning Arc

The chapter moves through function categories (7.1–7.5), then control flow (7.6, with four lettered stops), then reuse via named templates (7.7), then composition — pipelines, dynamic templates, debugging, cluster queries, and the full Sprig library (7.8–7.12).

7.1 String Functions

string functions
# quote: wrap in double quotes (safe for YAML strings with special chars)
name: {{ .Values.appName | quote }}               # → "easypj"

# upper / lower: case conversion
{{ "easypj" | upper }}                            # → EASYPJ
{{ "EASYpj" | lower }}                            # → easypj

# trim: remove whitespace from both ends
{{ "  hello  " | trim }}                          # → "hello"

# replace: replace a substring (old new string)
{{ "easypj-v1" | replace "-" "_" }}               # → "easypj_v1"

# nospace: remove all whitespace
{{ "e a s y p j" | nospace }}                     # → "easypj"

# trunc: truncate to N characters
{{ "easypj-production-deployment" | trunc 10 }}   # → "easypj-pro"

# indent: indent every line by N spaces
data:
  config.yaml: |
{{ .Files.Get "config.yaml" | indent 4 }}

7.2 Type Conversion

type conversion functions
# toYaml: convert an object to a YAML string
{{ .Values.resources | toYaml | indent 10 }}
# Output:
#           limits:
#             cpu: 500m
#             memory: 256Mi

# fromYaml: parse a YAML string into an object
{{ $config := .Files.Get "config.yaml" | fromYaml }}
port: {{ $config.server.port }}

# toJson / fromJson: same idea, but for JSON
{{ .Values.annotations | toJson }}
{{ $data := .Files.Get "data.json" | fromJson }}

# toString: force-convert to a string
{{ 42 | toString }}                              # → "42"

7.3 Default Values — Safety Nets

default value functions
# default: use a fallback if the value is empty/nil
replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount | default 2 }}
image: {{ .Values.image.repository | default "nginx" }}

# required: FAIL if the value is empty (for mandatory values)
{{ required "image.repository is required!" .Values.image.repository }}

# empty: returns true if the value IS "empty" (0, "", nil, false, empty list/map)
{{ if empty .Values.tolerations }}
  # No tolerations configured
{{ end }}

# coalesce: return the first non-empty value from a list
{{ coalesce .Values.customName .Chart.Name "default-name" }}
💡 "The Fail-Safe Function"

The official exam names default explicitly as the fail-safe: without it, a nil value produces "nil pointer evaluating interface {}.x" — the single most common template failure, both on the exam and in real production charts.

7.4 Math Functions

math functions
# Basic arithmetic
{{ add 2 3 }}         # → 5
{{ sub 10 3 }}        # → 7
{{ mul 3 4 }}         # → 12
{{ div 10 2 }}        # → 5
{{ mod 10 3 }}        # → 1

# min / max: find the min or max of several values
{{ min 1 5 3 9 }}     # → 1
{{ max 1 5 3 9 }}     # → 9

# Example: calculate a percentage
cpuPercent: {{ div .Values.usedCPU .Values.totalCPU | mul 100 }}

7.5 Date Functions

date functions
# now: current date/time (at template rendering time)
deployedAt: {{ now | quote }}

# date: format a date (layout reference: Mon Jan 2 15:04:05 MST 2006)
{{ date "2006-01-02" now }}

# dateModify: add/subtract time
{{ now | dateModify "-24h" | date "2006-01-02" }}

# htmlDate: ISO 8601 format
{{ now | htmlDate }}

7.6 Control Structures — if/else, with, range

Control structures let templates make decisions, iterate over data, and scope values — the four stops below cover every control-flow tool used throughout this guide.

7.6a if/else — Conditional Resource Inclusion

if/else examples
{{ if .Values.ingress.enabled }}
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
# ... ingress spec ...
{{ else }}
# Ingress disabled — no ingress resource created
{{ end }}

{{ if eq .Values.environment "production" }}
  replicas: 5
{{ else if eq .Values.environment "staging" }}
  replicas: 2
{{ else }}
  replicas: 1
{{ end }}

Comparison & Logical Operators Reference

OperatorMeaningExample
eqEqual{{ if eq .Values.env "production" }}
neNot equal{{ if ne .Values.env "dev" }}
ltLess than{{ if lt .Values.replicas 3 }}
gtGreater than{{ if gt .Values.replicas 1 }}
leLess than or equal{{ if le .Values.replicas 5 }}
geGreater than or equal{{ if ge .Values.memory 256 }}
andLogical AND{{ if and .Values.enabled .Values.ready }}
orLogical OR{{ if or .Values.debug .Values.verbose }}
notLogical NOT{{ if not .Values.disabled }}

7.6b with — Scoping Values

with examples
# with changes the scope (.) to the specified value
{{ with .Values.postgresql }}
  - name: POSTGRES_HOST
    value: {{ .host }}        # . now refers to .Values.postgresql
  - name: POSTGRES_PORT
    value: {{ .port | default 5432 | quote }}
{{ end }}

# If the value is empty/nil, the block is silently skipped
{{ with .Values.optionalConfig }}
  # This block only renders if optionalConfig is non-empty
{{ end }}

7.6c range — Iterating Over Lists & Maps

range examples
# Iterate over a list
{{ range .Values.ingress.hosts }}
  - host: {{ .host | quote }}
    http:
      paths:
      {{ range .paths }}
        - path: {{ .path }}
          pathType: {{ .pathType }}
      {{ end }}
{{ end }}

# Iterate over a map (key, value)
{{ range $key, $value := .Values.env }}
  - name: {{ $key }}
    value: {{ $value | quote }}
{{ end }}

7.6d Variable Assignment — $var := value

variable assignment
# Assign a variable with :=
{{ $appName := .Chart.Name }}
{{ $releaseName := .Release.Name }}

# Use the variable
name: {{ $appName }}-{{ $releaseName }}

# Variables are scoped — use $ to access the outer scope inside range
{{ $globalName := .Release.Name }}
{{ range .Values.services }}
  name: {{ $globalName }}-{{ .name }}
{{ end }}

7.7 Named Templates — define, template, include

Named templates are the reusable-function equivalent for Helm — define a chunk of template logic once, then call it from anywhere in the chart.

7.7a define vs template vs include — Key Differences

DirectivePurposePipeline supportUse case
defineDeclare a named template blockN/ACreating reusable snippets
templateExecute a named template inline❌ No pipelineSimple inclusion
includeExecute and return as a string✅ Yes — pipe to indent, quote, etc.Always use include!
named template example (_helpers.tpl)
{{/* _helpers.tpl */}}
{{- define "easypj.fullname" -}}
{{- .Release.Name }}-{{ .Chart.Name }}
{{- end -}}

{{/* Usage in deployment.yaml */}}
name: {{ include "easypj.fullname" . }}
# include returns a string — you can pipe it:
name: {{ include "easypj.fullname" . | trunc 63 | quote }}
📖 Why the Chart-Name Prefix Matters

Naming a template easypj.fullname rather than just fullname isn't cosmetic. Once a dependency chart loads into the SAME template namespace as its parent, an unprefixed name can collide with another chart's template of the same name. The prefix is how Helm's own docs recommend avoiding that collision entirely — always prefix every named template with the chart's own name.

7.8 Pipelines — Chaining Functions with |

pipeline examples
# Chain multiple functions with |
{{ .Values.appName | upper | quote }}
# → "EASYPJ"

# Common pipeline: get → indent
data:
  config.yaml: |
{{ .Files.Get "config.yaml" | indent 4 }}

# Complex pipeline: get → fromYaml → toYaml → indent
{{ .Files.Get "config.yaml" | fromYaml | toYaml | indent 4 }}

# Default + quote pipeline
{{ .Values.image.tag | default "latest" | quote }}

7.9 The tpl Function — Template Inside Template

tpl evaluates a string AS a template. This lets a user provide template expressions inside values.yaml that are rendered at deploy time — powerful, but use it sparingly.

tpl examples
# values.yaml:
# greeting: "Hello, {{ .Values.name }}!"
# name: "World"

# template:
{{ tpl .Values.greeting . }}
# → "Hello, World!"

7.10 Template Debugging

debug commands
# See rendered templates locally
helm template ./chart --debug

# Lint for syntax errors
helm lint ./chart

# Simulate an install/upgrade
helm install test ./chart --dry-run --debug
helm upgrade test ./chart --dry-run --debug

# Show computed values for a deployed release
helm get values myrelease --all

# Show rendered manifests for a deployed release
helm get manifest myrelease

7.11 Lookup Function — Querying the K8s API at Render Time

The lookup function queries the Kubernetes API during template rendering, letting a template read existing resources. Warning: this breaks Helm's declarative model — use sparingly.

lookup examples
# Check if a Secret exists
{{ $secret := lookup "v1" "Secret" .Release.Namespace "easypj-credentials" }}
{{ if $secret }}
  # Secret exists, use existing value
{{ else }}
  # Secret doesn't exist yet
{{ end }}

quote, upper, lower, trim, replace, nospace, trunc, indent, contains, hasPrefix, hasSuffix, repeat, substr, title

🔢
Math

add, sub, mul, div, mod, max, min, floor, ceil, round

📅
Date

now, date, dateModify, htmlDate, htmlDateInZone, dateInZone

📋
Lists

list, first, last, append, prepend, concat, reverse, uniq, has, slice, sortAlpha
