Under the Hood — battle-tested chart development tricks from the official docs

Four techniques go beyond "here's what a function does" into genuine production patterns real chart maintainers rely on constantly.

① Reading a Pipeline Like an Assembly Line

Every pipeline is a left-to-right chain — each stage's output becomes the next stage's input. Breaking a complex pipeline into its stages makes it far easier to read (and write):

   VALUE EXTRACTION + FORMATTING PATTERNS
   ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

   {{ .Values.image.tag | default "latest" | quote }}
       │                    │                   │
       └─ get value         └─ fallback         └─ wrap in quotes
       Result: "v2.0" or "latest"

   {{ include "easypj.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
       │                            │
       └─ render named template     └─ indent 4 + newline
       Result: (indented label block)

   {{ .Values.config | toYaml | indent 8 }}
       │                   │           │
       └─ get object       └─ to YAML  └─ indent 8 spaces
       Result: (indented YAML for ConfigMap data)
② tpl on External Config Files — Not Just Values Strings

tpl's most powerful use isn't rendering a one-line greeting from values — it's rendering an ENTIRE external config file as a template, letting users embed {{ .Values.x }}-style placeholders inside files bundled with the chart:

   # files/conf/app.conf (bundled in the chart, NOT in templates/):
   firstName={{ .Values.firstName }}
   lastName={{ .Values.lastName }}

   # Template:
   {{ tpl (.Files.Get "conf/app.conf") . }}

   # values.yaml: firstName: Peter / lastName: Parker
   # Output:
   firstName=Peter
   lastName=Parker
③ Auto-Rolling Deployments on Config Change (the checksum/config trick)

A ConfigMap or Secret change alone does NOT trigger a pod restart — Kubernetes has no built-in "restart on config change" behavior. The standard Helm workaround: hash the rendered config and stash it in a Deployment annotation, so a config change becomes a Deployment change:

kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}
        checksum/secret: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/secret.yaml") . | sha256sum }}
# Every time the ConfigMap or Secret content changes, this checksum changes too
# → the Pod template changes → a rolling update is triggered automatically
🔑 Library chart caveat. Inside a library chart, $.Template.BasePath isn't available the same way. Reference the named template directly instead: {{ include "mylibchart.configmap" . | sha256sum }}.
④ Preventing Helm From Deleting a Resource

The annotation helm.sh/resource-policy: keep tells Helm to NEVER delete this specific resource — not even during helm uninstall:

kind: Secret
metadata:
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/resource-policy": keep
  name: critical-data
# This Secret survives helm uninstall — it becomes ORPHANED
# (still exists, but no longer tracked/managed by Helm)
# ⚠️ helm install --replace can then conflict with the orphaned resource

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Functions are single-purpose tools; pipelines chain them — | feeds one function's output directly into the next function's input, left to right.
  • default is the fail-safe function — the single highest-value habit in this entire chapter is wrapping every optional .Values reference in it.
  • indent and nindent are NOT interchangeable — nindent adds the newline first, making it correct after a bare key:; indent doesn't, making it correct when text continues on the same line as its key.
  • Always prefer include over template — only include returns a pipeline-friendly string.
  • Named templates need a chart-name prefix (easypj.fullname, not fullname) to avoid collisions once a chart has subcharts sharing the same template namespace.
  • lookup breaks the declarative model — it makes helm template fail entirely (no live API server) and should be reached for rarely, deliberately.
  • The checksum/config annotation trick is the standard, production-grade way to auto-trigger a rolling update whenever a ConfigMap or Secret changes.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • indent where nindent belongs. indent 4 adds 4 spaces to EVERY line, including the first — usually leaving that first line under-indented relative to its own YAML key. Always ask: does the value need to start on the SAME line as its key (indent) or the NEXT line (nindent)?
  • Piping the output of template. {{ template "x.labels" | indent 4 }} is an error — template writes inline with zero pipeline support. Use include whenever a pipeline is needed, which in practice is almost always.
  • Skipping the chart-name prefix on a named template. A bare {{ define "fullname" }} works fine in isolation but silently collides the moment the chart gains a subchart defining its own fullname.
  • Reaching for lookup as a first resort. It breaks helm template entirely (no cluster to query) and makes chart behavior non-deterministic — reserve it for genuinely unavoidable "does this already exist" checks.
  • Using $.Template.BasePath inside a library chart. It isn't available the same way there — reference the named template directly with include instead.
  • Assuming a ConfigMap/Secret change alone restarts pods. It doesn't — Kubernetes has no built-in "restart on config change." The checksum/config annotation trick (Under the Hood, §③) is required to make that happen.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Reflex-wrap every optional .Values reference in | default the moment you type it — don't wait for the nil-pointer error to remind you.
  • "Same line as key" → indent. "Next line after key:" → nindent. A one-second mental check that prevents a whole class of "why won't my YAML parse" bugs.
  • Default to include, never template, even when you don't currently need a pipeline — you'll almost always add one later, and switching then means re-touching every call site.
  • Prefix every named template with the chart name as a fixed habit — easypj.labels, not labels — from the very first template you write, not retrofitted later.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 7)

verifying function output and pipeline behavior 
# Render everything locally, see exactly what functions/pipelines produced
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart --debug

# Narrow the output to one file — faster iteration while debugging a pipeline
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart --show-only templates/configmap.yaml

# Lint catches most function-usage mistakes before rendering even runs
helm lint --strict ./easypj-chart

# Confirm what values a deployed release actually computed
helm get values easypj --all

# See the exact rendered manifests Helm submitted for a deployed release
helm get manifest easypj

🧠 Chapter 7 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of functions, pipelines, and named templates — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
How do you provide a default value if .Values.replicas is not set?
Show Answer
Answer

{{ .Values.replicas | default 3 }}. default returns the fallback if the value is nil, empty, or zero.

Explanation

default is the #1 safety function in Helm templating — every nullable value reference should use it unless the value is genuinely mandatory (in which case use required instead).

Q2
What's the difference between template and include?
Show Answer
Answer

template executes and writes inline, with no pipeline support. include returns a string, supporting pipelines like | indent or | quote. Always prefer include.

Explanation

{{ template "x.labels" | indent 4 }} is a hard error; {{ include "x.labels" . | indent 4 }} works fine — this exact distinction is a frequently tested exam concept.

Q3
How do you conditionally include a resource only in the production environment?
Show Answer
Answer

{{ if eq .Values.environment "production" }}...resource spec...{{ end }}. Use eq, ne, and, or, not for comparisons.

Explanation

Wrapping the entire resource (not just parts of it) in the conditional is the standard pattern — it either exists completely or is fully absent from the rendered output.

Q4
How do you iterate over a list of values in a template?
Show Answer
Answer

{{ range .Values.ingress.hosts }}...{{ .host }}...{{ end }}. Inside the loop, . refers to the current item. For maps: {{ range $k, $v := .Values.env }}.

Explanation

Remember from Chapter 6: inside this loop, plain .Values is no longer reachable — use $.Values if you also need something from the root while iterating.

Q5
How do you convert a values object into properly-indented YAML inside a ConfigMap?
Show Answer
Answer

{{ .Values.appConfig | toYaml | indent 4 }}. toYaml serializes the object; indent 4 adds the indentation ConfigMap data expects.

Explanation

Here indent (not nindent) is correct, because the YAML block continues immediately after app.yaml: | on the next line already provided by the literal block scalar — the exact judgment call from this chapter's central gotcha.

Q6
What does the tpl function do?
Show Answer
Answer

It evaluates a string AS a template. {{ tpl .Values.dynamicGreeting . }} renders template expressions found inside a value, at deploy time.

Explanation

Without tpl, a values.yaml string like "Hello from {{ .Release.Name }}" renders LITERALLY, braces and all — tpl is what actually evaluates those embedded braces.

Q7
Which function forces a value to be required, failing the render if it's missing?
Show Answer
Answer

{{ required "Error message" .Values.mandatoryKey }}. If the key is empty or nil, Helm fails immediately with that custom error message.

Explanation

required is the deliberate opposite of default — use it for values with genuinely no safe fallback, like a database password.

Q8
How do you chain multiple functions together in one expression?
Show Answer
Answer

The pipe | operator: {{ .Values.name | upper | quote }}. Each function's output becomes the next function's input, left to right.

Explanation

This is the exact "kitchen tools, assembly line" mental model from the chapter opener — order matters, since each stage transforms whatever the previous stage produced.

Q9
What does the lookup function do, and when should you avoid it?
Show Answer
Answer

It queries the live Kubernetes API at render time. Avoid it in most cases — it breaks Helm's declarative model and makes helm template fail entirely, since there's no API server to query during a pure render.

Explanation

Prefer values/config-driven approaches wherever possible; reach for lookup only for genuinely unavoidable "does this already exist" checks, and document why when you do.

Q10
Where do you define named templates, and what naming convention identifies that kind of file?
Show Answer
Answer

In a file starting with an underscore, conventionally _helpers.tpl. Files starting with _ are NOT deployed as Kubernetes resources — they exist purely to hold reusable named templates.

Explanation

This mirrors NOTES.txt from Chapter 3 — another special file processed by the template engine but never submitted to Kubernetes as a resource.

⚙️ Chapter 7 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

A broken pipeline or function call, and you fix it using the mental models from this chapter.

Q1
A ConfigMap's data block renders with the first line correctly indented but every subsequent line under-indented by 4 spaces relative to where it should be. What's the likely bug?
Show Answer
Answer

The template almost certainly used indent where nindent belongs (or vice versa) — check whether the value is meant to start on the same line as its key or the next line, and match the function to that.

Explanation

This exact symptom is the signature of the indent/nindent mismatch — one function adds a leading newline, the other doesn't, and mixing them up shows up as consistently-wrong indentation, not a crash.

Q2
A template does {{ template "easypj.labels" | quote }} and Helm throws a parse error at that exact line. Diagnose it.
Show Answer
Answer

template doesn't support pipelines — piping its output to quote is invalid syntax. Fix by switching to include: {{ include "easypj.labels" . | quote }}.

Explanation

This is exactly why the chapter's speed tip says "default to include, never template" — even when you don't need a pipeline today, you'll likely add one later.

Q3
You add a second chart as a dependency, and both charts define a template called fullname. Templates start rendering with the wrong chart's naming logic. What's the root cause and the fix?
Show Answer
Answer

Both templates share the same global template namespace once loaded together — the unprefixed name collided. Fix: rename each to <chartname>.fullname (e.g. easypj.fullname and postgresql.fullname), and always follow that convention going forward.

Explanation

This is precisely the collision scenario §7.7a warns about — the prefix convention exists specifically to prevent this, not as arbitrary style guidance.

Q4
You update a ConfigMap's values and run helm upgrade, but the running pods never pick up the new config — they keep serving stale data until manually restarted. Diagnose and fix.
Show Answer
Answer

Kubernetes doesn't restart pods automatically when a mounted ConfigMap changes. Add the checksum/config annotation trick to the Deployment's pod template so a config change also changes the Deployment spec, triggering a real rolling update.

Explanation

See Under the Hood §③ for the exact annotation pattern — this is one of the most common "why isn't my config change taking effect" real-world issues.

Q5
A chart maintainer wants an easypj database password to be provided by the user with NO silent fallback — a missing value must hard-fail the install. Write the line.
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
password: {{ required "database.password must be set" .Values.database.password | quote }}
Explanation

required combined with quote is the standard pattern for mandatory string values — it fails loudly and specifically, rather than deploying with an empty password.

Q6
During a code review, you spot {{ $svc := lookup "v1" "Service" .Release.Namespace "easypj-svc" }} used purely to decide a default port number. Is this appropriate? What would you suggest instead?
Show Answer
Answer

Not appropriate — using lookup for something a values default could handle breaks helm template and makes the chart non-deterministic for no real benefit. Suggest a plain {{ .Values.service.port | default 8000 }} instead.

Explanation

Reserve lookup for cases with no values-driven alternative, like "only create this Secret if one doesn't already exist" — not as a general substitute for defaults.

Q7
Write a pipeline that takes .Values.appName, uppercases it, and safely quotes it for YAML — in one line.
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
name: {{ .Values.appName | upper | quote }}
Explanation

Three stages, left to right: get the value, transform it, format it for safe YAML output — the canonical pipeline shape used throughout this guide.

Q8
A values.yaml field is meant to let end users customize a startup banner message that itself references {{ .Release.Name }}. Plain interpolation renders the literal braces instead of the release name. What's missing?
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
banner: {{ tpl .Values.bannerMessage . }}
Explanation

Without tpl, a string pulled from values is inserted literally — including any {{ }} it happens to contain. tpl is specifically what evaluates those embedded expressions.

Q9
You need to permanently keep a specific Secret even after the whole release is uninstalled — it holds data other systems depend on. What's the one-line fix?
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
metadata:
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/resource-policy": keep
Explanation

Add this annotation to that specific resource only — everything else in the chart still gets cleaned up normally on uninstall; only this one resource is deliberately orphaned.

Q10
Design a named template call that generates standard Kubernetes labels, safely indented for insertion under a metadata.labels: key.
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
metadata:
  labels:
    {{- include "easypj.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
Explanation

nindent is correct here — the labels need to start on a NEW line after labels:, exactly the "next line after key:" case this chapter's central gotcha describes.

🔬 Practice Drill 7.1 — indent vs nindent, Side by Side

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Given data:\n config.yaml: | as a starting point, write the correct function call to embed {{ .Files.Get "config.yaml" }} beneath it at 4-space indentation, and explain in one sentence why it's indent and not nindent.

Hint: The | block scalar already puts you on a new line — does the function ALSO need to add one?
View Solution 
data:
  config.yaml: |
{{ .Files.Get "config.yaml" | indent 4 }}

Why indent, not nindent: the YAML | block scalar syntax already places the content on its own new line — adding nindent's extra leading newline here would create a stray blank line before the content. indent alone is correct.

🔬 Practice Drill 7.2 — Write a Named Template With the Correct Prefix

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Define a named template called easypj.selectorLabels that outputs app.kubernetes.io/name and app.kubernetes.io/instance, then call it correctly from a Deployment's spec.selector.matchLabels.

Hint: define creates it, include ... | nindent calls it.
View Solution
_helpers.tpl + deployment.yaml
# _helpers.tpl
{{- define "easypj.selectorLabels" -}}
app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
{{- end }}

# deployment.yaml
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      {{- include "easypj.selectorLabels" . | nindent 6 }}

Check yourself: the indentation level (6 spaces here, matching matchLabels:'s children) has to match wherever it's called FROM — the same named template gets a different nindent number depending on where it's included.

🔬 Practice Drill 7.3 — Build a Multi-Environment Replica Count with range/if

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Write a template snippet that sets replicas: 5 for production, 2 for staging, and 1 for everything else, based on .Values.environment.

Hint: if / else if / else — exactly the three-branch pattern from §7.6a.
View Solution
yaml
{{ if eq .Values.environment "production" }}
  replicas: 5
{{ else if eq .Values.environment "staging" }}
  replicas: 2
{{ else }}
  replicas: 1
{{ end }}

Check yourself: test all three branches by setting --set environment=production, =staging, and omitting it entirely — each should render a different replica count.

🔬 Practice Drill 7.4 — Add the Checksum/Config Auto-Rollout Annotation

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Add the checksum/config trick to a Deployment template so that any change to configmap.yaml automatically triggers a rolling update, then verify it actually changes across two renders with different config values.

Hint: the annotation value must be a hash of the RENDERED configmap, not the raw values.
View Solution
yaml + verification
annotations:
  checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}
bash
helm template easypj ./chart --set config.debug=true | grep checksum/config
helm template easypj ./chart --set config.debug=false | grep checksum/config
# the two hash values should differ

Check yourself: if the two hashes are IDENTICAL despite different values, the checksum is hashing something that doesn't actually change (a common copy-paste mistake) — double-check the file path passed to include.

🔬 Practice Drill 7.5 — Refactor a Fragile Template Into a Safe One

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

The following line will crash if .Values.image.pullPolicy is unset, and produces invalid YAML if the tag ever contains a colon: image: {{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}. Rewrite it to be fully safe.

Hint: This drill needs BOTH a default/required guard AND a quote.
View Solution
yaml
image: "{{ required "image.repository is required" .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag | default "latest" }}"

Check yourself: the repository is treated as mandatory (required, since there's no sensible default), the tag has a safe fallback (default "latest"), and the whole expression is wrapped in literal double quotes since it produces a compound string value with a colon in it.

📌 Chapter 7 Visual Summary — 70+ functions, one composition rule
  🔤 STRINGS               🔄 TYPES                🛡️ DEFAULTS
  ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐        ┌───────────────────┐
  │ quote, upper,│         │ toYaml,       │        │ default, required, │
  │ trim, indent │         │ fromYaml,     │        │ empty, coalesce    │
  │               │        │ toJson        │        │                     │
  └──────────────┘         └──────────────┘        └───────────────────┘

  🔀 FLOW                  📦 NAMED                ▶️ PIPELINE
  ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐        ┌───────────────────┐
  │ if/else,      │        │ define,       │        │ chain functions     │
  │ with, range   │        │ template,     │        │ left→right with |   │
  │               │        │ include       │        │                     │
  └──────────────┘         └──────────────┘        └───────────────────┘
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   THE ONE RULE: {{ get value | transform | format }} — every non-trivial
   template expression in this guide follows this same three-stage shape. ▶️

In words: Templates get their real power not from any single function, but from composing many small ones together with |. String, type, math, and date functions transform raw data; default/required/empty guard against missing values; if/with/range control what renders at all; define/template/include package logic for reuse across every template in the chart.

The recurring three-stage pipeline shape — get a value, transform or default it, format it safely for YAML — appears constantly once you start looking for it, and is worth internalizing as THE template-writing pattern for this entire guide.

The takeaway: Chapter 6 gave templates data to work with; this chapter gave them the vocabulary to actually DO something with that data. Chapter 8 puts both to work, building every template easypj's real chart needs from scratch.

Chapter 8 · Building the easypj Chart Templates — Real-World Practice

Now everything from Chapters 6 and 7 gets applied to build the complete easypj chart. Each template below is a real, working example directly adaptable for any Django application — this is where the abstract syntax and functions stop being abstract and become the actual chart reused in every remaining chapter and lab.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🛠️ Hands-On 🐍 easypj / jobpost 🎯 Chart Creation & Anatomy

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Build a parameterized, production-ready Deployment template for Django
  • ✅ Create Service, ConfigMap, Secret, Ingress, and HPA templates
  • ✅ Write helpful NOTES.txt for post-install guidance
  • ✅ Create reusable helper functions in _helpers.tpl
🎓 Helm Certification Relevance
Chart Creation & Anatomy HANDS-ON
🎯 Each Template Is a Cookie Cutter Shape

.Values is the dough — same cutter, different dough per environment, same shape of Kubernetes resource comes out every time. Two things to watch closely while building:

  • envFrom/configMapRef names must EXACTLY match the rendered ConfigMap/Secret name (produced via include "easypj.fullname" .). A typo here fails silently at pod-start, not at helm install — the pod goes CreateContainerConfigError, and the fix is always a name mismatch somewhere.
  • Test ONE template at a time. helm template ./chart -s templates/deployment.yaml isolates output and finds bugs far faster than scrolling a full multi-resource render.

🧭 Section Map — the Chapter 8 Learning Arc

Eight templates, one chart — each section builds one file, in the same order Helm itself processes a Deployment's dependencies: workload, network, config, secrets, external access, scaling, and the two non-resource files that round out a real chart.

easypj Template-to-Resource Map
   templates/deployment.yaml  ──▶  Deployment  (runs Django pods)
   templates/service.yaml     ──▶  Service     (internal networking)
   templates/configmap.yaml   ──▶  ConfigMap   (DEBUG, ALLOWED_HOSTS)
   templates/secret.yaml      ──▶  Secret      (DB password, keys)
   templates/ingress.yaml     ──▶  Ingress     (external HTTP entry)
   templates/hpa.yaml         ──▶  HPA         (auto-scale by load)
   templates/NOTES.txt        ──▶  (nothing — post-install message)
   templates/_helpers.tpl     ──▶  (nothing — shared logic only)
#SectionWhat It Builds
8.1Deployment TemplateThe Django pods themselves — parameterized, production-hardened
8.2Service TemplateStable internal networking to those pods
8.3ConfigMap TemplateNon-sensitive app settings
8.4Secret TemplateDatabase credentials, base64-encoded
8.5Ingress TemplateOptional external HTTP entry point
8.6HPA TemplateOptional CPU-based auto-scaling
8.7NOTES.txtUser-facing output shown right after install
8.8_helpers.tplThe shared naming/labeling logic every other template calls

8.1 Deployment Template — Parameterized for Flexibility

The production-ready version below layers in image pull secrets, a security context, liveness probing, and the checksum/config auto-rollout trick from Chapter 7 — not just the bare minimum.

templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ include "easypj.fullname" . }}
  labels:
    {{- include "easypj.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
  annotations:
    checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}
    # forces a pod restart whenever the ConfigMap changes
spec:
  {{- if not .Values.autoscaling.enabled }}
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  {{- end }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      {{- include "easypj.selectorLabels" . | nindent 6 }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        {{- include "easypj.selectorLabels" . | nindent 8 }}
    spec:
      {{- with .Values.imagePullSecrets }}
      imagePullSecrets:
        {{- toYaml . | nindent 8 }}
      {{- end }}
      securityContext:
        {{- toYaml .Values.podSecurityContext | nindent 8 }}
      containers:
      - name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
        image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
        imagePullPolicy: {{ .Values.image.pullPolicy }}
        ports:
        - name: http
          containerPort: {{ .Values.service.port }}
        {{- if .Values.probes.liveness }}
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: {{ .Values.probes.path }}
            port: http
          initialDelaySeconds: {{ .Values.probes.initialDelay }}
        {{- end }}
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: {{ include "easypj.fullname" . }}-config
        - secretRef:
            name: {{ include "easypj.fullname" . }}-secret
        env:
        {{- range .Values.env }}
        - name: {{ .name }}
          value: {{ .value | quote }}
        {{- end }}
        resources:
          {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 10 }}
💡 Note the if not .Values.autoscaling.enabled guard

When the HPA (§8.6) is active, it owns replicas — setting a fixed replicaCount here too would fight the autoscaler on every reconcile. Only set replicas when autoscaling is off.

8.2 Service Template — Ports, Type, Selectors

templates/service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: {{ include "easypj.fullname" . }}
  labels:
    {{- include "easypj.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
spec:
  type: {{ .Values.service.type }}
  ports:
  - port: {{ .Values.service.port }}
    targetPort: http
    protocol: TCP
  selector:
    {{- include "easypj.selectorLabels" . | nindent 4 }}

8.3 ConfigMap Template — appSettings from values.yaml

templates/configmap.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: {{ include "easypj.fullname" . }}-config
data:
  DEBUG: {{ .Values.config.debug | quote }}
  ALLOWED_HOSTS: {{ .Values.config.allowedHosts | quote }}
  DB_HOST: {{ .Release.Name }}-postgresql
  REDIS_HOST: {{ .Release.Name }}-redis-master

8.4 Secret Template — Database Credentials

templates/secret.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: {{ include "easypj.fullname" . }}-secret
type: Opaque
data:
  SECRET_KEY: {{ .Values.config.secretKey | b64enc | quote }}
  DB_PASSWORD: {{ .Values.postgresql.auth.password | b64enc | quote }}
⚠️ These Are Placeholders, Not Practice

Real production charts never put actual secret values in values.yaml — .Values.postgresql.auth.password here should be injected at deploy time (--set from a CI secret store) or managed via Sealed Secrets/External Secrets Operator, never committed as plaintext.

8.5 Ingress Template — Optional with Conditional

templates/ingress.yaml
{{ if .Values.ingress.enabled }}
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: {{ include "easypj.fullname" . }}
spec:
  rules:
  {{ range .Values.ingress.hosts }}
  - host: {{ .host | quote }}
    http:
      paths:
      {{ range .paths }}
      - path: {{ .path }}
        pathType: {{ .pathType }}
        backend:
          service:
            name: {{ include "easypj.fullname" $ }}
            port:
              number: {{ $.Values.service.port }}
      {{ end }}
  {{ end }}
{{ end }}
⚠️ Note the $ Inside the Nested Range

Two range blocks are nested here (hosts, then paths). Inside the inner one, plain . refers to a path item — include "easypj.fullname" . would be wrong. $ reaches back to the true root, exactly as Chapter 6/7 covered.

8.6 HPA Template — Auto-Scaling Configuration

templates/hpa.yaml
{{ if .Values.autoscaling.enabled }}
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: {{ include "easypj.fullname" . }}
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: {{ include "easypj.fullname" . }}
  minReplicas: {{ .Values.autoscaling.minReplicas }}
  maxReplicas: {{ .Values.autoscaling.maxReplicas }}
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: {{ .Values.autoscaling.targetCPUUtilizationPercentage }}
{{ end }}

8.7 NOTES.txt — User-Facing Output on Install

templates/NOTES.txt
🎉 Thank you for installing {{ .Chart.Name }}!

Your Django job board application has been deployed.

📋 Release: {{ .Release.Name }}
📦 Namespace: {{ .Release.Namespace }}
🔄 Replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}

{{ if .Values.ingress.enabled }}
🌐 Access your application at:
{{ range .Values.ingress.hosts }}
  http://{{ .host }}
{{ end }}
{{ else }}
🔧 To access the application, run:
  kubectl port-forward svc/{{ include "easypj.fullname" . }} 8000:{{ .Values.service.port }}
{{ end }}

📊 Check status: helm status {{ .Release.Name }}
📝 Run migrations: kubectl exec deploy/{{ include "easypj.fullname" . }} -- python manage.py migrate

8.8 _helpers.tpl — Reusable Template Helpers

Every other template calls into these four named templates — this is the single source of truth for naming and labeling across the entire chart.

templates/_helpers.tpl
{{/*
Expand the name of the chart.
*/}}
{{- define "easypj.name" -}}
{{- default .Chart.Name .Values.nameOverride | trunc 63 | trimSuffix "-" }}
{{- end }}

{{/*
Create a fully qualified app name. Truncated at 63 chars because
some Kubernetes name fields are limited to that length.
*/}}
{{- define "easypj.fullname" -}}
{{- if .Values.fullnameOverride }}
{{- .Values.fullnameOverride | trunc 63 | trimSuffix "-" }}
{{- else }}
{{- $name := default .Chart.Name .Values.nameOverride }}
{{- printf "%s-%s" .Release.Name $name | trunc 63 | trimSuffix "-" }}
{{- end }}
{{- end }}

{{/*
Common labels
*/}}
{{- define "easypj.labels" -}}
helm.sh/chart: {{ .Chart.Name }}-{{ .Chart.Version }}
{{ include "easypj.selectorLabels" . }}
{{- if .Chart.AppVersion }}
app.kubernetes.io/version: {{ .Chart.AppVersion | quote }}
{{- end }}
app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: {{ .Release.Service }}
{{- end }}

{{/*
Selector labels — the stable subset used for matchLabels/selectors,
which cannot change between releases (unlike the full label set above).
*/}}
{{- define "easypj.selectorLabels" -}}
app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ include "easypj.name" . }}
app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
{{- end }}
🎯 Naming Convention, Tested Frequently

Always call these with include "easypj.fullname" . — never template. include returns a pipeline-friendly string; template writes directly to output and cannot be piped through nindent, trunc, or anything else.

Under the Hood — the full testing workflow, and the container behind the chart

A chart is only half the picture — it deploys a container image that has to exist first, and it should never reach production without passing through a fixed validation sequence.

① Template Testing Workflow — Validate Before Deploying

Six steps, each one catching a different class of error before it can reach a real cluster:

1
Lint

helm lint ./easypj-chart — checks Chart.yaml syntax, template rendering, and best practices. Catches YAML errors before they reach the cluster.

2
Template (local render)

helm template easypj-test ./easypj-chart -f values-dev.yaml --debug — renders templates locally with zero cluster access. Verify the output YAML looks correct.

3
Dry-Run (cluster simulation)

helm install easypj-test ./easypj-chart --dry-run --debug — simulates the install against the live cluster, validating API versions and resource types without creating anything.

4
Deploy to Dev

helm install easypj-dev ./easypj-chart -f values-dev.yaml -n dev --create-namespace — deploy to a dev namespace first. Verify pods are running and healthy.

5
Run Tests

helm test easypj-dev -n dev — execute test pods to verify connectivity, DB access, and API endpoints respond correctly.

6
Promote to Production

helm upgrade --install easypj-prod ./easypj-chart -f values-prod.yaml -n production --atomic --wait --timeout 10m

🔑 Never skip steps 1–3. The certification exam specifically tests the ability to catch errors BEFORE deploying — a failed install wastes precious time that lint/template/dry-run would have saved for free.
② The Container Behind the Chart — a Production Dockerfile

Helm deploys Kubernetes resources, but the actual application runs inside a container built separately. A multi-stage build keeps the final image lean and non-root:

Dockerfile — multi-stage build for easypj
# Stage 1: build dependencies
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Stage 2: production image
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app

# Create a non-root user
RUN groupadd -r easypj && useradd -r -g easypj easypj

# Copy Python dependencies from the builder stage only — not the build tools
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /home/easypj/.local

# Copy application code
COPY --chown=easypj:easypj . .

ENV PATH=/home/easypj/.local/bin:$PATH \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=easypj.settings

RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

USER easypj
EXPOSE 8000

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s \
  CMD python manage.py check --deploy || exit 1

CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", \
     "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", \
     "--workers", "4", \
     "--access-logfile", "-"]
   BUILD → PUSH → DEPLOY PIPELINE
   ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐
   │ Docker   │     │ Container    │     │ Helm deploys      │
   │ Build    │────▶│ Registry     │────▶│ to Kubernetes     │
   │ docker   │     │ (Docker Hub, │     │ helm upgrade      │
   │ build -t │     │  ACR, ECR,   │     │ --install easypj  │
   │ easypj   │     │  GCR, etc.)  │     │ ./chart --set     │
   │          │     │ docker push  │     │ image.tag=v2.0.0  │
   └──────────┘     └──────────────┘     └──────────────────┘

   🔑 The image tag in values.yaml MUST match the tag you actually pushed —
      values.yaml: image.tag: "v2.0.0"  ←  must match `docker push` tag exactly

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Eight files, one chart — six render as real Kubernetes resources (Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, Ingress, HPA), two never do (NOTES.txt, _helpers.tpl).
  • Names must match exactly between templates. envFrom.configMapRef.name in deployment.yaml and the actual name in configmap.yaml both derive from include "easypj.fullname" . — as long as both call the SAME named template, they can never drift apart.
  • Autoscaling and a fixed replica count fight each other. The {{- if not .Values.autoscaling.enabled }}replicas: ...{{- end }} guard in the Deployment prevents that conflict.
  • Secrets need base64, never plaintext commitment. | b64enc | quote handles the encoding; the actual value should come from a deploy-time override, never a value baked into a tracked file.
  • Six manual validation steps exist for a reason — lint, template, dry-run, deploy-to-dev, test, promote. Each catches a different failure class, and skipping any of the first three wastes far more time than running them.
  • The Helm chart and the Docker image are separate, coordinated artifacts — the chart's image.tag value must exactly match whatever tag was actually pushed to the registry.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • envFrom/configMapRef name mismatch. If the ConfigMap/Secret name referenced in envFrom doesn't EXACTLY match the rendered name, the failure is silent at helm install time — it only surfaces later as CreateContainerConfigError when the pod actually tries to start. Always derive both sides from the same include "easypj.fullname" . call, never hand-type either one.
  • Setting replicas alongside an enabled HPA. Once autoscaling is active, it owns the replica count — a hardcoded value in the Deployment spec causes a tug-of-war on every reconcile loop.
  • Forgetting the nested-range $ in Ingress. With hosts nested inside paths, plain . inside the inner loop refers to a path item, not the root — include "easypj.fullname" $ is required, not include "easypj.fullname" ..
  • Treating values.yaml's secret fields as if they were real secrets. They're placeholders meant to be overridden at deploy time — committing an actual password there defeats the entire purpose of type: Opaque + b64enc.
  • Assuming NOTES.txt output persists. It's shown once, right after install/upgrade — helm status <release> is how you see it again later, not helm get notes run at some arbitrary future point (which DOES work, but people often don't realize NOTES.txt isn't stored anywhere they can casually browse).
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Test ONE template at a time. helm template ./chart -s templates/deployment.yaml isolates output and finds bugs far faster than scrolling a full multi-resource render every time.
  • Never skip lint → template → dry-run before a real install, even under exam time pressure — all three are free and instant, and catch the large majority of mistakes.
  • Copy the naming pattern, don't reinvent it. Every new resource template should start from the same include "easypj.fullname" . / include "easypj.labels" . | nindent 4 boilerplate as the templates already in this chapter.
  • When a pod won't start, check envFrom names first. A silent name mismatch is the single most common cause of a working chart that still produces a broken pod.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 8)

the full build-to-production sequence 
# 1. Build and push the container image
docker build -t myregistry.io/easypj:v2.0.0 .
docker push myregistry.io/easypj:v2.0.0

# 2. Validate the chart (steps 1-3 of the testing workflow)
helm lint ./easypj-chart
helm template easypj-test ./easypj-chart -f values-dev.yaml --debug
helm install easypj-test ./easypj-chart --dry-run --debug

# 3. Isolate a single template while debugging
helm template easypj-test ./easypj-chart -s templates/deployment.yaml

# 4. Deploy to dev, verify, then promote
helm install easypj-dev ./easypj-chart -f values-dev.yaml -n dev --create-namespace
helm test easypj-dev -n dev
helm upgrade --install easypj-prod ./easypj-chart -f values-prod.yaml -n production --atomic --wait --timeout 10m

🧠 Chapter 8 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of building real templates — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
How do you make an entire resource conditional — e.g., only create the Ingress if it's enabled?
Show Answer
Answer

{{ if .Values.ingress.enabled }}...full Ingress YAML...{{ end }}. Wrap the ENTIRE resource, from apiVersion to the last field.

Explanation

If ingress.enabled: false, the resource is completely skipped — no empty YAML, no error, nothing rendered at all for that file.

Q2
How do you reference a ConfigMap in a Deployment's envFrom, and why must the name be exactly right?
Show Answer
Answer

envFrom: [{ configMapRef: { name: {{ include "easypj.fullname" . }}-config } }]. Because the same computed name must exist in the actual ConfigMap resource — a mismatch fails silently at pod-start, not at install time.

Explanation

Always derive both sides (the ConfigMap's own metadata.name and the Deployment's configMapRef.name) from the exact same include call, so they can never drift independently.

Q3
What's the purpose of _helpers.tpl, and what naming rule applies to it?
Show Answer
Answer

It defines reusable named templates (names, labels, selectors). Files starting with _ are never deployed as Kubernetes resources — invoke their contents with {{ include "helperName" . }}.

Explanation

This is the file every OTHER template in the chart depends on — a bug in _helpers.tpl ripples into every resource that calls easypj.fullname or easypj.labels.

Q4
How do you safely pass a value from values.yaml into a Secret's data field?
Show Answer
Answer

{{ .Values.secretValue | b64enc | quote }}. Kubernetes Secret data fields require base64-encoded values — b64enc handles the encoding at render time.

Explanation

The value itself should still come from a deploy-time override or CI secret store, never a real credential hardcoded in values.yaml — b64enc solves the encoding requirement, not the security requirement.

Q5
How do you render resource limits/requests from values.yaml directly into a container spec?
Show Answer
Answer

resources: {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 10 }}. toYaml serializes the whole object; nindent 10 places it correctly on the line after resources:.

Explanation

The indentation number (10, here) has to match the container's actual nesting depth in the surrounding YAML — get this wrong and the resources block attaches to the wrong parent key.

Q6
Where does NOTES.txt output actually appear, and how do you see it again later?
Show Answer
Answer

It's printed to the terminal once, immediately after helm install/upgrade completes. To see it again later: helm get notes <release>.

Explanation

NOTES.txt is not a Kubernetes resource — it's purely user-facing text, rendered through the exact same template engine as every other file but never submitted to the cluster.

Q7
How do labels defined once in _helpers.tpl end up applied to every resource in the chart?
Show Answer
Answer

Each resource template calls {{- include "easypj.labels" . | nindent 4 }} under its own metadata.labels: key — the named template's returned string gets indented into that specific spot.

Explanation

This is why every template in this chapter looks structurally similar — they all share the same handful of include calls into the same handful of named templates.

Q8
In the Deployment template, why is replicas wrapped in {{- if not .Values.autoscaling.enabled }}...{{- end }} instead of being set unconditionally?
Show Answer
Answer

Because when the HPA (§8.6) is active, IT owns the replica count. A hardcoded replicas field would conflict with the autoscaler on every reconcile — omitting the field entirely when autoscaling is on avoids the fight.

Explanation

This exact pattern — a template field conditionally omitted based on a related feature flag — is common in real production charts wherever two controllers could otherwise both claim ownership of the same field.

Q9
The Ingress template has TWO nested range blocks (hosts, then paths). How do you reference the root context from inside the innermost one?
Show Answer
Answer

$ — it always refers to the true root context, regardless of how many range/with blocks are nested. include "easypj.fullname" $, not ..

Explanation

Two levels deep, plain . means "the current path item" — completely unrelated to the release/chart context the fullname template actually needs.

Q10
What's the complete workflow for validating a template CHANGE before it ever reaches a real cluster?
Show Answer
Answer

helm lint ./chart → helm template ./chart --debug → helm install test ./chart --dry-run --debug → only then a real install. Lint catches syntax, template shows exact rendered output, dry-run simulates the real thing.

Explanation

This is exactly Under the Hood's six-step workflow's first three steps — the part that happens before anything touches a real namespace.

⚙️ Chapter 8 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

A broken easypj deployment, and you diagnose it using this chapter's actual templates.

Q1
A pod is stuck in CreateContainerConfigError right after a fresh helm install that otherwise reported success. What do you check first?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>
kubectl get configmap,secret -n <namespace>
Explanation

This error means a referenced ConfigMap/Secret doesn't exist under the name the Deployment expects — almost always an envFrom name mismatch, exactly this chapter's central gotcha.

Q2
You edited only configmap.yaml and ran helm upgrade, but the running pods keep serving the OLD config. What's missing from the Deployment template?
Show Answer
Answer

The checksum/config annotation from §8.1 — without it, changing a ConfigMap alone doesn't change the Deployment's pod template, so Kubernetes has no reason to restart any pods.

Explanation

Add checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }} as a pod-template annotation — this is the Chapter 7 Under the Hood trick, applied for real here.

Q3
You enable autoscaling (autoscaling.enabled=true) but replicas keep resetting to the fixed replicaCount value every time you deploy. Diagnose the template bug.
Show Answer
Answer

The Deployment template is missing (or has a broken) {{- if not .Values.autoscaling.enabled }} guard around replicas: — it's setting replicas unconditionally, fighting the HPA on every reconcile.

Explanation

Verify with helm template ./chart --set autoscaling.enabled=true | grep replicas — the field should be entirely absent from the rendered output when autoscaling is on.

Q4
A teammate hardcodes DB_PASSWORD: cGFzc3dvcmQ= directly into secret.yaml, bypassing values.yaml entirely, because "it's already base64 anyway." What's wrong with this?
Show Answer
Answer

Base64 is encoding, not encryption — cGFzc3dvcmQ= trivially decodes to "password." Worse, it's now hardcoded directly in the template file (committed to Git), rather than injectable per-environment via values/overrides.

Explanation

The correct pattern keeps {{ .Values.postgresql.auth.password | b64enc | quote }} in the template, with the actual value supplied at deploy time — never a literal encoded string baked in.

Q5
Your Ingress renders with an empty rules: list even though values.yaml clearly has two hosts defined. What's the most likely template bug?
Show Answer
Answer

The outer {{ if .Values.ingress.enabled }} is probably evaluating false, OR .Values.ingress.hosts is empty/misspelled. Verify with helm template ./chart --show-only templates/ingress.yaml and check the ACTUAL computed values with helm get values --all.

Explanation

An empty-but-present rules: almost always traces back to the range source being empty, not a syntax error in the range itself — always verify the input before debugging the loop.

Q6
You want to confirm the Deployment template renders correctly for the production values file, without touching any other template. One command?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart -f values-prod.yaml -s templates/deployment.yaml
Explanation

-s/--show-only narrows a multi-template render to exactly one file — the Speed Tip "test one template at a time," applied.

Q7
A new engineer asks why _helpers.tpl doesn't show up as a resource when they run kubectl get all after installing the chart. What's the one-sentence answer?
Show Answer
Answer

Files starting with an underscore are never deployed as Kubernetes resources — they're processed by the template engine purely to define reusable logic other templates call into.

Explanation

This is exactly the same rule as NOTES.txt — both are special-cased by Helm's rendering pipeline (Chapter 6's Under the Hood) as non-resource output.

Q8
You changed the Docker image but forgot to update values.yaml's image.tag before deploying. What actually happens on helm upgrade?
Show Answer
Answer

Nothing new deploys — Kubernetes pulls whatever tag the chart specifies, which is still the OLD one. No error occurs; the "upgrade" silently redeploys the same old image.

Explanation

This is exactly why Under the Hood's build→push→deploy diagram flags the tag-matching requirement explicitly — a mismatched tag fails silently, not loudly.

Q9
Design the minimal command sequence to build a new image, push it, and deploy it to production via this chart — assuming the chart and values files already exist.
Show Answer
Answer
bash
docker build -t myregistry.io/easypj:v2.1.0 .
docker push myregistry.io/easypj:v2.1.0
helm upgrade --install easypj-prod ./easypj-chart \
  -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=v2.1.0 \
  -n production --atomic --wait --timeout 10m
Explanation

The --set image.tag=v2.1.0 overrides whatever values-prod.yaml currently has, which is exactly how a CI/CD pipeline injects a freshly-built tag without editing a tracked file per deploy.

Q10
Someone asks you to add a readiness probe to complement the existing liveness probe in the Deployment template, reusing the same path/port pattern. Sketch it.
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
{{- if .Values.probes.readiness }}
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: {{ .Values.probes.path }}
    port: http
  initialDelaySeconds: {{ .Values.probes.readinessInitialDelay | default 5 }}
{{- end }}
Explanation

Mirroring the existing livenessProbe's conditional-plus-values-driven shape keeps the template internally consistent — new fields should follow the established pattern, not introduce a different style.

🔬 Practice Drill 8.1 — Build & Deploy the Complete easypj Chart

⏱️ Target Time: 15 minutes
Scenario

Your team needs a Helm chart for the easypj Django app. Build it from scratch and deploy to a dev namespace:

  1. Scaffold: helm create easypj-chart, then delete the default templates.
  2. Chart.yaml: set name, appVersion: "2.1.0", type: application.
  3. values.yaml: set image.repository=easypj/easypj, image.tag=v2.1, service.port=8000, ingress.enabled=true.
  4. deployment.yaml: use the template from §8.1 with ConfigMap/Secret envFrom.
  5. service.yaml: ClusterIP, port 8000, selector labels from _helpers.tpl.
  6. configmap.yaml: DEBUG=false, ALLOWED_HOSTS=*, DB_HOST from the release name.
  7. secret.yaml: SECRET_KEY and DB_PASSWORD with b64enc.
  8. Validate: helm lint ./easypj-chart.
  9. Dry-run: helm install test ./easypj-chart --dry-run --debug.
  10. Deploy: helm install easypj-dev ./easypj-chart -n dev --create-namespace.
Hint: Every name reference (ConfigMap, Secret, Service) must trace back to the same include "easypj.fullname" . call.
View Solution
verification
# Verify the deployment
kubectl get all -n dev
helm list -n dev
helm status easypj-dev -n dev

# Confirm template rendering matches expectations
helm template easypj-dev ./easypj-chart -f values-dev.yaml --debug

# Check computed values
helm get values easypj-dev -n dev --all

# If something's broken, inspect the actual submitted manifest
helm get manifest easypj-dev -n dev | grep -A5 "kind:"

Check yourself: all pods should reach Running, helm status should show deployed, and every resource name in kubectl get all should match the pattern easypj-dev-easypj (release-name + chart-name, exactly as easypj.fullname computes it).

🔬 Practice Drill 8.2 — Break and Fix the envFrom Name

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Deliberately introduce a typo in configmap.yaml's name (add -cfg instead of -config), redeploy, and observe the exact failure mode. Then fix it.

Hint: The install itself will report success — the failure surfaces one layer down.
View Solution
bash
helm upgrade --install easypj-dev ./easypj-chart -n dev
kubectl get pods -n dev
# CreateContainerConfigError
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n dev
# Events: configmap "easypj-dev-easypj-cfg" not found

Check yourself: helm install reported success even though the ConfigMap name was wrong — this proves the mismatch is invisible until the pod actually tries to start, exactly this chapter's central gotcha.

🔬 Practice Drill 8.3 — Verify the Checksum/Config Trick Actually Works

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Deploy easypj, note the Deployment's current pod template hash, change config.debug in values, upgrade, and confirm a rolling restart actually happened.

Hint: kubectl rollout status and comparing checksum/config annotations before/after are both valid proof.
View Solution
bash
helm install easypj-dev ./easypj-chart -n dev --create-namespace
kubectl get deploy easypj-dev-easypj -n dev -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.metadata.annotations.checksum/config}'

helm upgrade easypj-dev ./easypj-chart -n dev --set config.debug=true
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-dev-easypj -n dev
kubectl get deploy easypj-dev-easypj -n dev -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.metadata.annotations.checksum/config}'
# the two checksum values should differ, and a rollout should have occurred

Check yourself: if the checksum DIDN'T change, double-check the ConfigMap template path passed to include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") — a wrong path silently hashes the wrong (unchanging) content.

🔬 Practice Drill 8.4 — Toggle Autoscaling and Confirm No Conflict

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Render the chart twice — once with autoscaling.enabled=false, once with true — and confirm replicas: appears in exactly one of the two outputs.

Hint: helm template ... | grep replicas: on both renders.
View Solution
bash
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart --set autoscaling.enabled=false | grep "replicas:"
# shows: replicas: 2  (or whatever replicaCount is)

helm template easypj ./easypj-chart --set autoscaling.enabled=true | grep "replicas:"
# shows: nothing — the Deployment's replicas field is entirely absent

Check yourself: if replicas: appears in BOTH renders, the {{- if not .Values.autoscaling.enabled }} guard is missing or broken — go fix the Deployment template before this drill "passes."

🔬 Practice Drill 8.5 — Trace a Resource Name End-to-End

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

For a release named easypj-prod installed from a chart named easypj, compute by hand (no helm template) what include "easypj.fullname" . would return, then verify it.

Hint: Trace through §8.8's easypj.fullname definition step by step — check fullnameOverride first, then fall back to the release+chart pattern.
View Solution

By hand: assuming no fullnameOverride is set, the template falls to printf "%s-%s" .Release.Name $name where $name defaults to .Chart.Name (assuming no nameOverride either) — so the result is easypj-prod-easypj.

bash
helm template easypj-prod ./easypj-chart | grep "name: easypj"

Check yourself: the actual rendered name should match your by-hand computation exactly — if it doesn't, walk back through the if/else branches in easypj.fullname to find where your assumption diverged from the real logic.

📌 Chapter 8 Visual Summary — eight files, one working chart
  📄 Deployment            🌐 Service                ⚙️ ConfigMap
  ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐          ┌───────────────────┐
  │ parameterized │        │ ports &        │         │ non-sensitive       │
  │ pod spec +    │        │ selectors      │         │ app settings        │
  │ checksum trick│        │                │         │                     │
  └──────────────┘         └──────────────┘          └───────────────────┘

  🔐 Secret                🚪 Ingress                📈 HPA
  ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐          ┌───────────────────┐
  │ credentials   │        │ conditional,   │         │ conditional,        │
  │ (b64enc)      │        │ nested range   │         │ owns replicas when  │
  │               │        │ + $ scope      │         │ enabled              │
  └──────────────┘         └──────────────┘          └───────────────────┘

  📝 NOTES.txt              🔧 _helpers.tpl
  ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ post-install  │        │ name / fullname / labels / selectorLabels │
  │ message only  │        │ — every other template calls into THESE   │
  └──────────────┘         └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   ALL SIX RESOURCE TEMPLATES SHARE ONE PATTERN:
   include "easypj.fullname" .  +  include "easypj.labels" . | nindent 4
   — consistent naming, everywhere, by construction. 🛠️

In words: Eight files make a real chart — six become actual Kubernetes resources, and two (NOTES.txt, _helpers.tpl) exist purely to support the other six. Every resource template follows the identical shape: compute a name via include "easypj.fullname" ., attach standard labels the same way, then add whatever's unique to that resource type.

The Deployment is the most complex file because it coordinates everything else — it references the ConfigMap and Secret by name (envFrom), reacts to config changes via the checksum trick, and defers to the HPA when autoscaling is on. Get its name references exactly right, and the rest of the chart follows the same pattern with far less to go wrong.

The takeaway: this chapter closes Part 3 — Chapters 6, 7, and 8 together took templates from "abstract syntax" to "a complete, real, working chart." Part 4 goes further: dependencies and subcharts (Ch9), lifecycle hooks (Ch10), and testing (Ch11).

🟡 Part 4 · Advanced Helm Techniques

Composition, Timing & Testing

Chapters 9–11 · Intermediate · "How do real, production-grade charts go beyond a single template set?"

🟡 Intermediate 📖 3 Chapters ⏱️ ~5 hours 🎯 Dependency Management · Lifecycle Hooks & Releases · Testing & Troubleshooting

Part 3 built a complete, working easypj chart in isolation. Part 4 makes it production-real: composing it with PostgreSQL and Redis as dependencies (Ch9), controlling exactly WHEN things happen during install/upgrade with lifecycle hooks (Ch10), and proving the chart actually works with automated tests (Ch11).

How the chapters fit — Part 4 mental model
   Ch 9 — COMPOSE                Ch 10 — SEQUENCE               Ch 11 — PROVE
   dependencies are        ───▶  hooks are stage        ───▶   helm test verifies
   ingredients you buy            directions — WHEN                the chart actually
   pre-made, not cook             things run, not WHAT             works, automatically
        │                              │                              │
        └──────────────────┬───────────┴──────────────┬───────────────┘
                            ▼                          ▼
              A chart that composes real dependencies, sequences operations
              correctly, and can prove its own correctness on demand.

Chapter 9 · Chart Dependencies & Subcharts

Real applications rarely live in isolation. easypj needs PostgreSQL for data and Redis for caching. Instead of bundling everything into one massive chart, Helm lets you declare dependencies — other charts your application needs, composed together instead of hand-rolled from scratch. This chapter covers the complete dependency system.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🔗 Dependencies 🐍 easypj / jobpost 🎯 Dependency Management

  • ✅ Manage dependencies with helm dependency update and helm dependency build

  • ✅ Share configuration across subcharts with Global Values
  • ✅ Import values from child charts into parent templates
  • ✅ Control dependency versions with SemVer constraints
🎓 Helm Certification Relevance
Dependency Management CORE DOMAIN
🎯 Dependencies Are Ingredients You Buy Pre-Made

Chart.yaml is the shopping list; helm dependency update is the trip to the store. Two things to get right immediately:

  • Editing Chart.yaml's dependencies block and running helm install immediately — without helm dependency update first — deploys with an EMPTY or stale charts/ directory. The chart "installs" but the dependency simply isn't there.
  • helm dependency list shows declared-vs-downloaded status in one command — check it before debugging "missing" subcharts the hard way.
