9.1 Chart.yaml Dependencies — Adding PostgreSQL, Redis, Nginx

Chart.yaml with dependencies
apiVersion: v2
name: easypj
version: 0.1.0
appVersion: "2.1.0"
dependencies:
  - name: postgresql
    version: "12.x.x"                              # SemVer range
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    condition: postgresql.enabled                   # toggle via values
    tags:
      - database
  - name: redis
    version: "~18.0.0"                             # ~ = patch-level flexibility
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    condition: redis.enabled
    tags:
      - cache
  - name: ingress-nginx
    version: "^4.0.0"                              # ^ = compatible releases
    repository: https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx
    condition: ingress-nginx.enabled

Conditions & Tags — Selective Subchart Enablement

Not every environment needs every dependency. condition and tags both toggle a subchart on/off — they compose, they aren't alternatives.

Using Conditions (per-dependency)
# Chart.yaml
dependencies:
  - name: postgresql
    condition: postgresql.enabled
  - name: redis
    condition: redis.enabled

# values.yaml
postgresql:
  enabled: true
redis:
  enabled: false   # skip redis in this env
Using Tags (bulk grouping)
# Chart.yaml
dependencies:
  - name: postgresql
    tags: [database]
  - name: redis
    tags: [cache]

# values.yaml
tags:
  database: true   # enable ALL db-tagged deps
  cache: false     # disable ALL cache-tagged deps
💡 Condition vs Tag Logic

For a subchart to be enabled: ALL its tags must be true AND its condition (if any) must be true. If both a condition and tags are set on the same dependency, the condition is checked first — if the condition path is defined and evaluates false, the chart is disabled regardless of what the tags say.

9.2 helm dependency update/build — Managing Dependencies

dependency commands
# Download dependencies (updates Chart.lock + downloads to charts/)
helm dependency update ./easypj-chart

# Build from an EXISTING Chart.lock (no network — faster)
helm dependency build ./easypj-chart

# List current dependencies — declared vs actually downloaded
helm dependency list ./easypj-chart
📖 update vs build — Not Interchangeable

helm dependency update reads Chart.yaml's dependencies block, resolves version constraints against the REPOSITORY (a network call), downloads .tgz files into charts/, and regenerates Chart.lock.

helm dependency build reads the EXISTING Chart.lock and fetches the EXACT pinned archives (from local cache if present, otherwise still a network call) WITHOUT re-negotiating version constraints against the repo. Use this in CI for reproducible builds — deterministic even if the repository's index has moved on.

🔑 Changed a version constraint in Chart.yaml? You need update. Just need charts/ repopulated from a committed Chart.lock? Use build — same pinned versions every time, no re-resolution.

⚠️ Always Commit Chart.lock

Chart.lock pins exact dependency versions. Without it, CI/CD builds may download different versions over time. charts/*.tgz is a build artifact — commit or .gitignore it either way, but Chart.lock should always be committed.

9.3 Subcharts vs Umbrella Charts — Pattern Comparison

📦 Subcharts (Recommended)
  • Each dependency is a separate chart
  • Parent chart declares deps in Chart.yaml
  • Clean separation of concerns
  • Dependencies can be updated independently
  • Standard for most Helm charts
☂️ Umbrella Charts
  • One chart that wraps multiple sub-apps
  • All templates in one chart
  • Simpler for small projects
  • Harder to version components separately
  • Consider if you have 2-3 tightly coupled services
📖 When to Use Each

Use a subchart when your app genuinely needs the dependency to run — easypj needs a database, not optionally. Use an umbrella chart when you're bundling unrelated apps for one-command deployment, like an entire platform stack.

9.4 Global Values — Sharing Config Across Subcharts

Use the global: key in values.yaml to share configuration with all subcharts automatically — every subchart can read .Values.global with no explicit import.

global values example
# Parent chart values.yaml
global:
  imageRegistry: myregistry.io
  imagePullSecrets:
    - name: regcred
  commonLabels:
    environment: production
    team: backend

postgresql:
  enabled: true
  # this subchart automatically has access to .Values.global.imageRegistry
  # with NO import statement needed

# In the subchart's own template:
image: {{ .Values.global.imageRegistry }}/postgresql:{{ .Values.image.tag }}
⚠️ Global Gotcha — Two Easy-to-Miss Rules

A subchart CAN override a global value in its own values.yaml, but the PARENT chart's global value always takes precedence — the parent wins. And global is NOT automatically available to the parent's OWN templates just because it's declared — the parent chart still has to reference it explicitly as .Values.global.xxx, exactly like any subchart would.

9.5 Importing Values from Child Charts

Global values flow ONE direction only — parent to children. Sometimes the parent needs the OPPOSITE: reading a value a child chart generates or exposes. That's what import-values is for.

import-values example
dependencies:
  - name: postgresql
    version: "12.x.x"
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    import-values:
      - child: service.ports.postgresql   # from the subchart
        parent: dbPort                    # accessible as .Values.dbPort
      - child: auth
        parent: dbAuth                    # the entire auth section, imported
Child-to-Parent Value Flow
CHILD CHART (postgresql):            PARENT CHART (easypj):
┌───────────────────────────┐        ┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ values.yaml:               │        │ Chart.yaml:                  │
│   auth:                    │        │ dependencies:                │
│     password: changeme     │        │   - name: postgresql         │
│                             │        │     import-values:           │
│ CHILD exports "auth"       │        │       - child: auth.password │
│ to the parent via import   │───────▶│         parent: db.password  │
└───────────────────────────┘        │                              │
                                     │ templates/deployment.yaml:   │
                                     │   env:                       │
                                     │     - name: DB_PASSWORD      │
                                     │       value: {{ .Values.db.  │
                                     │         password }}          │
                                     └─────────────────────────────┘
🎯 Exam Scenario

"You have a WordPress chart that depends on MariaDB. How do you pass the MariaDB-generated password to the WordPress deployment?" Answer: use import-values in Chart.yaml to map the child's exported value to a parent value, then reference it normally in the WordPress template.

📖 Beyond name/version/repository/condition

A dependency entry also supports: tags (group multiple deps under one on/off switch), alias (install the same dependency chart twice under different names), import-values (pull specific child values up into the parent's scope, as shown above).

🔑 Resolution rule: if BOTH a tag and a condition are set on the same dependency, the condition always wins.

9.6 Dependency Version Constraints

Helm uses SemVer 2 for dependency version constraints — understanding the ranges precisely is critical for reproducible deployments.

ConstraintMeaningMatches
12.0.0Exact versionOnly 12.0.0
>=12.0.0 <13.0.0Version range12.0.0 through 12.x.x
~12.0.0Patch-level flex (~)>=12.0.0, <12.1.0
^12.0.0Minor-level flex (^)>=12.0.0, <13.0.0
12.x.xWildcard (x = any)Any 12.x.x
>=12.0.0 || 18.x.xOR condition12+ OR any 18.x
*Any versionAll versions (use sparingly!)
⚠️ Version Constraint Warning

Always use explicit version ranges or pin to specific versions. Using * or overly broad ranges can silently pull in breaking changes on a future helm dependency update. Remember: update respects an EXISTING Chart.lock if present — it won't re-resolve unless the constraint itself changed or the lock file is deleted.

Under the Hood — how helm dependency update actually resolves versions, and a third composition pattern

Two things go deeper than the surface-level commands: the exact mechanics behind dependency resolution, and a composition pattern that isn't "subchart" or "umbrella chart" at all.

① How helm dependency update Actually Works — Step by Step

Understanding the internal mechanics helps debug "chart not found" and version-conflict errors instead of guessing:

1
Read Chart.yaml Dependencies

Helm reads the dependencies array. For each entry, it checks: name, version constraint, repository URL, optional condition, and tags.

2
Check Chart.lock (if it exists)

If Chart.lock exists, Helm compares its entries against Chart.yaml. If they match, it uses the locked versions (reproducible). If they differ, it downloads new versions. If Chart.lock is missing entirely, it resolves fresh.

3
Fetch the Repository Index

For each repository URL, Helm downloads index.yaml (cached locally). The index lists every available chart version with its URL and digest.

4
Solve Version Constraints

Helm finds all versions matching the constraint (e.g. >=12.0.0 <13.0.0) and picks the HIGHEST one. That version's .tgz URL is recorded in Chart.lock with its SHA256 digest.

5
Download .tgz to charts/

The archive is downloaded into charts/. These files are typically NOT committed to Git (add charts/*.tgz to .gitignore) — Chart.lock IS committed, so the same versions can always be re-downloaded.

🔑 "Highest matching version" is the whole algorithm. Step 4 is deterministic: given a constraint and an index, there's exactly one answer — the highest version satisfying the range. Version-conflict confusion almost always traces back to a constraint that's looser (or tighter) than the author actually intended.
② A Third Pattern: Independent Releases

Beyond "subchart" and "umbrella chart," production teams commonly use a third composition strategy — deploying each piece as its OWN separate Helm release, connected only by service discovery:

☂️ Umbrella Chart Pattern

ONE chart that declares OTHER charts as dependencies. The umbrella chart owns everything.

easypj-umbrella/
  Chart.yaml:
    dependencies:
    - name: postgresql
    - name: redis
    - name: easypj-app
  values.yaml:
    postgresql: {auth: {password: xxx}}
    redis: {enabled: true}
    easypj-app: {replicaCount: 3}

INSTALL: helm install full-stack ./umbrella
ONE command deploys everything.
All releases share ONE namespace.
🔗 Independent Release Pattern

EACH chart is deployed as a SEPARATE release. They're connected via service discovery, not a shared Chart.yaml.

# Deploy infrastructure first:
helm install postgresql bitnami/postgresql -n infra
helm install redis bitnami/redis -n infra

# Deploy the application:
helm install easypj ./easypj-chart -n app \
  --set db.host=postgresql.infra.svc

Each release is INDEPENDENT.
Can upgrade/rollback individually.
Can span multiple namespaces.
FactorUmbrella ChartIndependent Releases
DeploymentSingle commandMultiple commands
RollbackAll or nothingPer-component
Version couplingTight (one Chart.lock)Loose (independent)
NamespaceShared namespaceSeparate namespaces possible
Best forSimple apps, demos, devProduction, microservices
③ Dependency Troubleshooting Reference
🔧
"dependency not found"

Run helm dependency update to download missing charts. Check the repository URL is correct and accessible. Verify the chart name matches exactly.

🔧
Version conflict

The SemVer constraint is too loose or too tight. Use helm dependency list to see resolved versions. Pin exact versions in Chart.lock for reproducible builds.

🔧
Conditional dependency not disabling

Check the condition: key in Chart.yaml matches a value in values.yaml. The value must be exactly boolean false — NOT the string "false", which is truthy.

🔧
Using tags for bulk control

Use tags: in dependencies plus tags.database: false in values.yaml to disable every database-tagged dependency at once — more flexible than toggling individual conditions.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Dependencies are declared, then resolved — Chart.yaml's dependencies: block is just intent; helm dependency update/build is what actually populates charts/.
  • update hits the network and re-resolves; build reads the lock file offline. CI/CD should almost always use build for determinism.
  • Global values flow one direction only — parent to every child, automatically. Getting data back OUT of a child requires the explicit import-values mechanism.
  • Condition beats tags when both are set — and a subchart needs ALL its tags true AND its condition true to be enabled.
  • Three composition patterns exist, not two — subcharts (one app, real dependencies), umbrella charts (bundle unrelated apps, one command), and independent releases (loosest coupling, best for production microservices).
  • SemVer constraints have real teeth — * or overly broad ranges can silently pull in breaking changes on a future resolve; prefer explicit ranges.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Editing Chart.yaml's dependencies and running helm install immediately — without helm dependency update first — deploys with an EMPTY or stale charts/ directory. The install itself doesn't fail; the dependency just silently isn't there.
  • A condition value set as a string "false" instead of boolean false. The string is truthy — the subchart stays enabled even though the author clearly intended to disable it.
  • Assuming global is available to the parent chart's own templates automatically. It isn't special-cased for the parent — reference it explicitly as .Values.global.xxx, exactly like a subchart would.
  • Forgetting that global values flow only downward. A subchart cannot push a value back up to its parent or sideways to a sibling subchart — that direction requires import-values, an explicit opt-in per dependency.
  • Committing charts/*.tgz but not Chart.lock, or vice versa without a clear policy. At minimum, Chart.lock should always be committed — reproducibility depends on it.
  • Using * as a "quick fix" for a version constraint that wasn't matching. It resolves, but removes all protection against a future breaking change silently entering the dependency tree.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • helm dependency list shows declared-vs-downloaded status in one command — check it before debugging "missing" subcharts the hard way.
  • Reflex: changed a constraint → update. Just need charts/ repopulated → build. This one distinction resolves most "which command do I run" hesitation.
  • When a subchart won't disable, check the values.yaml TYPE first — enabled: false (boolean) vs enabled: "false" (string) is a one-character difference with completely different behavior.
  • Default to the subchart pattern unless you have a specific reason for an umbrella chart or independent releases — it's the path of least surprise for most real applications.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 9)

declaring, resolving, and inspecting dependencies 
# Resolve + download (network required, re-negotiates versions)
helm dependency update ./easypj-chart

# Rebuild from an existing Chart.lock (CI-friendly, deterministic)
helm dependency build ./easypj-chart

# See declared vs actually downloaded, in one view
helm dependency list ./easypj-chart

# Add a LOCAL (file-path) dependency — useful for monorepos
# Chart.yaml:
#   dependencies:
#     - name: my-common-chart
#       version: 0.1.0
#       repository: file://../common-chart

# Toggle a dependency at install time without editing values.yaml
helm install easypj ./easypj-chart --set redis.enabled=false

🧠 Chapter 9 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of dependency management — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Where do you declare a chart's dependencies?
Show Answer
Answer

In Chart.yaml under the dependencies: key. Each entry specifies name, version (a SemVer constraint), and repository.

Explanation

Dependencies are only resolved when helm dependency update actually runs — declaring them in Chart.yaml alone does nothing to charts/.

Q2
What's the practical difference between helm dependency update and helm dependency build?
Show Answer
Answer

update fetches from remote repositories (network required) and regenerates Chart.lock. build reads from an EXISTING Chart.lock (no re-resolution) and downloads the exact pinned archives.

Explanation

Use update when a version constraint changed; use build in CI/CD for fast, deterministic, reproducible builds off a committed lock file.

Q3
How do you add a dependency from a local file path instead of a remote repository?
Show Answer
Answer

repository: file://../path/to/chart in Chart.yaml — relative to the chart's own directory. Useful for monorepos and testing before publishing.

Explanation

The local chart is COPIED into charts/ during helm dependency update, exactly like a remote dependency would be — its version must match its own Chart.yaml.

Q4
Your umbrella chart has 3 subcharts. How do you deploy all of them to the same namespace?
Show Answer
Answer

No explicit configuration needed — subcharts automatically inherit the release's namespace. helm install myapp ./umbrella -n prod puts every resource, umbrella and subcharts alike, into prod.

Explanation

If different namespaces per component are genuinely needed, that requires switching to the Independent Release pattern (Under the Hood, §②) — an umbrella chart cannot split its subcharts across namespaces.

Q5
Should Chart.lock be committed to Git? What about charts/*.tgz?
Show Answer
Answer

Chart.lock: YES, always. It pins exact versions and SHA256 digests for reproducible builds. charts/*.tgz: optional — either commit for offline builds, or .gitignore it and have CI run helm dependency build.

Explanation

Without Chart.lock, helm dependency update could resolve a different version months later if a new matching release lands upstream — the lock file is what makes builds reproducible over time.

Q6
How do you completely and conditionally disable a subchart?
Show Answer
Answer

Set a condition in Chart.yaml mapped to a values key (e.g. condition: redis.enabled), then set that value to boolean false in values.yaml — the subchart is skipped entirely.

Explanation

It must be a real boolean, not the string "false" — a classic gotcha covered in this chapter's Gotchas section.

Q7
What is an umbrella chart, in one sentence?
Show Answer
Answer

A meta-chart with no meaningful templates of its own that wraps multiple related sub-applications as dependencies, deploying a complete stack via a single helm install.

Explanation

Contrast with a subchart relationship, where the PARENT chart is a real application (easypj) that merely depends on infrastructure (postgresql, redis) to function.

Q8
How do you import one specific value generated by a child chart into the parent's scope?
Show Answer
Answer

Use import-values on that dependency's entry: { child: auth.password, parent: db.password } makes the child's value available as .Values.db.password in the parent.

Explanation

This is the ONLY sanctioned way for data to flow child-to-parent — global values only ever flow the opposite direction.

Q9
What files does helm dependency update create or modify?
Show Answer
Answer

It downloads .tgz archives into charts/, and creates or updates Chart.lock with the exact resolved versions and SHA256 digests.

Explanation

These two effects together are the entire observable output of the command — if neither changed after running it, either everything was already up to date, or something failed silently (check the exit code).

Q10
If BOTH a condition and tags are set on the same dependency and they disagree, which one wins?
Show Answer
Answer

The condition — it's checked first. If the condition path is defined and evaluates to false, the dependency is disabled regardless of what its tags say.

Explanation

This resolution order is worth memorizing explicitly, since it's easy to assume tags and conditions are simply ANDed together with equal weight — they're not; condition has priority.

⚙️ Chapter 9 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

A broken dependency setup, and you fix it using this chapter's mental models.

Q1
A teammate adds a new PostgreSQL dependency to Chart.yaml and immediately runs helm install easypj ./chart. The install reports success but no PostgreSQL pod exists. Diagnose it.
Show Answer
Answer

They skipped helm dependency update — the charts/ directory is empty or stale, so Helm had nothing to deploy for that dependency. Fix: helm dependency update ./chart, then reinstall/upgrade.

Explanation

This is exactly this chapter's central exam-tip gotcha — editing Chart.yaml alone changes intent, not the actual downloaded archives.

Q2
Your CI pipeline needs deterministic, offline-safe dependency resolution — no surprises from an upstream repo publishing a new version overnight. Which command, and why?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm dependency build ./easypj-chart
Explanation

build uses the committed Chart.lock's exact pinned versions — no re-negotiation against the live repository index, so a new upstream release can't silently change what CI deploys.

Q3
You set redis.enabled: "false" (with quotes) in values.yaml, expecting Redis to be skipped, but it still deploys. Diagnose it.
Show Answer
Answer

The value is a STRING "false", not a boolean — and a non-empty string is truthy in Go templates. Fix: remove the quotes so YAML parses it as an actual boolean: redis.enabled: false.

Explanation

This exact type mismatch is the most common reason a condition: "isn't working" despite looking correct at a glance.

Q4
You need to disable BOTH the database and cache subcharts at once for a lightweight dev environment, without touching Chart.yaml. One values.yaml block?
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
tags:
  database: false
  cache: false
Explanation

This assumes the dependencies were tagged database/cache in Chart.yaml (§9.1) — tags let you flip a whole GROUP of dependencies at once instead of listing each one's individual condition.

Q5
A subchart's template references .Values.commonLabels (no global. prefix) and gets nothing. The parent's values.yaml clearly has global.commonLabels set. What's wrong?
Show Answer
Answer

The subchart template is missing the required global. prefix — it should read .Values.global.commonLabels. Subcharts only automatically see their own dedicated section plus the special global namespace, never the parent's arbitrary top-level keys.

Explanation

This is the same scoping rule from Chapter 4's Under the Hood, applied concretely to a real dependency scenario.

Q6
Design a Chart.yaml import-values entry that exposes a Redis subchart's generated port as .Values.cachePort in the parent.
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
dependencies:
  - name: redis
    version: "~18.0.0"
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    import-values:
      - child: service.ports.redis
        parent: cachePort
Explanation

The exact child key path depends on that specific chart's own values.yaml structure — always check the dependency's helm show values output before writing the mapping.

Q7
You want to quickly confirm which dependencies are DECLARED in Chart.yaml versus which are ACTUALLY sitting in charts/ right now, without manually comparing two things by hand. One command?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm dependency list ./easypj-chart
Explanation

Its output flags any dependency that's declared but not yet downloaded — exactly the Speed Tip from this chapter, applied.

Q8
A version constraint "12.x.x" just resolved to a version with a breaking config change nobody expected. What went wrong with the constraint choice itself?
Show Answer
Answer

The wildcard constraint was too loose — it allows ANY 12.x.x release, including minor version bumps that can (and, per SemVer convention, are allowed to) introduce new backward-compatible-but-still-behavior-changing features. A tighter ~12.5.0 (patch-only) would have been safer.

Explanation

This is exactly the "Version Constraint Warning" from §9.6 — overly broad ranges trade convenience for surprise.

Q9
You're building a monorepo where a shared "common" chart lives alongside easypj's own chart, not published anywhere yet. How do you declare that dependency?
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
dependencies:
  - name: easypj-common
    version: 0.1.0
    repository: file://../easypj-common
Explanation

file:// paths are resolved relative to the chart directory and copied into charts/ on helm dependency update, exactly like a remote dependency — no repository server needed for local development.

Q10
Your team is debating umbrella chart vs independent releases for a new 4-service platform. What's the one factor that should decide it?
Show Answer
Answer

How tightly the services need to be versioned and rolled back together. If they must always move in lockstep (one Chart.lock, one release), umbrella. If any service needs independent upgrade/rollback cycles or its own namespace, independent releases.

Explanation

Production microservice architectures almost always favor independent releases for exactly this reason — the tight coupling an umbrella chart provides becomes a liability once services genuinely need to evolve at different speeds.

🔬 Practice Drill 9.1 — Add PostgreSQL as a Real Dependency

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Starting from the easypj-chart built in Chapter 8, declare a PostgreSQL dependency, resolve it, and confirm it's actually present before deploying anything.

Hint: Declare → resolve → verify — in that order, never skip the middle step.
View Solution
bash
# 1. Declare in Chart.yaml (edit the file):
#   dependencies:
#     - name: postgresql
#       version: "12.x.x"
#       repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
#       condition: postgresql.enabled

# 2. Resolve
helm dependency update ./easypj-chart

# 3. Verify BEFORE deploying
helm dependency list ./easypj-chart
ls easypj-chart/charts/

Check yourself: helm dependency list should show postgresql with a status of "ok," and charts/ should contain an actual postgresql-*.tgz file — if either is missing, do NOT proceed to helm install.

🔬 Practice Drill 9.2 — Toggle Redis On and Off via Tags

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Tag both PostgreSQL and Redis dependencies appropriately, then render the chart twice — once with the cache tag on, once off — and confirm Redis resources appear/disappear accordingly.

Hint: helm template ... | grep -i redis is the fastest verification.
View Solution
bash
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart --set tags.cache=true | grep -i "kind: .*redis" -i
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart --set tags.cache=false | grep -i "kind: .*redis" -i
# first should show Redis resources, second should show nothing

Check yourself: if Redis resources appear in BOTH renders, the tag isn't actually wired to a tags: block in Chart.yaml's redis dependency — go back and add it.

🔬 Practice Drill 9.3 — Share a Registry via Global Values

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Set a global.imageRegistry value and confirm BOTH easypj's own templates AND the PostgreSQL subchart's rendered output reference it — without editing the PostgreSQL subchart at all.

Hint: easypj's OWN templates need an explicit .Values.global.imageRegistry reference too — it isn't automatic just because you're the parent.
View Solution
bash
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart --set global.imageRegistry=myregistry.io \
  | grep -A1 "image:"

Check yourself: both easypj's own container image AND postgresql's should show myregistry.io/... — if only the subchart picked it up, easypj's own deployment.yaml is missing an explicit .Values.global.imageRegistry reference.

🔬 Practice Drill 9.4 — Import a Child Value and Use It

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Add an import-values entry that exposes PostgreSQL's auth.database as .Values.dbName in the parent, then reference .Values.dbName in easypj's ConfigMap.

Hint: Check the child chart's actual values.yaml structure first — the child: path must match exactly.
View Solution
yaml
# Chart.yaml
dependencies:
  - name: postgresql
    import-values:
      - child: auth.database
        parent: dbName

# templates/configmap.yaml
data:
  DB_NAME: {{ .Values.dbName | quote }}

Check yourself: helm template ./chart | grep DB_NAME should show the value pulled straight from PostgreSQL's own defaults, with zero duplication of that value anywhere in easypj's own values.yaml.

🔬 Practice Drill 9.5 — Choose the Right Composition Pattern

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

For each situation, name which of the THREE composition patterns (subchart, umbrella, independent releases) fits best, in one sentence each: (1) easypj needs its own database. (2) A demo environment bundling easypj + 3 supporting services for one-click setup. (3) A microservices platform where each of 8 services is owned by a different team with its own release cadence.

Hint: Necessity, convenience, and independence are the three deciding factors, one per scenario.
View Solution

(1) Subchart — the database is a genuine, non-optional dependency of one application. (2) Umbrella chart — the priority is one-command convenience for a demo, and tight coupling is fine there. (3) Independent releases — 8 teams needing independent upgrade/rollback cadences is exactly the scenario umbrella charts and even subcharts handle poorly.

Check yourself: if your answer for (3) was "umbrella chart," reconsider — tight version coupling across 8 independently-owned services is a coordination bottleneck, not a convenience.

📌 Chapter 9 Visual Summary — composing easypj with real dependencies
  📋 Chart.yaml deps        ⬇️ helm dep update         🌐 global values
  ┌──────────────┐          ┌──────────────┐           ┌───────────────────┐
  │ declare       │         │ download &     │          │ parent → ALL       │
  │ postgresql,   │  ────▶  │ lock exact     │  ────▶   │ children,           │
  │ redis         │         │ versions       │          │ automatically       │
  └──────────────┘          └──────────────┘           └───────────────────┘

  📥 import-values           🔒 Chart.lock              🏷️ SemVer constraints
  ┌──────────────┐          ┌──────────────┐           ┌───────────────────┐
  │ child → parent│         │ ALWAYS commit  │          │ ~ patch · ^ minor   │
  │ (explicit only)│        │ for reproducible│         │ x.x wildcard ·      │
  │               │         │ builds         │          │ pin explicitly       │
  └──────────────┘          └──────────────┘           └───────────────────┘
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   THREE PATTERNS, ONE DECISION: does this dependency need to run WITH
   my app (subchart), get bundled for convenience (umbrella), or evolve
   completely independently (separate releases)? 🔗

In words: A dependency starts as pure intent — a line in Chart.yaml — and becomes real only after helm dependency update resolves it against a repository and downloads the exact matching archive into charts/. Chart.lock is what makes that resolution repeatable: commit it, and helm dependency build can restore the exact same dependency tree anywhere, offline.

Configuration flows in one clear direction by default — global values cascade from parent to every child automatically — and only flows the other way (child to parent) through the explicit import-values mechanism. Nothing crosses those boundaries by accident.

The takeaway: easypj is no longer a chart in isolation — it's a small dependency tree with PostgreSQL and Redis, composed deliberately rather than hand-rolled. Chapter 10 adds the last missing piece: controlling exactly WHEN things happen during that composition's install and upgrade lifecycle.

Chapter 10 · Hooks & Lifecycle Management

Some operations can't be a plain Kubernetes resource — running a database migration BEFORE new pods start is a timing problem, not a resource problem. Hooks give control over when things happen during a Helm operation: back up data before deleting, migrate a schema before an upgrade, validate a deployment on demand. This chapter covers the complete hook system.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🪝 Hooks 🐍 easypj / jobpost 🎯 Lifecycle Hooks & Releases

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand what Helm Hooks are and when to use them
  • ✅ Master all 8 hook types (pre/post-install, upgrade, delete, rollback, test)
  • ✅ Control hook execution with policies and weights
  • ✅ Create Job-based hooks for database migrations and backups
  • ✅ Build a real DB migration hook for easypj
🎓 Helm Certification Relevance
Lifecycle Hooks & Releases CORE DOMAIN
🎯 Hooks Are Stage Directions in a Play Script

"Before Act 2 begins, dim the lights" — hooks run at a specific MOMENT in the install/upgrade lifecycle, not as part of the cast. Three things to get right immediately:

  • Hook resources are NOT tracked by helm uninstall or helm rollback the way normal resources are. A failed hook Job can be left behind and needs manual cleanup. Two sanctioned cleanup paths beyond hook-delete-policy: the helm.sh/resource-policy: keep annotation (prevents Helm from EVER deleting a resource — a different mechanism entirely) or Kubernetes' own Job field ttlSecondsAfterFinished (auto-cleanup independent of Helm).
  • hook-weight defaults to 0 if the annotation is omitted — hooks without an explicit weight still execute, just at the "0" position relative to weighted ones.
  • kubectl logs job/<hook-name> is faster than digging through helm get hooks output when a hook fails — go straight to the source.

🧭 Section Map — the Chapter 10 Learning Arc

The arc: what a hook is (10.1) → the 8 types (10.2) → cleanup policy (10.3) → ordering via weights (10.4) → the Job shape hooks almost always take (10.5) → a complete, real migration hook for easypj (10.6).

Helm Install Lifecycle With Hooks
   helm install myapp ./chart
        │
        ▼
   ┌─────────────────┐
   │ pre-install     │  ← Hook: Job/ConfigMap (weight: -5)
   │ (run DB backup) │
   └────────┬────────┘
            ▼
   ┌─────────────────┐
   │ Render & Apply  │  ← All non-hook resources
   │ K8s Manifests   │    (Deployment, Service, ConfigMap...)
   └────────┬────────┘
            ▼
   ┌─────────────────┐
   │ post-install    │  ← Hook: Job (weight: 5)
   │ (run DB migrate)│
   └────────┬────────┘
            ▼
   ┌─────────────────┐
   │ test            │  ← helm test (test pods)
   │ (verify app)    │
   └─────────────────┘

   HOOK TYPES: pre-install, post-install, pre-delete,
               post-delete, pre-upgrade, post-upgrade,
               pre-rollback, post-rollback, test

   WEIGHTS: Lower numbers run FIRST (-5 before 0 before 5)
   DELETION: hook-succeeded, hook-failed, before-hook-creation

10.1 What are Helm Hooks? — Pre/Post Operations

A Hook is a Kubernetes resource (usually a Job) annotated with "helm.sh/hook": <hook-type>. Instead of being deployed as part of the normal release, hooks run at specific lifecycle events — before install, after upgrade, before delete, and so on.

📖 The 3 Hook Annotations, Verbatim
metadata:
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade          ← WHEN it runs
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-5"           ← execution ORDER,
                                              lower runs first,
                                              string not integer
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": before-hook-creation
                                            ← FALLBACK deletion
                                              policy for old Job
                                              objects

🔑 hook-weight values are STRINGS ("-5", not -5) — a common exam typo that silently fails YAML type validation.

10.2 Hook Types — All 8 Variants

📥
pre-install

Runs BEFORE resources are created. Use for: init scripts, DB schema setup.

✅
post-install

Runs AFTER all resources are created. Use for: data seeding, notifications.

🔄
pre-upgrade

Runs BEFORE upgrade applies. Use for: DB backups, pre-migration checks.

📤
post-upgrade

Runs AFTER upgrade completes. Use for: DB migrations, cache warming.

🗑️
pre-delete

Runs BEFORE resources are deleted. Use for: graceful shutdown, data export.

🧹
post-delete

Runs AFTER deletion. Use for: cleanup of external resources.

⏪
pre-rollback

Runs BEFORE rollback. Use for: compatibility checks.

🔙
post-rollback

Runs AFTER rollback. Use for: notification, validation.

Hook Decision Flowchart — Which Hook Do I Need?
  Need to run something BEFORE resources are created?
  ──YES──▶ pre-install (init scripts, schema setup)

  Need to run something AFTER resources are created?
  ──YES──▶ post-install (data seeding, notifications)

  Need to run BEFORE an upgrade takes effect?
  ──YES──▶ pre-upgrade (DB backup, compatibility check)

  Need to run AFTER an upgrade completes?
  ──YES──▶ post-upgrade (DB migration, cache warming, smoke tests)

  Need to clean up BEFORE resources are deleted?
  ──YES──▶ pre-delete (data export, deregister from load balancer)

  Need to validate the deployment works?
  ──YES──▶ test (connectivity check, API endpoint test)

  🔑 KEY: hooks run SYNCHRONOUSLY — they BLOCK the release until complete.
     Use --timeout to prevent a hung hook from blocking forever.
⚠️ Hook Timeout Warning

If a hook hangs (e.g. a migration Job can't reach the DB), it blocks the ENTIRE release operation. Always consider --timeout on install/upgrade. The default is 5 minutes — long enough for most operations, but adjust for large migrations.

10.3 Hook Execution Policy — Controlling Deletion & Failure Behavior

PolicyWhen resource is deletedUse case
before-hook-creationRight before a new hook of the same type runsReplacing temporary resources — the default, since Jobs are immutable once created
hook-succeededImmediately after the hook completes successfullyOne-time migration jobs; keeps the cluster clean
hook-failedImmediately after the hook failsRarely used alone — usually you WANT to inspect a failure first
combining multiple policies
metadata:
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "5"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded,before-hook-creation
    # multiple policies can be combined with commas —
    # this means: delete on success AND delete before the next hook runs

10.4 Hook Weights — Controlling Execution Order

Multiple hooks of the same type run in weight order — lowest first. The default weight is 0. Negative weights run before positive ones.

Hook Weight Execution Order
WEIGHT:  -10           -5            0             5             10
         |              |             |             |              |
pre-install:  [init-secret]  [create-ns]  [default-job]  [migrate-db]  [seed-data]
                (runs first)                                  (runs last)

SAME WEIGHT hooks execute in an undefined order (don't rely on it!)
Use DIFFERENT weights whenever ordering actually matters.
hook weight example
# Backup runs FIRST (weight: -5), then Migration (weight: 5)
annotations:
  "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade
  "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-5"    # Backup Job
---
annotations:
  "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade
  "helm.sh/hook-weight": "5"     # Migration Job
🎯 Exam Scenario

"You need to run a DB backup (Job A), then a schema migration (Job B), then a data seed (Job C) before installing the app. How do you guarantee that order?" Answer: three pre-install hooks with weights -10, -5, and 0 respectively. Weight ordering is tested frequently.

10.5 Job-Based Hooks — Running Batch Operations

hook Job template
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-db-migrate
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "5"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: migrate
        image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
        command: ["python", "manage.py", "migrate"]

10.6 easypj DB Migration Hook — Pre-Upgrade Migration Job

A complete, real-world hook for running Django database migrations before every upgrade of easypj:

templates/db-migrate-hook.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: {{ include "easypj.fullname" . }}-db-migrate
  labels:
    {{- include "easypj.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "5"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded,before-hook-creation
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: migrate
        image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
        command: ["python", "manage.py", "migrate", "--noinput"]
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: {{ include "easypj.fullname" . }}-config
        - secretRef:
            name: {{ include "easypj.fullname" . }}-secret
💡 Reusing the Chapter 8 Naming Pattern

This hook calls include "easypj.fullname" . and include "easypj.labels" . — the exact same named templates every other resource in the chart uses. Hooks are regular templates with special annotations; nothing about naming/labeling changes for them.

Under the Hood — the precise 13-step hook lifecycle, concurrency, CRDs, and rollback hooks

Four things go well beyond "hooks run at specific moments": the exact official sequence, what actually runs concurrently, how CRDs are handled entirely differently, and a rollback-specific gotcha worth knowing before it bites you in production.

① The Complete Hook Lifecycle — 13 Steps (from Official Docs)

The official Helm documentation defines an exact 13-step lifecycle for helm install with hooks. Knowing this precise sequence is what turns "why did my hook not run" into a two-second diagnosis:

1
User runs helm install

helm install foo ./chart — the Helm client sends the install request to the Helm library (SDK).

2
Helm library install API is called

The SDK's install function runs with the chart, values, and options.

3
CRDs in crds/ are installed

Any Custom Resource Definitions in the crds/ directory are applied FIRST, before any templates render. CRDs are NOT managed as part of the release — never updated or deleted by Helm.

4
Templates are rendered

The library renders every file in templates/ (except _*.tpl helpers and NOTES.txt).

5
Pre-install hooks are prepared

Resources annotated helm.sh/hook: pre-install are identified and loaded into Kubernetes.

6
Hooks are sorted by weight

Default weight 0. Sorted ascending by weight, then by resource kind, then by name. Lower weights execute FIRST.

7
Lowest-weight hook is loaded

The hook with the lowest (most negative) weight is applied to Kubernetes first.

8
Helm waits until the hook is "Ready"

For Jobs/Pods: wait for successful completion (exit 0). If ANY hook fails, the ENTIRE install fails right here.

9
Non-hook resources are loaded

Once all pre-install hooks succeed, the actual release resources (Deployments, Services, etc.) are applied. With --wait, Helm waits for them to be ready before proceeding.

10
Post-install hooks are prepared

Resources annotated helm.sh/hook: post-install are identified.

11
Post-install hooks execute

Run in weight order, AFTER all release resources are deployed (and ready, if --wait).

12
Release object is returned

The library returns the release object (metadata, status, notes) to the Helm client.

13
Client exits

helm install completes. The release is now deployed (or failed if any hook or resource failed).

🔑 Three questions, three step numbers. "When does a pre-install hook run?" → steps 5–8, before any release resources exist. "Why did my hook fail?" → step 8, check the hook's own logs. "Can I have multiple hooks of the same type?" → yes, step 6 — they're sorted by weight, same-weight order is undefined.
② Concurrency & Parallelism — What Actually Runs at the Same Time
   HOOK EXECUTION ORDER (DEFAULT: SERIAL ACROSS WEIGHTS)
   ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
   pre-install hooks:
     [Weight: -10] → Job A runs → completes → Job B starts
     [Weight: -5]  → Job B runs → completes → Job C starts
     [Weight: 0]   → Job C runs → completes
     (ALL hook resources of one weight complete before the next weight starts)

   SAME-WEIGHT BEHAVIOR (since Helm 3.2+):
     [Weight: 0] Job A ──┐
     [Weight: 0] Job B ──┤  started TOGETHER — concurrent, not sequential
     [Weight: 0] Job C ──┘

   TIMEOUT:
     Default: 5 minutes for ALL hooks of an operation, COMBINED
     Override: --timeout 10m
     Per-hook timeout: NOT supported by Helm — use the Job's own
       activeDeadlineSeconds field instead

   FAILURE:
     One hook fails → the ENTIRE operation fails
     --atomic → auto-rollback on ANY hook failure
     Failed hooks are preserved for debugging UNLESS hook-failed policy is set
🔑 Weights create BARRIERS, not a strict global order. Every hook at one weight must finish before the next weight starts — but hooks sharing a weight run concurrently, not one-by-one. Give two hooks the same weight only when they're genuinely safe to run in parallel.
③ CRDs and Hooks — A Deliberately Different Mechanism

Custom Resource Definitions are NOT hooks, and don't behave like them — they use the dedicated crds/ directory instead:

crds/ Directory (Helm 3+)
  • Files in crds/ are applied BEFORE any templates (lifecycle step ③ above)
  • CRDs are NOT managed as part of the release
  • They are NEVER updated or deleted by Helm — ever
  • No template rendering — raw YAML only
  • The old crd-install hook from Helm 2 was removed entirely in Helm 3
CRD Best Practices
  • Place EXACTLY ONE CRD per file
  • Keep CRDs minimal — only what's actually needed
  • Use a SEPARATE chart for CRDs in production
  • CRDs survive helm uninstall — always
  • Manual deletion required: kubectl delete crd <name>
🔑 If you change a CRD template and upgrade, nothing happens to the existing CRD. This is deliberate — it prevents an accidental breaking change to a custom resource type that other tools or teams might depend on. Apply CRD changes manually, or manage them in their own chart with its own release lifecycle.
④ Rollback Hook Patterns — A Gotcha Worth Knowing Ahead of Time

Rollback hooks are often overlooked but critical for data integrity — they run during helm rollback and can prevent data corruption:

⏪
Pre-Rollback: Backup Current State
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-pre-rollback-backup
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-rollback
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-10"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: backup
        image: postgres:15
        command: ["pg_dump", "-h",
          "{{ .Release.Name }}-postgresql",
          "-U", "easypj", "-f",
          "/backup/pre-rollback-{{ .Release.Revision }}.sql"]
🔄
Post-Rollback: Verify & Restore
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-post-rollback-verify
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": post-rollback
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "5"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: verify
        image: easypj:{{ .Values.image.tag }}
        command: ["python", "manage.py",
          "check", "--deploy"]
🔑 .Release.Revision inside a rollback hook is the NEW revision, not the target. During rollback, Helm creates a NEW revision using the old configuration — pre-rollback hooks run BEFORE the old resources are restored, post-rollback hooks run AFTER. The revision number in the template always refers to this new, forward-moving revision, never the historical one you're rolling back to.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • A hook is a normal Kubernetes resource with special annotations — helm.sh/hook is the only thing that distinguishes it from a regular chart resource.
  • Hooks are synchronous and blocking — the entire install/upgrade/delete operation waits for a hook to finish before proceeding, and a failed hook fails the whole operation.
  • hook-weight must be a quoted string ("-5"), not a bare integer — a subtle YAML-typing mistake that fails validation silently.
  • Hooks live OUTSIDE the release manifest — helm get manifest never shows them, and neither helm uninstall nor helm rollback automatically cleans them up the way normal resources are cleaned up.
  • Same-weight hooks run concurrently, not sequentially (since Helm 3.2+) — different weights create true ordering barriers; the same weight does not.
  • CRDs use an entirely separate mechanism (the crds/ directory) — never updated or deleted by Helm, ever, by design.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • hook-weight written as a bare number. "helm.sh/hook-weight": -5 (unquoted) is invalid — it must be the string "-5". This is a common, silent exam typo.
  • Assuming helm uninstall/helm rollback clean up hook resources automatically. They don't — hooks are managed entirely independently, via their own hook-delete-policy (or manual cleanup).
  • Expecting a hook to appear in helm get manifest. It never will — hooks are deliberately excluded from the tracked release manifest.
  • Changing a hook's template and expecting helm upgrade to "update" the existing hook resource. Hooks aren't updated in place — Helm deletes and RE-CREATES the hook resource on every relevant operation, even if nothing in the hook actually changed.
  • Changing a CRD template and expecting the live CRD to update on upgrade. It won't — CRDs are never touched by Helm after initial install, by design. Apply CRD changes manually.
  • Reading .Release.Revision inside a rollback hook as "the revision I'm rolling back TO." It's actually the NEW revision number rollback is creating — not the historical target.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • kubectl logs job/<hook-name> is faster than digging through helm get hooks when a hook fails — go straight to the container's own output.
  • Two sanctioned cleanup paths beyond hook-delete-policy: helm.sh/resource-policy: keep (never delete, a completely different mechanism) or Kubernetes' own ttlSecondsAfterFinished on the Job (auto-cleanup independent of Helm entirely).
  • Distinct weights whenever order matters, same weight only when parallel execution is genuinely safe. Don't rely on same-weight ordering — it's explicitly undefined.
  • Reach for --atomic whenever hooks are involved in production — a hook failure without it leaves the release in a failed state that needs manual recovery.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 10)

debugging hooks — check status, logs, and force a re-run 
# List hook-created Job resources
kubectl get jobs -l helm.sh/hook

# Read a specific hook's own output — the fastest debug step
kubectl logs job/<hook-job-name>

# See the full event history for a hook Job
kubectl describe job/<hook-job-name>

# Force a hook to re-run by deleting its (already-completed) resource first
kubectl delete job/<hook-job-name>
helm upgrade myapp ./chart  # re-creates and re-runs the hook

# See hook-related errors surfaced in the release itself
helm status myapp

🧠 Chapter 10 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of hooks and lifecycle timing — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What annotation marks a Kubernetes resource as a Helm hook?
Show Answer
Answer

"helm.sh/hook": <hook-type> (e.g. pre-install, post-upgrade). Jobs are by far the most common hook resource type.

Explanation

The resource is otherwise completely ordinary — the annotation alone tells Helm to manage it differently, running it at a lifecycle event instead of deploying it as part of the normal release.

Q2
Can a single resource be more than one hook type at once?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes — use comma-separated values: "helm.sh/hook": post-install,post-upgrade. The resource runs on both events independently.

Explanation

This is common for DB migrations that need to run after BOTH a fresh install and every subsequent upgrade — one template definition, reused across both events.

Q3
Do hook resources get automatically deleted during helm uninstall?
Show Answer
Answer

No — hook resources are NOT managed as part of the release, so they persist unless they carry a hook-succeeded or similar delete policy. (The exception: pre/post-delete hooks, which run DURING uninstall itself.)

Explanation

Leftover completed hook Jobs are common in clusters that never set a delete policy — periodic manual cleanup via kubectl delete job -l helm.sh/hook is a reasonable fallback.

Q4
How do you limit a hook Job's maximum execution time, independent of Helm's own --timeout?
Show Answer
Answer

Set the Kubernetes Job's own activeDeadlineSeconds in the hook's spec. If exceeded, the Job is terminated and the hook fails — distinct from Helm's --timeout, which caps the ENTIRE operation.

Explanation

Use both together for defense in depth: a per-hook ceiling via activeDeadlineSeconds, and an overall operation ceiling via helm upgrade --timeout 10m.

Q5
Do hooks have access to .Values, .Release, and the other built-in objects?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes, full access — hooks are regular templates with special annotations, rendered at the same time and in the same context as every other file: .Values, .Release, .Chart, .Files, .Capabilities, .Template.

Explanation

This is why the easypj migration hook (§10.6) can call include "easypj.fullname" . and reference .Values.image.tag exactly like a Deployment template would.

Q6
Between hook weight -5 and +5, which runs first, and why would you use each?
Show Answer
Answer

-5 runs first — lower weights always execute before higher ones. Negative weights suit early operations (backups, pre-checks); positive weights suit late operations (notifications, post-processing).

Explanation

Weights are compared numerically even though they're written as strings — "-10" still sorts before "-5", which sorts before "0".

Q7
How are test hooks fundamentally different from every other hook type?
Show Answer
Answer

They only run when explicitly invoked via helm test <release> — never automatically during install/upgrade/delete. Every other hook type fires automatically at its named lifecycle moment.

Explanation

This makes test ideal for on-demand smoke tests (API health checks, DB connectivity) that a human or a CI pipeline triggers deliberately, not as a blocking step of every deploy.

Q8
Why are Jobs preferred over bare Pods for hooks?
Show Answer
Answer

Jobs run to completion and natively track success/failure — exactly what a hook needs. Pods just run indefinitely with no built-in completion semantics, retry count, or deadline.

Explanation

Jobs also offer backoffLimit (auto-retry) and activeDeadlineSeconds (deadline) — both genuinely useful for batch-style hook operations, and both absent from a plain Pod.

Q9
What happens to a release if one of its hooks fails?
Show Answer
Answer

The entire operation (install/upgrade/delete) fails, and the release enters a failed state. The failed hook's Job pod typically remains for debugging (unless a hook-failed delete policy removed it). With --atomic, Helm automatically rolls back instead.

Explanation

A single hook failure is never "partial" — it aborts the whole operation, which is exactly why production installs/upgrades should almost always include --atomic.

Q10
What annotation controls when a completed hook resource gets deleted, and what values does it accept?
Show Answer
Answer

"helm.sh/hook-delete-policy". Values: hook-succeeded, hook-failed, before-hook-creation — multiple values can be comma-separated.

Explanation

Without any delete policy set, hook Jobs simply accumulate in the cluster forever — always set at least one for production hooks.

⚙️ Chapter 10 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

A hook that isn't behaving as expected, and you diagnose it with this chapter's mental model.

Q1
A hook Job written with "helm.sh/hook-weight": -5 (no quotes) fails chart validation. What's wrong?
Show Answer
Answer

hook-weight must be a quoted STRING, not a bare YAML integer. Fix: "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-5".

Explanation

Kubernetes annotations are always string-valued — an unquoted number in YAML can be interpreted as a different type depending on context, which is exactly the "common exam typo" this chapter's exam-tip warns about.

Q2
Three months after deploying easypj, you notice dozens of completed *-db-migrate Job pods still sitting in the namespace. What's missing from the hook template, and what's the fix?
Show Answer
Answer

A hook-delete-policy. Add "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded so completed Jobs clean themselves up automatically going forward (existing ones still need manual kubectl delete).

Explanation

Without an explicit policy, nothing removes a hook Job automatically — this accumulation is one of the most common real-world hook maintenance issues.

Q3
A pre-upgrade migration hook is hanging — it's been running for 20 minutes with no output. What's your first diagnostic command?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
kubectl logs job/easypj-db-migrate
Explanation

Going straight to the container's own logs is faster than parsing helm get hooks output — exactly this chapter's central Speed Tip.

Q4
You need Job A (backup) to always finish completely before Job B (migration) even starts, both as pre-upgrade hooks. Is giving them the same weight safe?
Show Answer
Answer

No — same-weight hooks run CONCURRENTLY since Helm 3.2+, not sequentially. Give Job A a lower weight (e.g. -10) and Job B a higher one (e.g. -5) to guarantee A fully completes before B starts.

Explanation

Weights create true barriers only ACROSS different weight values — within one weight, order is explicitly undefined and may run in parallel.

Q5
You updated the migration hook's container image tag and ran helm upgrade, but the hook still ran the OLD command. Is Helm caching something, or is this expected?
Show Answer
Answer

This would be unexpected — hooks are deleted and RE-CREATED on every relevant operation, so a template change should always take effect on the very next run. If it didn't, check that the template edit actually landed in the chart being installed (a stale local chart copy is the most common real cause).

Explanation

Hooks are the OPPOSITE of "not updated" in this specific sense — unlike CRDs (which genuinely never update), hooks are fully re-rendered and re-applied fresh every time their triggering event fires.

Q6
You add a new CRD to crds/, run helm install, then later change that same CRD file and run helm upgrade. What actually happens to the live CRD?
Show Answer
Answer

Nothing — the live CRD is completely unaffected by the upgrade. CRDs in crds/ are applied once, at install, and never touched again by Helm. Apply the change manually with kubectl apply -f crds/....

Explanation

This is deliberate, not a bug — it prevents Helm from silently making a breaking change to a cluster-wide custom resource type other tools might depend on.

Q7
A pre-rollback backup hook references {{ .Release.Revision }} in its backup filename, expecting it to name the file after the revision being rolled back TO. Is that correct?
Show Answer
Answer

No — .Release.Revision inside a rollback hook is the NEW revision number the rollback operation is creating, not the historical target revision. The filename will reflect the wrong number if the author assumed otherwise.

Explanation

This exact misunderstanding is called out as a named gotcha in Under the Hood §④ — worth double-checking any hook template that references .Release.Revision during a rollback.

Q8
A teammate wants to guarantee a specific Secret NEVER gets deleted, even by a well-intentioned helm uninstall — but it's not a hook resource at all, just a normal chart Secret. What's the right annotation, and how is it different from a hook-delete-policy?
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
metadata:
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/resource-policy": keep
Explanation

resource-policy: keep works on ANY resource (hook or not) and means "never delete, ever." hook-delete-policy only applies to hook resources and controls cleanup timing, not permanent preservation.

Q9
Design a post-install hook that seeds initial data ONLY on a truly fresh install, never on any subsequent upgrade.
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
metadata:
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": post-install
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "0"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
Explanation

Using ONLY post-install (not post-install,post-upgrade) is what limits this to fresh installs — Chapter 6's .Release.IsInstall boolean would be the equivalent guard if this logic instead lived inside a shared template.

Q10
Design the full ordering for three pre-upgrade hooks that must run in this exact sequence: backup, then migrate, then notify — with migrate and notify allowed to overlap since they touch unrelated systems.
Show Answer
Answer
yaml
# backup:   "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-10"
# migrate:  "helm.sh/hook-weight": "0"
# notify:   "helm.sh/hook-weight": "0"
Explanation

Backup at a strictly lower weight guarantees it fully completes first; giving migrate and notify the SAME weight (0) is exactly how you deliberately opt them into concurrent execution — this is the one case in this chapter where "same weight" is the correct, intentional choice rather than an accident.

🔬 Practice Drill 10.1 — Add and Verify a Real Migration Hook

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

Add the §10.6 migration hook to easypj-chart, upgrade a running release, and confirm from kubectl alone (not Helm output) that the hook actually ran before the new Deployment pods started.

Hint: kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp shows the real chronological order of what Kubernetes actually did.
View Solution
bash
helm upgrade easypj-dev ./easypj-chart -n dev
kubectl get jobs -l helm.sh/hook -n dev
kubectl logs job/easypj-dev-easypj-db-migrate -n dev
kubectl get events -n dev --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | grep -E "Job|Deployment"

Check yourself: the events timeline should show the migration Job's completion event BEFORE any new ReplicaSet/Pod creation events for the Deployment — that ordering, observed directly from Kubernetes rather than trusted from Helm's own output, is the actual proof the hook worked.

🔬 Practice Drill 10.2 — Force a Hook Failure and Watch --atomic Recover

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Temporarily break the migration hook's command (typo the Django management command) and run an upgrade with --atomic. Confirm the release ends up healthy anyway.

Hint: --atomic implies --wait — give it enough --timeout to actually observe the failure and rollback.
View Solution
bash
helm upgrade easypj-dev ./easypj-chart -n dev \
  --set command_typo=true --atomic --timeout 3m
# expect: "upgrade failed... rolling back"
helm status easypj-dev -n dev
# should show "deployed", not "failed"

Check yourself: the failed hook's Job pod should still be visible via kubectl get jobs -l helm.sh/hook -n dev for post-mortem debugging, even though the release itself recovered to deployed.

🔬 Practice Drill 10.3 — Order Three Hooks Correctly

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Write three pre-install hook annotation blocks (weights only, not full Jobs) that guarantee: a namespace-prep step runs first, a secret-seeding step runs second, and a smoke-test step runs strictly last — no two ever run in parallel.

Hint: Three DISTINCT weights, since "no two run in parallel" rules out any shared weight.
View Solution
yaml
# namespace-prep:  "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-10"
# seed-secrets:    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-5"
# smoke-test:      "helm.sh/hook-weight": "0"

Check yourself: if any two of your three weights are equal, you've violated the "no two run in parallel" requirement — go back and make all three strictly distinct.

🔬 Practice Drill 10.4 — Add a CRD and Confirm It Survives Uninstall

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Add a minimal CRD to crds/, install the chart, then uninstall it, and confirm the CRD is STILL present in the cluster afterward.

Hint: kubectl get crd before and after the uninstall should show identical results for this CRD.
View Solution
bash
helm install easypj-crd-test ./easypj-chart -n dev --create-namespace
kubectl get crd jobposts.easypj.example.com
helm uninstall easypj-crd-test -n dev
kubectl get crd jobposts.easypj.example.com
# still there — CRDs are NEVER deleted by Helm
kubectl delete crd jobposts.easypj.example.com  # manual cleanup, only if truly done with it

Check yourself: if the CRD disappeared after helm uninstall, something in the chart is managing it as a regular template resource rather than placing it correctly under crds/.

🔬 Practice Drill 10.5 — Write a Post-Rollback Verification Hook

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Write a post-rollback hook that runs Django's check --deploy command after any rollback, to catch configuration problems introduced by reverting to an old release.

Hint: Model it directly on Under the Hood §④'s post-rollback example.
View Solution
yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-post-rollback-verify
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": post-rollback
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "5"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: verify
        image: easypj:{{ .Values.image.tag }}
        command: ["python", "manage.py", "check", "--deploy"]

Check yourself: this hook fires on EVERY rollback automatically, with zero manual step required — that's the entire value of a lifecycle hook over a manual runbook step someone might forget.

📌 Chapter 10 Visual Summary — controlling WHEN, not just WHAT
  🪝 8 Hook Types           ⚖️ Weights                 📋 Delete Policies
  ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐           ┌───────────────────┐
  │ pre/post ×    │        │ lower runs    │           │ hook-succeeded      │
  │ install/      │        │ FIRST,        │           │ hook-failed          │
  │ upgrade/      │        │ same weight = │           │ before-hook-creation │
  │ delete/       │        │ concurrent    │           │ (combine w/ commas)  │
  │ rollback, test│        │               │           │                     │
  └──────────────┘         └──────────────┘           └───────────────────┘

  🏗️ Job (the shape)        🔍 CRDs (different!)       ⏪ Rollback hooks
  ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐           ┌───────────────────┐
  │ restartPolicy:│        │ crds/ dir,     │          │ .Release.Revision   │
  │ Never, tracks │        │ NEVER updated  │          │ = the NEW revision,  │
  │ success/fail  │        │ or deleted     │          │ not the target one   │
  └──────────────┘         └──────────────┘           └───────────────────┘
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   THE ONE RULE: hooks BLOCK synchronously, run in weight order (same
   weight = concurrent), and live entirely outside the tracked release
   manifest — a parallel system, deliberately. 🪝

In words: A hook is an ordinary Kubernetes resource — almost always a Job — wearing one special annotation that tells Helm "don't deploy me as part of the normal release; run me at this specific moment instead." Eight moments exist, weights control order within a moment, and delete policies control cleanup afterward.

Hooks deliberately live in a parallel system from the rest of the release: they're not in helm get manifest, not cleaned up by helm uninstall, and not updated in place — they're deleted and recreated fresh every time. CRDs go even further, using their own crds/ mechanism that Helm never touches again after the very first install.

The takeaway: Part 4's last piece, testing (Chapter 11), builds directly on the test hook type introduced here — proving a chart actually works is the natural next step after controlling exactly when everything else happens.

Chapter 11 · Testing & Validation — Ship with Confidence

"It rendered" and "it works" are different claims. Helm provides multiple layers of validation — linting, template rendering, dry-run simulation, schema validation, and test hooks — that together form a safety net catching errors before they reach production. This chapter closes Part 4 by covering every validation technique available.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🧪 Testing 🐍 easypj / jobpost 🎯 Testing & Troubleshooting

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Run chart tests with helm test
  • ✅ Write test pod definitions for connectivity and smoke testing
  • ✅ Catch errors early with helm lint
  • ✅ Preview rendered YAML with helm template
  • ✅ Simulate operations with --dry-run — and know exactly what each of its three values proves
  • ✅ Validate values with JSON Schema
  • ✅ Integrate testing into CI/CD pipelines
🎓 Helm Certification Relevance
Testing & Troubleshooting CORE DOMAIN
🎯 lint Is Spell-Check, template Is Dress Rehearsal, test Is Opening Night

Each validation layer proves a genuinely different thing — confusing them is the single biggest mistake in this chapter's domain:

  • A chart that passes helm lint AND helm template can still fail on install. Neither checks against your ACTUAL cluster's API versions or live resource conflicts — only --dry-run=server does.
  • --dry-run is a 3-VALUED FLAG, not a simple switch — the single most-corrected fact in this chapter (Under the Hood covers it in full).
  • Lint output has two tiers — ERRORS (will actually fail install) vs WARNINGS (break convention, chart still installs). Use --strict to make warnings fail too — the exam-day-safe default for CI pipelines.

🧭 Section Map — the Chapter 11 Learning Arc

The arc follows the actual validation pyramid: on-demand tests (11.1–11.2) → static checks that need no cluster (11.3–11.4) → cluster-aware simulation (11.5) → input validation (11.6) → tying it all together into a pipeline (11.7).

Validation Pipeline — Catch Errors Before Production Sees Them
   helm lint          helm template        helm install
   (syntax &     ──▶  --debug         ──▶  --dry-run=server   ──▶
    best-practice)    (does it render?)     (would K8s accept it?)
        │                    │                      │
        ▼                    ▼                      ▼
   Chart.yaml valid?    Real YAML out?        API server validates
   values.yaml exists?  Values substituted?   without applying
                                                (bare --dry-run does
                                                 NOT hit the API!)
                                                       │
                                                       ▼
                                              helm install (for real)
                                                       │
                                                       ▼
                                              helm test (verify it
                                               actually WORKS, not
                                               just that it deployed)

   ⚡ SPEED TIP: chain all 3 pre-flight checks in one line:
   helm lint ./chart && helm template ./chart --debug &&
   helm install test ./chart --dry-run=server --debug
