11.1 Chart Tests — helm test

helm test
# Run all tests for a release
helm test easypj-dev -n dev

# Run tests and show logs
helm test easypj-dev --logs

# Run with a timeout
helm test easypj-dev --timeout 5m

11.2 Test Pods — Writing Test Cases

templates/tests/test-connection.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: "{{ include "easypj.fullname" . }}-test-connection"
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": test
spec:
  containers:
  - name: wget
    image: busybox
    command: ['wget']
    args: ['{{ include "easypj.fullname" . }}:{{ .Values.service.port }}']
  restartPolicy: Never

Two Test Pod Design Patterns

💨
Smoke Test

Verify the application started and responds — a quick HTTP GET to the service endpoint. Runs fast (~5s).

containers:
- name: smoke-test
  image: curlimages/curl
  command: ["curl", "-f",
    "http://{{ .Release.Name }}-svc/health"]
🔗
Integration Test

Verify database connectivity and basic CRUD operations — validates the full stack. Takes longer (~30s).

containers:
- name: integration-test
  image: easypj-test:latest
  command: ["./run-tests.sh"]
  env:
  - name: DB_HOST
    value: {{ .Release.Name }}-postgresql

11.3 helm lint — Catching Template Errors Early

linting
# Lint a chart
helm lint ./easypj-chart

# Lint with strict mode (warnings become errors)
helm lint ./easypj-chart --strict

# Lint against specific values
helm lint ./easypj-chart -f values-prod.yaml
📖 Two Tiers of Lint Output

Lint output has two tiers: ERRORS (will actually cause helm install to fail) versus WARNINGS (break convention, but the chart still installs). Use --strict to make warnings fail too — the exam-day-safe default for CI pipelines (§11.7).

11.4 helm template — Rendering Without Installing

template rendering
# Render templates locally (no cluster needed)
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart -f values-prod.yaml

# Render with debug output
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart --debug

# Render and validate with an external YAML/K8s schema tool
helm template ./chart | kubeval --strict

11.5 --dry-run — Simulating Install/Upgrade

dry-run simulation
# Simulate an install
helm install easypj-test ./chart --dry-run --debug

# Simulate an upgrade
helm upgrade easypj ./chart --dry-run --debug

# Dry-run is NOT purely a template render — depending on its value,
# it can talk to the API server too (see below)
⚠️ CORRECTED — --dry-run Is a 3-Valued Flag, Not a Switch

The official domain names this exact skill: verifying a chart is safe WITHOUT ever touching a running cluster. Three tools, three different guarantees — know which one proves what:

  • helm lint → Chart.yaml/values.yaml structure + template best-practice rules. Does NOT render full YAML.
  • helm template → fully renders YAML locally. Proves templates produce SYNTACTICALLY VALID output. No cluster contacted.
  • --dry-run=client (or bare --dry-run) → renders locally only, does NOT contact the API server. Same guarantee as template.
  • --dry-run=server → ALSO submits to the API server for validation (needs cluster connectivity) — the ONLY mode that proves Kubernetes would actually ACCEPT the result. Still creates nothing.

🔑 Bare --dry-run does NOT hit the cluster — you must write --dry-run=server explicitly to get real server-side validation.

11.6 Schema Validation — values.schema.json Deep Dive

values.schema.json
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["replicaCount", "image"],
  "properties": {
    "replicaCount": {
      "type": "integer",
      "minimum": 1,
      "maximum": 100,
      "description": "Number of replicas (1-100)"
    },
    "image": {
      "type": "object",
      "required": ["repository", "tag"],
      "properties": {
        "repository": { "type": "string", "pattern": "^[a-z0-9./-]+$" },
        "tag": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 },
        "pullPolicy": { "enum": ["Always", "IfNotPresent", "Never"] }
      }
    },
    "ingress": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "enabled": { "type": "boolean" },
        "host": { "type": "string", "format": "hostname" }
      },
      "if": { "properties": { "enabled": { "const": true } } },
      "then": { "required": ["host"] }
    }
  }
}
⚠️ Conditional Validation, Read Carefully

The if/then block above says: IF ingress.enabled is true, THEN host becomes required. This prevents a user from enabling ingress without specifying a hostname. JSON Schema Draft 7 features like if/then/else and $ref are fully supported by Helm 3.

11.7 CI/CD with helm test — Integrating into Pipelines

1
Lint

helm lint ./chart --strict — fail fast on syntax errors (~1s).

2
Template

helm template ./chart -f values-ci.yaml — render locally (~2s).

3
Dry-Run

helm install test ./chart --dry-run=server — validate against the cluster (~3-5s).

4
Install

helm upgrade --install test ./chart -n ci --atomic — deploy to a CI namespace (~30-120s).

5
Test

helm test test -n ci --logs — run test hooks (~30-60s).

6
Cleanup

helm uninstall test -n ci — remove the CI deployment (~10s).

💡 CI/CD Best Practices
  • Always run lint first — catches ~80% of issues in one second
  • Use a dedicated CI namespace — never test in production namespaces
  • Auto-cleanup — uninstall test releases after every run
  • Set timeouts — helm test --timeout 5m prevents hung CI jobs
  • Parallelize — test multiple charts at once using different namespaces
MethodSpeedNeeds cluster?CatchesPriority
helm lint⚡ Instant❌ NoSyntax errors, missing required fields, deprecated APIs🔴 ALWAYS FIRST
helm template⚡ Fast❌ NoTemplate rendering errors, missing values, nil pointers🟡 SECOND
--dry-run=server🐢 Moderate✅ YesAPI version mismatches, webhook rejections, resource conflicts🟢 THIRD
helm test🐢 Slow✅ YesApplication-level issues (connectivity, API responses, DB access)🔵 AFTER DEPLOY
Schema validation⚡ Instant❌ NoInvalid value types, out-of-range values, missing required fields🟡 AUTOMATIC
Under the Hood — the testing pyramid, helm test internals, and reading errors like an expert

Three things separate someone who runs these commands from someone who genuinely understands WHY the layers exist and how to read what they say when something breaks.

① The Helm Testing Pyramid

Just like software testing, chart validation has layers — each catches different errors at different speeds, and running only one layer leaves real gaps:

   HELM TESTING PYRAMID (Fastest → Most Thorough)
   ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
                       ┌─────┐
                       │ E2E │  helm test (real cluster, real data)
                       │     │  SLOW (30-120s) — catches: integration, connectivity
                       ├─────┤
                       │DRY  │  helm install --dry-run=server --debug
                       │RUN  │  MEDIUM (3-5s) — catches: API validation, K8s errors
                       ├─────┤
                       │TMPL │  helm template --debug
                       │     │  FAST (1-2s) — catches: render errors, nil pointers
                       ├─────┤
                       │LINT │  helm lint --strict
                       │     │  INSTANT (<1s) — catches: YAML syntax, missing fields
                       └─────┘

   EVERY CI PIPELINE SHOULD RUN ALL FOUR LAYERS, IN ORDER.
   If lint fails, stop — don't waste time on template/dry-run.
   If template fails, stop — don't waste time on dry-run.
   If dry-run fails, stop — don't waste time on helm test.
🔑 Fail fast, in pyramid order. Each layer is strictly more expensive (in time and, for the top two, real cluster resources) than the one below it — there's never a good reason to run helm test against a chart that hasn't already passed lint.
② Understanding helm test Internals
1
Test Discovery

Helm looks for resources annotated helm.sh/hook: test in the release's stored manifest. These were deployed during install/upgrade but are NOT normal resources — they're hook resources, exactly like Chapter 10's lifecycle hooks.

2
Test Execution

Tests run in weight order, like any other hook. Each test pod/job is created, and Helm waits for it to complete successfully (exit code 0). Tests can be Pods (run once) or Jobs (restartPolicy: Never).

3
Result Collection

Helm collects exit codes and logs from each test resource. helm test --logs prints logs even for successful tests; failed tests show their error output automatically.

4
Test Cleanup

Tests with hook-delete-policy: hook-succeeded are deleted after passing. Failed tests are preserved for debugging. Tests can be re-run any time — they execute fresh against the CURRENT release state, not a snapshot from install time.

🔑 Tests run against the LIVE cluster, not a sandbox. A poorly-written test can genuinely corrupt data if it performs writes. Always ensure test pods carry appropriate RBAC and resource limits, and keep them read-only unless the test is explicitly, deliberately validating a write path.
③ Tracking Down Error Paths & Output Validation Routines

Two exam-named skills worth knowing by their official terminology, not just by feel:

Tracking down error paths means reading a Helm error's file:line reference back to its source. A message like template: easypj/templates/deployment.yaml:14:23: executing... nil pointer tells you exactly where to look — open deployment.yaml, go to line 14. The error ALWAYS names the file; there's no guessing required.

Output validation routines means applying a repeatable check sequence to RENDERED YAML, not just confirming "does it render." A common pattern: pipe helm template output through kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f - or a dedicated YAML/K8s schema validator (like kubeval) to confirm structural correctness one more layer beyond what helm template alone proves.

an output validation routine, chained
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart -f values-prod.yaml \
  | kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f -
🔑 This is genuinely a different check than helm template alone. helm template proves the Go template syntax rendered without error. Piping the OUTPUT through kubectl apply --dry-run=client additionally proves the resulting YAML is structurally valid Kubernetes — a subtly different, complementary guarantee.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Five distinct validation layers exist, each proving something different — lint (structure), template (renders), dry-run (cluster would accept), install (actually deployed), test (actually works).
  • --dry-run is a 3-valued flag — bare/=client never touches the cluster; only =server does real API validation. This single distinction is the most commonly misunderstood fact in the whole chapter.
  • Passing lint and template does NOT guarantee a successful install — only --dry-run=server or a real install proves the cluster would actually accept the result.
  • Test hooks only run on demand via helm test — unlike lifecycle hooks, they never block a normal install/upgrade.
  • The testing pyramid should always run in order, failing fast — instant lint before fast template before moderate dry-run before slow real tests.
  • Every Helm error names its own file and line — reading that reference directly is always faster than guessing.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Assuming a chart that passes helm lint AND helm template is production-safe. Neither checks against your ACTUAL cluster's API versions or live resource conflicts — a chart can pass both and still fail on real install.
  • Believing bare --dry-run validates against the cluster. It doesn't — it behaves identically to --dry-run=client, rendering locally with zero API contact. Only the explicit --dry-run=server talks to Kubernetes.
  • Treating helm test as a safe, sandboxed operation. It runs against the LIVE cluster and live data — a test pod that performs writes can genuinely corrupt production state if not carefully scoped.
  • Running helm test before lint/template/dry-run pass. It's the slowest, most expensive layer — always fail fast on the cheaper checks first.
  • Forgetting --strict on helm lint in CI. Without it, WARNINGS don't fail the pipeline — a convention violation can silently ship.
  • Assuming schema validation only checks types. Draft-7 if/then/else conditional rules let a schema express real cross-field business logic, not just "is this a string."
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Chain all 3 pre-flight checks in one line: helm lint ./chart && helm template ./chart --debug && helm install test ./chart --dry-run=server --debug — one command, fails fast at whichever stage breaks.
  • Lint always first, no exceptions. It's instant and catches roughly 80% of real-world chart mistakes before anything more expensive runs.
  • Read the file:line in every error before doing anything else. Helm's error messages are more precise than they first appear.
  • Use a dedicated CI namespace for helm test — never point a test run at anything resembling production.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 11)

the complete validation pipeline, layer by layer 
# 1. Lint — instant, no cluster
helm lint ./easypj-chart --strict

# 2. Template — fast, no cluster
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart -f values-prod.yaml --debug

# 3. Dry-run — moderate, NEEDS a cluster (note the =server!)
helm install easypj-test ./easypj-chart --dry-run=server --debug

# 4. Real install/upgrade
helm upgrade --install easypj ./easypj-chart -n ci --atomic --wait

# 5. Test — slow, verifies it actually WORKS
helm test easypj -n ci --logs

# 6. Cleanup (CI namespaces only)
helm uninstall easypj -n ci

🧠 Chapter 11 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of validation layers — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What command runs chart tests for an already-deployed release?
Show Answer
Answer

helm test <release> -n <namespace>. This executes every test hook resource (usually test Pods). Add --logs to see their output.

Explanation

Test hooks only run on demand, never automatically during install/upgrade — this deliberately separates "did it deploy" from "does it work."

Q2
What's the fundamental difference between helm lint and helm template?
Show Answer
Answer

helm lint validates Chart.yaml/values.yaml structure and template best-practice rules without producing rendered output. helm template actually renders every template to real YAML. Lint validates; template renders.

Explanation

A one-second lint catches structural issues before a two-second template render even attempts to substitute values — running both, in that order, costs almost nothing.

Q3
How does --dry-run=server differ from helm template?
Show Answer
Answer

helm template renders entirely locally/offline. --dry-run=server connects to the live Kubernetes API server and validates API versions, resource types, and admission webhooks — without creating anything.

Explanation

Only =server proves the cluster would genuinely accept the result — bare --dry-run/=client gives no more guarantee than helm template already did.

Q4
Where are test pod definitions conventionally placed inside a chart?
Show Answer
Answer

In templates/tests/. Common filenames: test-connection.yaml (HTTP smoke check), test-db.yaml (database connectivity check).

Explanation

This is purely a directory convention — what actually makes a resource a test is the helm.sh/hook: test annotation, not its file location.

Q5
Which JSON Schema keywords constrain a numeric value to a range, and a string to a set of allowed values?
Show Answer
Answer

minimum/maximum for numbers; enum for a restricted set of allowed strings. minLength/maxLength constrain string length specifically.

Explanation

These are checked automatically at install/upgrade time whenever a chart ships a values.schema.json — no extra flag needed to trigger the check.

Q6
What specifically makes a Pod a "test pod" that only runs via helm test?
Show Answer
Answer

The annotation "helm.sh/hook": test. This tells Helm to run the Pod ONLY on an explicit helm test invocation, never during normal install/upgrade.

Explanation

Unlike other lifecycle hooks, test hooks never block a deploy — they're purely opt-in, run-when-you-ask validation.

Q7
How does Helm validate user-supplied values against values.schema.json — do you need a separate command?
Show Answer
Answer

No separate command — Helm automatically validates against values.schema.json at install/upgrade time. Running helm lint also triggers the same schema validation.

Explanation

This is why schema validation is marked "AUTOMATIC" priority in §11.7's comparison table — it's not an opt-in step you have to remember to run.

Q8
In a CI/CD pipeline, what's the correct order for lint, template, and dry-run — and why?
Show Answer
Answer

Lint → Template → Dry-run. Each is progressively more expensive (in time, and for dry-run, real cluster contact), so failing fast on the cheapest check first saves the most time overall.

Explanation

This exactly mirrors the Testing Pyramid from Under the Hood — cheapest/fastest layer at the bottom, most expensive at the top.

Q9
Can helm template run with no Kubernetes cluster available at all?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes — helm template is purely local. It renders templates to YAML using only the chart files and values, with zero cluster connection required.

Explanation

This makes it ideal for CI environments and offline development where no live cluster is available — contrast with --dry-run=server, which errors immediately without one.

Q10
What flag shows the actual output/logs of test pods, not just a pass/fail summary?
Show Answer
Answer

helm test <release> --logs. Without it, you only see a status summary; with it, you see each test's real stdout — HTTP responses, error messages, assertion output.

Explanation

Always reach for --logs when a test fails and you need to know WHY, not just THAT it failed.

⚙️ Chapter 11 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

A validation gap, and you close it with the right layer of testing.

Q1
A chart passes helm lint and helm template cleanly in CI, but the real install fails with an API version error. Was the CI pipeline wrong to trust those two checks?
Show Answer
Answer

Not wrong, but incomplete — neither lint nor template ever contacted a real cluster, so neither could catch an API-version mismatch. Add a --dry-run=server step before the real install to close this exact gap.

Explanation

This is precisely the "chart passes lint and template but still fails install" gotcha this chapter opens with.

Q2
A teammate says they "already dry-ran it" using bare helm install test ./chart --dry-run and it looked fine, then the real install still failed with a webhook rejection. What did their dry-run actually prove?
Show Answer
Answer

Nothing about the live cluster — bare --dry-run behaves as --dry-run=client, never contacting the API server. It only proved the same thing helm template would have. They needed --dry-run=server to actually catch the webhook rejection ahead of time.

Explanation

This is the single most commonly misunderstood fact in the entire chapter — always write the explicit value.

Q3
A test pod's write operation accidentally deleted real data during a helm test run against a shared cluster. What two design mistakes led here?
Show Answer
Answer

(1) The test wasn't scoped to a dedicated, isolated CI namespace — it ran somewhere with real data reachable. (2) The test performed a write/delete operation when it should have been read-only, since it wasn't explicitly testing a write path.

Explanation

Both are named directly in this chapter's Gotchas and Under the Hood §② — helm test runs against the live cluster, with no sandboxing provided automatically.

Q4
Your CI pipeline runs all five validation layers on every single commit, even trivial doc-only changes, and it's slow. What's the one-line optimization that preserves safety?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm lint ./chart --strict && helm template ./chart --debug && helm install test ./chart --dry-run=server --debug
Explanation

Chaining with && means the pipeline stops at the FIRST failing layer instead of always running all three to completion — a chart with a lint error never wastes time on a cluster round-trip.

Q5
You get the error template: easypj/templates/secret.yaml:9:15: executing "easypj/templates/secret.yaml" at <.Values.postgresql.auth.password>: nil pointer evaluating interface {}.postgresql. Where do you look, and what's likely wrong?
Show Answer
Answer

Open templates/secret.yaml at line 9 — the error names the exact file and line. The likely cause: .Values.postgresql is missing or nil in whatever values file/overrides are currently active.

Explanation

This is "tracking down error paths" from Under the Hood §③ applied directly — the file:line reference removes all guesswork about where the problem lives.

Q6
You want to validate that helm template's output is not just syntactically valid Go-template output, but genuinely well-formed Kubernetes YAML. What extra step proves that?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart | kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f -
Explanation

This is an "output validation routine" — piping rendered YAML through a separate structural check gives a guarantee helm template alone doesn't provide.

Q7
A chart's values.schema.json requires host only when ingress.enabled is true — but a values file sets enabled: true with no host and passes validation anyway. What's the schema bug?
Show Answer
Answer

The schema is likely missing the if/then conditional block entirely, or the condition's property path doesn't match the actual values structure. The correct shape: "if": {"properties": {"enabled": {"const": true}}}, "then": {"required": ["host"]}.

Explanation

Without the conditional, host can only ever be marked required or optional GLOBALLY — there's no way to express "required, but only sometimes" without if/then.

Q8
You need to prove a chart renders correctly for values-prod.yaml specifically, entirely offline, before a teammate with cluster access runs the real dry-run. One command?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart -f values-prod.yaml --debug
Explanation

Entirely local, entirely offline — proves the templates render without error for that specific values file, independent of anyone's cluster access.

Q9
A helm test run shows "1 test PASSED" but gives no detail about what it actually checked. How do you see the real output?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm test easypj-dev -n dev --logs
Explanation

Without --logs, a passing test tells you nothing beyond its exit code — always add it, even for passing tests, to build confidence in what was actually verified.

Q10
Design a complete, minimal CI script for easypj that stops immediately at the first failure and cleans up after itself regardless of outcome.
Show Answer
Answer
bash
set -e
helm lint ./easypj-chart --strict
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart --debug
helm install ci-test ./easypj-chart --dry-run=server --debug -n ci
helm upgrade --install ci-test ./easypj-chart -n ci --atomic --wait --timeout 5m
helm test ci-test -n ci --logs
helm uninstall ci-test -n ci
Explanation

set -e makes the whole script exit on the first failing command — a real CI system would additionally wrap the uninstall in a cleanup trap so it runs even if an earlier step fails, but the linear happy-path sequence above is the core pattern.

🔬 Practice Drill 11.1 — Run the Full Pyramid, In Order

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

Starting from easypj-chart, run all four static/simulation layers in the correct order (lint, template, dry-run=server, install), stopping immediately if any layer fails.

Hint: Chain with &&, cheapest layer first.
View Solution
bash
helm lint ./easypj-chart --strict && \
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart --debug && \
helm install easypj-test ./easypj-chart --dry-run=server --debug -n dev

Check yourself: if you accidentally wrote bare --dry-run instead of --dry-run=server, the third command never actually contacted the cluster — go back and verify you used the explicit value.

🔬 Practice Drill 11.2 — Write and Run a Smoke Test

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Add the §11.2 test-connection.yaml to easypj-chart, install a release, and run helm test with logs to confirm the smoke test actually passes.

Hint: The test pod must be inside templates/tests/ to be discovered.
View Solution
bash
helm install easypj-dev ./easypj-chart -n dev --create-namespace
helm test easypj-dev -n dev --logs

Check yourself: the logs should show the wget command's actual HTTP response — if the test pod can't resolve the service name, double-check it uses the exact same include "easypj.fullname" . the Service itself uses.

🔬 Practice Drill 11.3 — Break the Chart, Read the Error, Fix It

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Deliberately introduce a typo referencing a nonexistent values key in deployment.yaml, run helm template, and use the error's file:line reference to fix it — without opening any other file first.

Hint: The error message tells you exactly which file and line to open — trust it.
View Solution
bash
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart --debug
# Error: template: easypj/templates/deployment.yaml:23:14: ...
# Open deployment.yaml, go to line 23, fix the typo'd key
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart --debug
# Should now render cleanly

Check yourself: if you found yourself scanning multiple files to find the bug, re-read the error message more carefully — it always names the exact location.

🔬 Practice Drill 11.4 — Add a Conditional Schema Rule

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Write a values.schema.json rule for easypj requiring autoscaling.maxReplicas to be present and greater than autoscaling.minReplicas whenever autoscaling.enabled is true.

Hint: JSON Schema can express "field required when a sibling is true," but comparing two sibling fields directly needs more advanced composition — a simpler required is a reasonable partial solution worth attempting first.
View Solution
json
{
  "properties": {
    "autoscaling": {
      "properties": {
        "enabled": {"type": "boolean"},
        "minReplicas": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1},
        "maxReplicas": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1}
      },
      "allOf": [{
        "if": {"properties": {"enabled": {"const": true}}},
        "then": {"required": ["minReplicas", "maxReplicas"]}
      }]
    }
  }
}

Check yourself: this solution enforces both fields are PRESENT when autoscaling is on — it does NOT yet enforce max > min (that requires custom validation logic JSON Schema alone can't express cleanly). Recognizing that limit is itself part of the drill.

🔬 Practice Drill 11.5 — Write a Complete CI Script From Memory

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Without looking back at §11.7, write the 6-step CI/CD sequence for easypj-chart from memory: lint, template, dry-run, install, test, cleanup.

Hint: Each step should be strictly more "real" (closer to production) than the one before it.
View Solution
bash
helm lint ./easypj-chart --strict
helm template easypj ./easypj-chart -f values-ci.yaml
helm install ci-test ./easypj-chart --dry-run=server -n ci
helm upgrade --install ci-test ./easypj-chart -n ci --atomic
helm test ci-test -n ci --logs
helm uninstall ci-test -n ci

Check yourself: if you wrote this from memory correctly, including remembering --dry-run=server (not bare --dry-run), this chapter's central lesson has genuinely landed.

📌 Chapter 11 Visual Summary — five layers, one pyramid, closing Part 4
  🔍 lint                  📄 template               🧪 dry-run
  ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐          ┌───────────────────┐
  │ instant,      │        │ fast, offline, │         │ =client: offline    │
  │ no cluster    │        │ real YAML out  │         │ =server: hits API   │
  │ (ALWAYS FIRST)│        │                │         │ (creates nothing)   │
  └──────────────┘         └──────────────┘          └───────────────────┘

  📐 schema validation      🏃 helm test
  ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐
  │ automatic,    │        │ on-demand,    │
  │ instant,      │        │ LIVE cluster, │
  │ input rules   │        │ slowest layer │
  └──────────────┘         └──────────────┘
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   THE ONE RULE: fail fast, cheapest layer first — lint → template →
   dry-run=server → install → test. Never skip to the top of the pyramid. 🧪

In words: "It rendered" and "it works" are genuinely different claims, and Helm gives five distinct tools to prove each layer in between. Lint and template never touch a cluster and catch the majority of real mistakes almost instantly. Dry-run — specifically --dry-run=server, not the bare flag — is the only pre-install check that proves Kubernetes would actually accept the result. helm test, run only on demand against a real deployed release, is the final proof the application genuinely works, not just that it deployed.

Reading errors well matters as much as running the right command — every Helm template error names its own file and line, and piping rendered output through an external validator adds one more layer of structural confidence beyond what Helm's own tools check.

The takeaway: Part 4 is now complete — dependencies (Ch9), lifecycle timing (Ch10), and validation (Ch11) together turn a chart from "it's a folder of templates" into "it's a tested, production-grade deployable unit." Part 5 goes further still: running Helm safely and observably in actual production.

Chapter 12 · Chart Repositories & Distribution

A chart that only lives on your laptop helps no one else. This chapter is how charts get shared, versioned, and consumed — by a team internally, or by the public. Whether consuming community charts or distributing your own, repositories are Helm's distribution mechanism, covering everything from public registries to private OCI repositories, chart signing, and version rollout strategies.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 📦 Distribution 🐍 easypj / jobpost 🎯 Chart Creation & Anatomy

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Navigate public repositories: Bitnami, Artifact Hub, and community charts
  • ✅ Set up your own chart repository with ChartMuseum, Harbor, or an OCI registry
  • ✅ Push and pull charts using OCI-compliant container registries
  • ✅ Sign charts and verify provenance with GPG keys
  • ✅ Configure private repositories with authentication
  • ✅ Manage chart versions and rollout strategies
🎓 Helm Certification Relevance
Chart Creation & Anatomy CORE + PRODUCTION DEPTH
🎯 A Repository Is a Library, Artifact Hub Is the Card Catalog

The actual repo is the shelf the book (chart) sits on. Sections 12.1–12.2 (repo basics, helm repo index) map directly to the official Chart Creation & Anatomy domain; 12.3–12.6 (OCI, signing, private auth, version rollout) are beyond-the-exam, genuinely production-grade depth. Two things to get right immediately:

  • Adding a repo with helm repo add does NOT auto-refresh it later. Forgetting helm repo update after a chart is republished means you keep installing a stale cached version.
  • helm search repo only searches ALREADY-ADDED repos. If a chart "doesn't exist," check helm repo list before assuming the chart itself is missing.

🧭 Section Map — the Chapter 12 Learning Arc

The arc moves from consuming (12.1) to hosting your own (12.2), through the two dominant distribution mechanisms (12.3 OCI, 12.4 signing), to access control (12.5) and version discipline (12.6).

Chart Repository Types — Which One for Which Job
   TYPE                │ EXAMPLE               │ BEST FOR
   ────────────────────│───────────────────────│──────────────────────────
   Public HTTP repo    │ Bitnami, ingress-nginx│ Third-party software
   Artifact Hub        │ artifacthub.io        │ Discovery/search only
                        │                        │  (not a repo itself)
   OCI Registry        │ ghcr.io, ECR           │ Charts alongside your
                        │                        │  container images
   ChartMuseum/Harbor  │ self-hosted            │ Private org charts
   Local .tgz          │ file://path            │ Testing, air-gapped

   🧭 DECISION: Publishing YOUR OWN charts internally? → OCI Registry
      (Helm 3.8+, same infra as your Docker images).
      Consuming THIRD-PARTY software? → Bitnami/Artifact Hub.

12.1 Public Repositories — Bitnami, Artifact Hub, Stable

RepositoryFocusStatusURL
BitnamiCurated, production-ready charts✅ Activecharts.bitnami.com/bitnami
Artifact HubGlobal search engine (aggregator)✅ Activeartifacthub.io
StableLegacy Helm 2 community charts❌ Deprecatedcharts.helm.sh/stable
Ingress-NginxOfficial NGINX ingress✅ Activekubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx
Cert-ManagerTLS certificate automation✅ Activecharts.jetstack.io
working with public repos
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo update
helm search repo bitnami/postgresql
helm search hub wordpress  # global search on Artifact Hub
⚠️ CORRECTED — Stable Is a Read-Only Archive

The old "Stable" repository was deprecated in November 2020 and is now a read-only archive — don't use it as a live example or a real dependency source. Use Bitnami or Artifact Hub instead.

12.2 Creating Your Own Chart Repository

🏛️
ChartMuseum

Lightweight, open-source Helm chart repository server. Supports S3, GCS, Azure, and local storage. Simple HTTP API for pushing charts.

🏗️
Harbor

Enterprise-grade container + Helm chart registry. Built-in RBAC, vulnerability scanning, replication, and OCI support.

☁️
OCI Registries

Use any OCI-compliant registry (Docker Hub, ECR, ACR, GCR) to store Helm charts. No separate chart server needed!

Deploying ChartMuseum or Harbor

🏛️
ChartMuseum
helm repo add chartmuseum \
  https://chartmuseum.github.io/charts
helm install chartmuseum \
  chartmuseum/chartmuseum \
  --set env.open.DISABLE_API=false
🏗️
Harbor
helm repo add harbor \
  https://harbor.mycompany.com/chartrepo/library \
  --username admin --password xxx

# Or via OCI:
helm registry login harbor.mycompany.com
helm push chart.tgz oci://harbor.mycompany.com/library
📖 EXAM-CORE COMMAND: helm repo index

Every HTTP chart repository is just a folder of .tgz packages PLUS one generated file: index.yaml. helm repo index ./repo-dir (re)generates that index.yaml by scanning every .tgz in the folder — it's what makes helm repo add/helm search repo work at all. Run it again after adding a new packaged chart to the folder, or the new version won't be discoverable.

bash
helm repo index ./repo-dir --url https://charts.example.com
# --url sets the base URL baked into index.yaml

# For CI adding ONE chart at a time — merge into an existing index
# instead of fully regenerating it:
helm repo index ./dir --merge existing-index.yaml

12.3 OCI-Based Charts — helm push to Container Registry

Helm 3.8+ supports OCI registries natively. Store charts alongside container images in the same registry — simpler infrastructure, one less service to manage.

OCI chart operations
# Login to an OCI registry
helm registry login registry.example.com -u myuser -p mypass

# Package and push
helm package ./easypj-chart
helm push easypj-0.1.0.tgz oci://registry.example.com/charts

# Pull from OCI
helm pull oci://registry.example.com/charts/easypj --version 0.1.0

# Install directly from OCI — no helm repo add needed
helm install easypj oci://registry.example.com/charts/easypj --version 0.1.0

# Inspect chart metadata
helm show chart oci://registry.example.com/charts/easypj
💡 OCI = Simpler Infrastructure

With OCI support, no separate chart repository server is needed. The existing container registry (Docker Hub, ECR, ACR, GCR) now stores both images AND charts.

📖 OCI Artifact Anatomy

A chart pushed via OCI is still a gzipped tarball underneath — it's just stored as a digest-addressed layer (media type application/vnd.cncf.helm.chart.content.v1.tar+gzip) alongside a config layer and an optional provenance layer, rather than as a static .tgz file on a web server.

Traditional HTTP vs OCI — Which Commands Change

FeatureOCITraditional HTTP
StorageAny OCI registryHTTP server + index.yaml
AuthRegistry-native (docker login-style)Basic auth / TLS
VersioningOCI tagsSemVer entries in the index
Toolinghelm push/pullhelm repo add/index

12.4 Chart Signing & Provenance — helm package --sign

signing charts
# Generate a GPG key (one-time)
gpg --full-generate-key

# Package and sign
helm package ./easypj-chart --sign --key 'devops@easypj.com' --keyring ~/.gnupg/secring.gpg

# Verify a signed chart
helm verify easypj-0.1.0.tgz
# Output: Signed by: DevOps Team <devops@easypj.com>
Chart Signing Workflow — Author to Consumer
CHART AUTHOR                                CHART CONSUMER
┌─────────────────────┐                    ┌─────────────────────┐
│ 1. Generate keypair │                    │ 1. Import public key │
│    gpg --full-       │                    │    gpg --import key  │
│    generate-key      │                    │                       │
└──────────┬───────────┘                    └──────────┬───────────┘
           │                                          │
           ▼                                          ▼
┌─────────────────────┐                    ┌─────────────────────┐
│ 2. Package + Sign   │                    │ 2. Verify signature │
│    helm package      │  ── .tgz.prov ──▶  │    helm verify       │
│    --sign --key '..' │                    │    chart-0.1.0.tgz  │
│    --keyring ~/.gnupg│                    │    --keyring pubring │
└─────────────────────┘                    └─────────────────────┘

helm package --sign produces: chart-0.1.0.tgz + chart-0.1.0.tgz.prov
The .prov file is a detached signature (OpenPGP clearsigned)
🎯 Provenance on the Exam

You may be asked to verify a chart's integrity. Remember: helm verify checks the provenance file. helm install --verify does verification during installation. The keyring path must be correct, or verification fails even for a genuinely valid signature.

12.5 Private Repositories — Authentication & Access Control

private repository auth
# Add a private repo with basic auth
helm repo add myprivate https://charts.mycompany.com --username admin --password secret

# Add with a username only — Helm prompts for the password (safer)
helm repo add myprivate https://charts.mycompany.com --username admin

# OCI registry login
helm registry login myregistry.azurecr.io -u myuser -p mytoken

# Token-based (Bearer) auth
helm repo add private https://charts.company.com \
  --username token --password "$GITLAB_TOKEN"

# TLS client certificates
helm repo add secure https://charts.secure.com \
  --cert-file client.crt \
  --key-file client.key \
  --ca-file ca.crt

12.6 Chart Version Management & Rollout Strategies

📌
Semantic Versioning

Follow MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Bump MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for new features, PATCH for fixes.

🔄
Canary Releases

Deploy a new chart version to a subset of users first. Monitor metrics, then promote. helm install canary ./chart --set canary.enabled=true

🔙
Rollback Ready

Every release is versioned. helm rollback restores any previous version in seconds. Keep --history-max high enough to actually have somewhere to roll back to.

Under the Hood — HTTP vs OCI architecture, air-gapped distribution, Artifact Hub, and troubleshooting

Four things go beyond "here's the command" into genuinely understanding how chart distribution works under different constraints.

① Traditional HTTP vs OCI — Full Architecture Comparison

Understanding the underlying architecture helps choose the right repository type and debug connection issues when something goes wrong:

Traditional HTTP Repository
ARCHITECTURE:
┌────────┐     ┌────────────┐     ┌──────────┐
│ Helm   │────▶│ HTTP Server│────▶│ Storage  │
│ CLI    │     │ (nginx, S3)│     │ (.tgz    │
└────────┘     └────────────┘     │  files)  │
                                  └──────────┘
KEY FILE: index.yaml
- Lists all charts + versions
- Contains URLs + SHA256 digests
- Downloaded on helm repo update
- Cached locally at ~/.cache/helm

COMMANDS:
helm repo add NAME URL
helm repo update
helm search repo NAME
helm pull REPO/CHART --version X
OCI-Based Repository
ARCHITECTURE:
┌────────┐     ┌────────────┐     ┌──────────┐
│ Helm   │────▶│ OCI        │────▶│ Blob     │
│ CLI    │     │ Registry   │     │ Storage  │
└────────┘     │ (Docker,   │     └──────────┘
               │ Harbor,    │
               │ ECR, GCR)  │
               └────────────┘
KEY CONCEPT: Charts as OCI artifacts
- Charts stored as OCI manifests
- Tags used for versioning
- Same auth as Docker (docker login)
- No index.yaml — registry API for listing

COMMANDS:
helm registry login REGISTRY
helm push FILE.tgz oci://REGISTRY/REPO
helm pull oci://REGISTRY/REPO/CHART --version X
helm show chart oci://REGISTRY/REPO/CHART --version X
🔑 OCI is the future. The Helm project recommends OCI for new chart repositories. OCI registries provide better security (built-in auth, RBAC), immutability (digest-based), and integration with existing container infrastructure. Traditional HTTP repos remain fully supported but are no longer the recommended default for NEW distribution setups.
② Air-Gapped & Offline Environments

Some environments have no internet access at all — distributing charts there needs a deliberate offline workflow:

1
Download Charts for Offline Use
# Download chart + dependencies to a local .tgz:
helm pull bitnami/postgresql --version 12.1.0 --destination ./offline-charts/

# Download WITH all dependencies unpacked:
helm pull bitnami/postgresql --version 12.1.0 --untar
cd postgresql && helm dependency update
cd .. && helm package postgresql
2
Set Up a Local Repository
# Create an index for the local charts:
helm repo index ./offline-charts/

# Serve with any HTTP server:
python3 -m http.server 8080 --directory ./offline-charts/

# Add to Helm and install:
helm repo add local http://localhost:8080
helm install myapp local/mychart
3
Use OCI for Air-Gapped Environments
# Push to an internal OCI registry:
helm push mychart-0.1.0.tgz oci://internal-registry.local/charts

# Pull and install:
helm pull oci://internal-registry.local/charts/mychart --version 0.1.0
helm install myapp ./mychart-0.1.0.tgz
③ Artifact Hub — The Helm Chart Marketplace
   ARTIFACT HUB (artifacthub.io)
   ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
   A centralized discovery platform for cloud-native artifacts

   SUPPORTED ARTIFACT TYPES:
   ┌──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┐
   │ Helm     │ OPA      │ Falco    │ Tinkerbell│ KubeArmor│
   │ Charts   │ Policies │ Rules    │ Templates │ Profiles │
   ├──────────┼──────────┼──────────┼──────────┼──────────┤
   │ OLM      │ Tekton   │ KCL      │ Inspektor │ Headlamp │
   │ Operators│ Tasks    │ Packages │ Gadget    │ Plugins  │
   └──────────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────┘

   CHART SUBMISSION:
   1. Package chart: helm package ./mychart
   2. Push to OCI or HTTP repo
   3. Add repository URL to Artifact Hub
   4. Artifact Hub scans index.yaml and lists your chart
🔑 Artifact Hub is a discovery INDEX, not storage. It never hosts your chart's actual bytes — it just crawls your repository's index.yaml (or OCI registry) and presents it in a searchable UI. Removing your repo from Artifact Hub does nothing to the underlying chart storage, and vice versa.
④ Repository Troubleshooting Reference
SymptomDiagnosisFix
Error: no repositories foundNo repos configuredhelm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
Error: looks like "URL" is not a valid chart repositoryindex.yaml missing or malformedVerify the URL; curl -s URL/index.yaml | head
Error: failed to fetchNetwork issue or repo downhelm repo update --debug; check proxy settings
Error: no cached repository for ...Repo added but never updatedhelm repo update
Error: chart not foundChart name or version doesn't exist in the local indexhelm search repo REPO/CHART --versions
Certificate errorsTLS verification failedAdd --ca-file (never --insecure-skip-tls-verify in production)

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • A repository is just charts plus an index — index.yaml for HTTP repos, or the registry's own API for OCI. Neither exists without a chart being packaged and published first.
  • helm repo add is one-time; helm repo update is ongoing. Adding a repo doesn't create a refresh subscription — you must re-run update to see newly published versions.
  • OCI is the recommended direction for new distribution setups — same infrastructure as container images, built-in registry auth, digest-based immutability.
  • Signing proves integrity, not trustworthiness of content — helm verify confirms a chart wasn't tampered with after signing, not that the chart itself is safe to run.
  • Air-gapped distribution is a real, supported workflow — helm pull --untar + a local HTTP server or internal OCI registry covers fully offline environments.
  • Artifact Hub indexes, it doesn't host — it crawls your repository's own index.yaml or OCI registry rather than storing chart bytes itself.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Adding a repo with helm repo add does NOT auto-refresh it later. Forgetting helm repo update after a chart is republished means you keep installing a stale cached version indefinitely.
  • helm search repo only searches ALREADY-ADDED repos. If a chart "doesn't exist," check helm repo list first — the chart may simply live in a repo you never added.
  • Assuming the "Stable" repo is still a valid example or dependency source. It's a read-only archive since November 2020 — genuinely deprecated, not just "less popular."
  • A wrong --keyring path silently fails verification even for a genuinely valid signature — helm verify needs to find the right public key to check against.
  • Confusing OCI push/pull with traditional repo add/search. They're two entirely different command families — helm repo add never works with an oci:// URL, and OCI charts need no repo add step at all.
  • Forgetting to re-run helm repo index after adding a new packaged chart to a local repo folder. The new version simply won't be discoverable until the index is regenerated.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • helm search repo only searches ALREADY-ADDED repos — reach for helm search hub instead when you're not sure a repo has been added yet.
  • Use helm repo index ./dir --merge existing-index.yaml in CI pipelines that add one chart at a time — it folds the new chart INTO the existing index instead of fully regenerating it.
  • OCI needs no repo add at all — helm install/pull/show all accept an oci:// URL directly, once you're logged in.
  • When debugging a "chart not found," check helm repo list before anything else — it's usually a missing repo, not a missing chart.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 12)

every repository command, in one place 
# ADD REPOSITORIES
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo add myrepo https://myrepo.io/charts --username user --password pass

# LIST & SEARCH
helm repo list                          # show all configured repos
helm search repo nginx                  # search ALL added repos for "nginx"
helm search repo bitnami/nginx          # search one specific repo
helm search repo --versions bitnami/nginx  # show ALL versions
helm search hub nginx                   # search Artifact Hub (broader)

# UPDATE & REMOVE
helm repo update                        # refresh all repo indexes
helm repo remove bitnami                # remove a repo
helm repo index ./charts                # generate index.yaml for a local repo

# SHOW CHART DETAILS (before installing)
helm show chart bitnami/nginx           # Chart.yaml contents
helm show values bitnami/nginx          # default values.yaml
helm show readme bitnami/nginx          # README.md
helm show all bitnami/nginx             # everything

# OCI OPERATIONS
helm registry login REGISTRY
helm push FILE.tgz oci://REGISTRY/REPO
helm pull oci://REGISTRY/REPO/CHART --version X

🧠 Chapter 12 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of repositories and distribution — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What command pushes a chart to an OCI registry?
Show Answer
Answer

helm push mychart-0.1.0.tgz oci://registry.example.com/charts. Requires helm registry login first.

Explanation

OCI support (Helm 3.8+) stores charts alongside container images in the same registry — no separate chart server needed, simplifying infrastructure considerably.

Q2
What's the difference between helm search hub and helm search repo?
Show Answer
Answer

search hub queries Artifact Hub globally. search repo searches only the repositories already added locally with helm repo add.

Explanation

This distinction from Chapter 1/2 keeps recurring throughout the guide — it's genuinely one of the most-tested facts across multiple chapters.

Q3
How do you sign a Helm chart?
Show Answer
Answer

helm package ./chart --sign --key 'your-key' --keyring ~/.gnupg/secring.gpg, requiring a pre-generated GPG key. Verify later with helm verify chart.tgz.

Explanation

Signing produces a companion .prov file — that's what helm verify actually checks against, not hidden metadata inside the .tgz itself.

Q4
What's the primary infrastructure benefit OCI registries provide for Helm charts?
Show Answer
Answer

Charts live alongside container images in the SAME registry — no separate chart server needed, meaning simpler infrastructure overall.

Explanation

This is why the Helm project now recommends OCI as the default for new distribution setups — one less moving piece to operate and secure.

Q5
How do you add a private repository that requires a username and password?
Show Answer
Answer

helm repo add myrepo https://charts.example.com --username user --password pass. Omitting --password triggers an interactive prompt instead — the safer option to avoid leaving a credential in shell history.

Explanation

The same pattern extends to token-based (Bearer) auth by passing the token as the password value, and to TLS client certs via separate --cert-file/--key-file/--ca-file flags.

Q6
What is ChartMuseum, and what makes it different from Harbor?
Show Answer
Answer

ChartMuseum is a lightweight, open-source Helm chart repository server (S3/GCS/Azure/local backends). Harbor is a heavier, enterprise-grade combined container + chart registry with built-in RBAC, scanning, and replication.

Explanation

Choose ChartMuseum for a quick, standalone chart server; choose Harbor when enterprise features (RBAC, vulnerability scanning) genuinely matter.

Q7
How do you install a chart directly from an OCI registry, without ever running helm repo add?
Show Answer
Answer

helm install myapp oci://registry.example.com/charts/mychart --version 1.0.0. OCI charts are referenced by full URL directly — no repository registration step exists for them.

Explanation

This is one of the structural differences between the two repository families — OCI genuinely has no equivalent of helm repo add/update at all.

Q8
Is the "Stable" repository still a recommended source for production charts?
Show Answer
Answer

No — it was deprecated alongside the Helm 2 era (November 2020) and is now a read-only archive. Use Bitnami or Artifact Hub instead.

Explanation

Any tutorial or blog post still recommending charts.helm.sh/stable as a live example is outdated — treat it as a signal the source material predates 2020.

Q9
What does helm verify actually prove about a chart?
Show Answer
Answer

It checks the cryptographic signature and provenance file, confirming the chart hasn't been tampered with since it was signed — it does NOT independently prove the chart's content is safe or correct.

Explanation

Integrity (unmodified since signing) and safety (the content itself is trustworthy) are two different guarantees — signing only provides the first.

Q10
What's the recommended chart version strategy for production rollouts?
Show Answer
Answer

Follow SemVer strictly (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, bumping MAJOR only for breaking changes), consider canary releases for high-risk changes, and keep --history-max generous enough that a real rollback target always exists.

Explanation

These three practices work together — accurate versioning tells consumers what changed, canaries limit blast radius, and adequate history makes "undo" actually possible when something goes wrong.

⚙️ Chapter 12 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

A distribution problem, and you solve it with the right repository mechanics.

Q1
A teammate published a new version of an internal chart to your private HTTP repo an hour ago, but helm search repo internal/mychart --versions still shows only the old version. What's the fix?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm repo update
Explanation

helm repo add is one-time — it never subscribes to future changes. The local cached index only refreshes on an explicit helm repo update.

Q2
You're certain a chart called "redis-cluster" exists publicly, but helm search repo redis-cluster returns nothing. What's the fastest next check?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm search hub redis-cluster
helm repo list
Explanation

search repo only searches locally-added repos — the chart likely exists in a repository you simply haven't added yet, which search hub would reveal.

Q3
You just packaged a new chart version into your local ChartMuseum folder, but the new version doesn't show up in helm search repo. What single command did you forget?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm repo index ./charts --url https://charts.mycompany.com --merge existing-index.yaml
Explanation

A new .tgz file sitting in the folder does nothing on its own — index.yaml is the ONLY thing helm repo update actually downloads and reads, and it must be regenerated to reflect the new file.

Q4
Your company is choosing between a fresh ChartMuseum deployment and using the existing ECR registry (already used for Docker images) for a NEW internal chart repository. Which would you recommend, and why?
Show Answer
Answer

ECR via OCI — it reuses existing registry auth, RBAC, and infrastructure rather than standing up and securing an entirely new service. This is exactly the "OCI is the future" recommendation from this chapter.

Explanation

ChartMuseum remains a reasonable choice when no existing OCI-capable registry is available — but when one already exists, adding a second, separate chart-only service is usually unnecessary overhead.

Q5
A completely air-gapped cluster needs PostgreSQL from Bitnami installed, with zero internet access at deploy time. Design the offline workflow.
Show Answer
Answer
bash
# On a machine WITH internet access:
helm pull bitnami/postgresql --version 12.1.0 --destination ./offline-charts/
helm repo index ./offline-charts/
# Transfer ./offline-charts/ into the air-gapped environment

# Inside the air-gapped environment:
python3 -m http.server 8080 --directory ./offline-charts/
helm repo add local http://localhost:8080
helm install mydb local/postgresql
Explanation

The chart and its index are downloaded ONCE where internet exists, then physically transferred and served locally — no step in the air-gapped environment itself ever needs external connectivity.

Q6
A consumer runs helm verify easypj-0.1.0.tgz and gets a verification failure, even though the author insists they signed it correctly. What's the most common cause?
Show Answer
Answer

The consumer likely hasn't imported the author's public key, or is pointing --keyring at the wrong location. helm verify needs the correct public key available locally to check the signature against.

Explanation

A valid signature plus a missing/wrong public key produces the same failure symptom as an actually-invalid signature — always confirm the key was imported before assuming tampering.

Q7
You need to mirror the entire Bitnami repository into a private internal repo for compliance reasons. Sketch the approach.
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo update
for chart in $(helm search repo bitnami -l -o json | jq -r '.[].name'); do
  helm pull "$chart" --destination ./mirror/
done
helm repo index ./mirror/
# Host ./mirror/ via nginx, S3, or an internal registry
Explanation

Mirroring is really just "pull every chart, then re-index" — the same primitives as air-gapped distribution, applied to an entire repository instead of one chart.

Q8
You're seeing Error: looks like "https://charts.internal.com" is not a valid chart repository or cannot be reached. What's your first diagnostic command?
Show Answer
Answer
bash
curl -s https://charts.internal.com/index.yaml | head
Explanation

This isolates whether the problem is network/DNS-level, or specifically that index.yaml is missing/malformed at that URL — a genuinely different fix for each case.

Q9
Your team wants to publish an internal chart to Artifact Hub for internal discoverability, but keep the actual chart storage private. Is this possible?
Show Answer
Answer

Not directly for public listing — Artifact Hub indexes are typically public. For internal-only discoverability, run an equivalent internal tool or simply rely on helm repo list/documentation, since Artifact Hub itself doesn't host or gate access to the underlying chart bytes either way.

Explanation

Remember Artifact Hub is a discovery index, not storage — access control genuinely lives at the repository/registry layer, not at the discovery layer.

Q10
Design the minimal command sequence to package, sign, and push a new easypj chart version to an internal OCI registry.
Show Answer
Answer
bash
helm package ./easypj-chart --sign --key 'devops@easypj.com'
helm registry login registry.example.com -u myuser -p mypass
helm push easypj-0.2.0.tgz oci://registry.example.com/charts
Explanation

Signing happens at package time (producing the .tgz plus a .prov file); the OCI push is a separate, later step — order matters, since you can't sign a chart that hasn't been packaged yet.

🔬 Practice Drill 12.1 — Add, Update, Search, in Order

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

From a clean Helm install, add the Bitnami repo, refresh it, and confirm PostgreSQL is discoverable — in the correct three-step order.

Hint: Skipping the middle step is the single most common repository mistake in this chapter.
View Solution
bash
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo update
helm search repo bitnami/postgresql

Check yourself: the search should return at least one row — if it doesn't, you likely skipped helm repo update.

🔬 Practice Drill 12.2 — Package and Push to a Local OCI Registry

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

If you have Docker available, run a local OCI-compatible registry, then package and push easypj-chart to it, and pull it back to confirm round-trip integrity.

Hint: docker run -d -p 5000:5000 registry:2 gives you a throwaway local OCI registry.
View Solution
bash
docker run -d -p 5000:5000 --name local-registry registry:2
helm package ./easypj-chart
helm push easypj-0.1.0.tgz oci://localhost:5000/charts
helm pull oci://localhost:5000/charts/easypj-chart --version 0.1.0

Check yourself: the pulled .tgz should be byte-identical to what was pushed — OCI storage is content-addressed, so any corruption in transit would surface as a digest mismatch.

🔬 Practice Drill 12.3 — Diagnose Three Repository Errors

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

For each error, name the fix from memory: (1) Error: no repositories found. (2) Error: no cached repository for bitnami. (3) A search that returns stale/old versions only.

Hint: All three map to one of: add, update, or list.
View Solution

(1) helm repo add <name> <url> — no repos configured at all. (2) helm repo update — the repo was added but its index was never fetched. (3) helm repo update again — the local cache is simply out of date.

Check yourself: (2) and (3) have the SAME fix — both stem from a missing/stale helm repo update, just at different points in the lifecycle.

🔬 Practice Drill 12.4 — Write an Offline-Ready values-airgap.yaml Plan

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Without running anything, write out the exact 4-command sequence to prepare easypj-chart and its PostgreSQL dependency for a fully air-gapped install, from a machine WITH internet access.

Hint: Dependencies need to be resolved locally BEFORE the chart is packaged for transfer.
View Solution
bash
helm dependency update ./easypj-chart
helm package ./easypj-chart
mkdir ./offline-charts && mv easypj-*.tgz ./offline-charts/
helm repo index ./offline-charts/

Check yourself: the resulting .tgz already contains PostgreSQL bundled in its own charts/ directory (Chapter 9) — the air-gapped environment needs no separate step to fetch that dependency.

🔬 Practice Drill 12.5 — Choose a Repository Strategy and Justify It

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Your 5-person startup already uses Docker Hub for container images and has no dedicated platform team. Recommend a chart distribution strategy and justify it in two sentences.

Hint: "No dedicated platform team" strongly favors the option requiring the LEAST new infrastructure to operate.
View Solution

Sample answer: "Use OCI via the existing Docker Hub account — helm push/pull against oci://registry-1.docker.io/... reuses infrastructure and credentials the team already manages. Standing up ChartMuseum or Harbor would add a new service to operate and secure, which a 5-person team without dedicated platform staff should avoid unless a specific feature (like Harbor's vulnerability scanning) is genuinely required."

Check yourself: the deciding factor here is operational overhead, not raw feature count — the "best" option on paper isn't always the right one for a given team's actual capacity.

📌 Chapter 12 Visual Summary — from laptop chart to distributed, trusted artifact
  🌐 Public Repos           🏛️ Private Repos           📦 OCI
  ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐           ┌───────────────────┐
  │ Bitnami,      │        │ ChartMuseum,   │          │ same registry as    │
  │ Artifact Hub  │        │ Harbor          │          │ your container      │
  │ (discovery)   │        │                │          │ images — the future │
  └──────────────┘         └──────────────┘           └───────────────────┘

  🔏 Signing                🔐 Auth                     📌 Versioning
  ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐           ┌───────────────────┐
  │ GPG + .prov,  │        │ basic/token/   │          │ SemVer + canary +   │
  │ proves        │        │ TLS certs      │          │ --history-max for   │
  │ integrity     │        │                │          │ real rollback       │
  └──────────────┘         └──────────────┘           └───────────────────┘
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   THE ONE RULE: repo add is one-time, repo update is forever — every
   "chart not found" or "stale version" traces back to this distinction. 📦

In words: Distributing a chart means picking where it lives (public, private, or OCI), optionally proving its integrity (GPG signing), gating who can pull it (repository auth), and disciplined versioning so consumers know what changed and can always roll back. Every repository — HTTP or OCI — boils down to charts plus a way to list what's available; for HTTP that's index.yaml, for OCI it's the registry's own API.

OCI is where the ecosystem is heading — same infrastructure, same auth, one less service — but traditional HTTP repos and dedicated servers like ChartMuseum/Harbor remain fully valid choices, especially for teams with existing investment there.

The takeaway: a chart isn't truly "shipped" until it's discoverable, trustworthy, and correctly versioned somewhere other than your own laptop. Chapter 13 goes further into what "trustworthy" really means — securing Helm itself against misuse.
